title: Returning the Deposit: One Month, Itemized Statement, Penalties
bodyText:
Louisiana requires you to return a residential tenant's deposit within one month after the lease ends. You may keep only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default (such as unpaid rent) or unreasonable wear to the property, and if you keep anything you must send an itemized statement of what you kept and why.

Since August 1, 2026 the statute allows the statement within one month after the tenancy ends or within fifteen days after that one-month date, but the deposit itself is still due within one month, so the cautious course is to send the refund and the statement together within one month. The tenant must give you a forwarding address. The return rule does not apply if the tenant abandons the property without giving the notice required (by the lease or by law) or before the lease ends.

If you willfully fail to comply, the tenant can recover the amount wrongfully kept plus $300 or twice that amount, whichever is greater; failing to refund within 30 days after the tenant's written demand counts as willful, and the court may award attorney fees to the winner. A lease clause waiving these rights is void. If you sell the property during a lease, you must transfer the deposit to the buyer, who then owes its return.

title: Louisiana Eviction: Notice to Vacate and Court Timeline
bodyText:
To evict in Louisiana you must first deliver a written notice to vacate giving the tenant at least five days from delivery to leave, unless the lease contains the tenant's written waiver of that notice. Because the period is shorter than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays are not counted, so allow at least five business days after delivery (the Attorney General's landlord-tenant guide also says five business days); the same counting applies to the three-day wait before the hearing. If the property is abandoned or closed, or you do not know where the tenant is, you may attach the notice to a door of the property. For a month-to-month or other indeterminate lease, the written termination notice itself serves as the notice to vacate; for a fixed-term lease, the notice to vacate may be given no more than 30 days before the term ends.

If the tenant does not leave, you file a rule to show cause in court; the hearing can be set no earlier than the third day after service, and if you win the court renders a judgment of eviction, which stays effective for at least 90 days. If the tenant does not leave within 24 hours of the judgment, the court issues a warrant for the sheriff, constable or marshal to put you in possession. A tenant can suspend the eviction by appeal only by answering the rule under oath with an affirmative defense and filing the appeal and bond within 24 hours of the judgment.

After the required notice, you may retake possession without further court process only on a reasonable belief that the tenant has abandoned the property (for example, keys returned and belongings removed); in a parish under a federal disaster declaration, a tenant's absence is not evidence of abandonment for 30 days after the declaration, and violating these rules exposes you to $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater. A tenant's application for or receipt of rent subsidy is not payment of rent and is not a defense.

Federal law can require a longer 30-day notice for some properties (see the CARES Act row). If you know the tenant takes part in the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program for abuse victims, court papers such as the rule to show cause must be served on the Secretary of State, not at the home, and service delays run ten days longer (La. R.S. 44:57). City courts and justices of the peace may have their own filing practices (for example, attaching the lease and the notice to the filing), so check with the court where you file.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in Louisiana
bodyText: Louisiana has no just-cause or good-cause eviction law. A lease with a fixed term ends when the term expires, without any notice, unless it is extended or reconducted; a month-to-month lease ends on written notice given at least 10 calendar days before the end of a month (30 days before the end of the period for periods longer than a month). After that you still need a notice to vacate (unless waived in the lease) and a court eviction. Some limits apply regardless of the lease: in buildings of six or more units you may not end or refuse to renew a lease because of domestic abuse, stalking or cyberstalking against the tenant or a household member (with exceptions for repeated violent disturbances), parishes and cities may not make you evict for a tenant's calls for police or emergency help, and fair-housing law bars ending a tenancy for a discriminatory reason. Louisiana statutes contain no general retaliatory-eviction ban.

title: Bad Checks: Service Charge, Demand Letter and Double Damages
bodyText: If a tenant's rent check bounces for insufficient funds, Louisiana lets you charge a service charge of up to $25 or 5% of the check, whichever is greater, when you make written demand for payment, but only if you post a notice of the charge at your business premises in a place where people entering will see it. If the tenant does not pay within fifteen working days after receiving a written demand sent by certified or registered mail, you can sue for twice the amount owed (at least $100) plus attorney fees and court costs. The demand must be in substantially the form the statute prescribes, mailed to the address printed on the check. These rules cover checks only; a failed electronic payment has no statutory charge, so any charge for it must come from your lease.

title: Foreclosure: Disclose Before Signing, Notify Within Seven Days
bodyText: Before a residential lease is signed, and throughout it, you must tell the tenant and any prospective tenant in writing about any pending foreclosure against the property and about the tenant's right to be notified of a foreclosure. Give this disclosure before signing (for example with the application or the lease draft), not only in the signed lease. If you are served with a notice of seizure in a foreclosure, you must give every tenant a signed written notice within seven calendar days, naming the court, case name and docket number and containing the statute's exact statement that the notice is not a notice to vacate. A tenant who proves a violation recovers $200 plus any other damages and costs. The rule applies to all residential lessors, including Section 8 landlords, but not to a federally insured bank acting as assignee or mortgage holder.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors at Lease (One- and Two-Family Homes)
bodyText: When you lease a one- or two-family dwelling in Louisiana, it must contain at least an operable ten-year, sealed lithium battery smoke detector and an operable carbon monoxide detector with a long-life sealed battery (a combined unit is allowed). Check both before each new lease. Larger buildings fall under the state fire code and fire marshal rules. The statute does not say who maintains or replaces detectors during the tenancy; your lease can assign testing and battery checks to the tenant, but the duty to have them in place at the time of lease is yours. Failing to comply is not a reason for an insurer to refuse to pay a claim (La. R.S. 40:1581(D)).

title: Holdover: Reconduction After One Week, No Statutory Penalty
bodyText:
If a tenant stays after a fixed-term lease ends and you do nothing, Louisiana law renews the lease automatically: when the tenant remains in possession for one week after the end of a term longer than a week, without a notice to vacate or terminate or other opposition from you or the tenant, the lease is "reconducted" from month to month on all the same terms. To prevent that, give the tenant written notice to vacate (or other written opposition) at the end of the term or within that week; a notice to vacate for a fixed-term lease may be given up to 30 days before the term ends. Once reconducted, the lease ends only on written notice given at least 10 calendar days before the end of a month.

Louisiana sets no statutory holdover penalty such as double rent; you recover your actual damages, usually the rental value for the days the tenant stays, unless your lease sets an agreed daily holdover charge. Whether a sentence in the lease itself can stand as your advance opposition is not settled in the statutes, so give the notice.

title: Warranty Against Defects: What a Lease Can and Cannot Waive
bodyText:
Louisiana makes you warrant that the property is suitable for its purpose and free of defects that prevent that use, including defects that arise after move-in and are not the tenant's fault and defects you did not know about; in a residential lease the warranty protects everyone who lives there under the lease. A lease can waive this warranty only in clear and unambiguous language that is brought to the tenant's attention, and even then the waiver does not work for defects you knew or should have known about that the tenant did not, for defects that seriously affect health or safety in a residential lease, or to excuse your intentional or gross fault or liability for physical injury. A broad "as is" sentence buried in a lease is unlikely to work.

Separately, a statute lets an owner avoid liability for injuries caused by defects to the tenant or anyone on the property through the tenant if the tenant expressly assumes responsibility for the property's condition, unless the owner knew or should have known of the defect, or was notified of it and failed to fix it within a reasonable time. This library offers both as narrow optional clauses.

title: Late Fees: No Statutory Cap, but a Court Can Cut an Unreasonable One
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that caps residential late fees, sets a grace period, or requires a notice before a late fee. A late fee in your lease is treated as stipulated damages for late payment: you do not have to prove your actual loss, rent becomes late automatically on its fixed due date, and a court may reduce the fee only if it is so manifestly unreasonable as to be contrary to public policy. Set a modest, fixed fee and charge it once per late payment; a large or compounding daily fee invites a court to cut it. Charge a late fee only if your lease provides one.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month or Other Periodic Lease
bodyText:
If a lease has no fixed end date, Louisiana treats it as month to month (unless it is agricultural), and either party ends it by written notice given at least 10 calendar days before the end of a month; the lease then ends at the end of that month. For rental periods longer than a month the notice is 30 calendar days before the end of the period; for periods of a week to a month, 5 calendar days; for shorter periods, any time before the period ends. A notice that names no date ends the lease at the end of the first period for which it is timely. The tenant can also give notice simply by moving out and surrendering possession at the right time.

A fixed-term lease ends on its end date without notice, but if the tenant stays a week after a term longer than a week without a notice to vacate or terminate or other opposition from you or the tenant, it renews month to month. If your lease lets either party end it early, you must give the longer of the notice in your lease or these statutory periods, and the right to that notice cannot be waived in advance.

title: Lessor's Privilege on the Tenant's Belongings
bodyText: Louisiana gives you a privilege (a kind of lien) on the tenant's movable belongings in or on the leased property to secure rent and other lease obligations. It extends to a subtenant's belongings only up to what the subtenant owes the tenant, and it can reach a third person's belongings in the property unless you know they are not the tenant's. You enforce it only through the court, by a writ of sequestration, which you can get without posting security and even before rent is due if you have good reason to believe the tenant will remove the property; you may seize the belongings while they are in the property and for 15 days after removal if they are still the tenant's and can be identified. You may not seize them yourself. Many household items are exempt from seizure under any writ, including clothing, bedding, most furniture, kitchen and laundry appliances, family portraits, pets, and certain tools of the trade; and a court must order any sale.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant: What Louisiana Law Already Gives You
bodyText: If the tenant, or anyone on the property with the tenant's consent, damages the property, Louisiana law already makes the tenant liable for the damage and obliges the tenant to repair it, along with any deterioration beyond normal or agreed use. The tenant's rights to a rent reduction or to end the lease after the property is damaged or its use is impaired apply only when the damage happened without the tenant's fault, and the rule that a lease ends when the property is totally destroyed applies only when neither party is at fault. If the tenant misuses the property or uses it in a way that may damage it, you can seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages. Because the law covers these points, this library does not add a separate tenant-caused-damage clause for Louisiana; the optional casualty clause uses the same fault rule.

title: No Rent Payment Method Rule
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes and codes do not tell you which payment methods you must accept for rent. Nothing in Louisiana's statutes and codes requires you to take cash, requires a paper option such as a check or money order, or bars you from requiring an online portal or electronic payment. You set the accepted methods in the lease. If the lease says nothing, rent is payable at the address you give the tenant, and if you give none, at the tenant's address (La. Civ. Code art. 2703). Fees for paying by debit card are a separate question: see the note on Louisiana's 2026 debit-card surcharge ban.

title: Debit Card Surcharge Ban
bodyText:
Since August 1, 2026, Louisiana bars a business engaged in the sale of goods or services from adding a surcharge when a customer pays with a debit card instead of cash, check, credit card or a similar method (2026 La. Acts No. 751, enacted as R.S. 51:3081). The law does not mention rent or leases, and it is not settled whether renting a home counts as a sale of services. Until that is clear, the cautious course is not to charge a tenant extra for paying rent or other lease charges by debit card.

A tenant who is charged a surcharge must give you written notice first; if you refund it within thirty days, no lawsuit is allowed unless the violation was willful or repeated, and the attorney general may also enforce the law. This act governs debit cards only. No Louisiana statute addresses credit-card surcharges for rent.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that specifically addresses setting rents with algorithmic or revenue-management pricing software, or sharing rent and occupancy data with other landlords. That does not make coordinated pricing safe. Louisiana's antitrust law makes every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade illegal, with criminal penalties and triple damages plus attorney fees for anyone injured (La. R.S. 51:122, 51:137), and the Unfair Trade Practices Act bars unfair methods of competition (La. R.S. 51:1405). Whether using a shared pricing tool that pools competitors' nonpublic data is an unlawful combination depends on the facts and on court decisions, so get legal advice before relying on one; federal antitrust law also applies.

title: Application Fee Notice
bodyText: Before you accept an application fee from someone applying to rent a home they will use as their primary residence, give them a written notice that states: (1) the amount of the fee; (2) whether you consider credit scores, employment history, criminal history or eviction records in deciding whether to rent to them; and (3) that they may share, in good faith, a statement of 200 words or less explaining financial hardship from a state or federally declared disaster or emergency and how it affected their credit, employment or rental history. The hardship part of the notice must mention the COVID-19 pandemic and hurricanes. You may deliver the notice electronically if you meet Louisiana's electronic transactions law (La. R.S. 9:3258.1). This does not apply to an owner-occupied building of no more than four units, or to a home that will not be the applicant's primary residence. The statute gives applicants no right to sue over a violation, but it is still the law, so build the notice into your application process.

title: No Application Fee Cap or Refund Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not cap rental application or screening fees, does not require you to refund a fee if you don't rent to the applicant, does not require you to hold fees while earlier applicants are screened, and does not bar a fee for a minor household member. The one Louisiana rule is the written notice you must give before accepting an application fee for a primary residence, unless you live in a building of no more than four units (La. R.S. 9:3258.1; see the application fee notice note). Charge a fee you can justify and state it in that notice.

title: How Payments Are Applied
bodyText:
Louisiana has no landlord-tenant rule on the order in which you apply a tenant's payments; the Civil Code's general rules on applying payments to debts apply. The tenant has the right to say which debt a payment is for, at the time of payment or by circumstances you know (La. Civ. Code art. 1864), though not to a debt that is not yet due without your consent (art. 1865). If neither of you designates, the payment goes to the debt already due, and among due debts by the Code's order, ending with the debt that became due first (art. 1868). If you give a receipt that applies the payment to a particular debt and the tenant accepts it, the tenant generally cannot later ask you to apply it to another debt (art. 1867).

The library's application-of-payments clause applies payments to rent first and then to other charges, unless the tenant directs otherwise in writing for a particular payment. That fits Louisiana law: it sets the agreed order while keeping the tenant's right to direct a payment. Honor any direction a tenant gives with a payment, and show on your receipts how each payment was applied. This applies the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Collection Fee
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that lets you add a collection-agency fee to a tenant's unpaid rent or damages, and the library does not offer a collection-fee clause for Louisiana. The reason is the Civil Code's rule for money debts: when a payment is late, your damages for the delay are the interest on the amount owed, at the rate the lease sets or otherwise at the legal rate, and you can recover no more than that, whatever your actual loss. The one addition the Code allows is attorney fees, when a written contract expressly makes the tenant liable for them in a fixed or determinable amount (La. Civ. Code art. 2000). A collection-agency fee is neither, and whether a court would enforce one written as stipulated damages is unsettled. If you want to recover the cost of collecting, use a written attorney-fee term with a fixed or determinable amount and a late fee you can justify, and pursue interest on unpaid sums. If you hire a collection agency, it must register with the Louisiana secretary of state (La. R.S. 9:3534.1).

title: No Limit on Up-Front Payments
bodyText:
Louisiana does not limit what you may collect when the lease is signed or before the tenant moves in. There is no list of permitted up-front charges, no cap on the security deposit and no limit on how much rent may be paid in advance. Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is due at the start of the term, or at the start of each rent period if rent is paid by the month or another interval (La. Civ. Code art. 2703). List in the lease each amount due up front and when it is due.

One rule shapes how you label what you collect: any advance or deposit of money a tenant gives you to secure performance of the lease is a security deposit under Louisiana law, whatever you call it, and must be returned or accounted for within one month after the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)). If you collect last month's rent up front, say in the lease that it is rent for that named month.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that specifically bars you from charging a tenant a fee for a service you don't provide. General contract law still makes it a bad idea. An obligation needs a cause, the reason a party binds himself (La. Civ. Code arts. 1966-1967), and when you fail to perform what you promised the tenant may refuse to perform the matching obligation, ask a court to dissolve the agreement, or recover damages (La. Civ. Code arts. 1994, 2013, 2022). So if the lease charges a fee for a service such as trash pickup, pest control or an amenity, provide the service, or stop charging the fee while it is unavailable. Charging for something the tenant does not receive could also be challenged as an unfair practice under Louisiana's Unfair Trade Practices Act (La. R.S. 51:1405).

title: Fees and Rent
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that defines rent to include fees, and none that makes a fee rent because the lease calls it "additional rent". You and the tenant set the rent: it may be money or other performance, fixed at a sum that is certain or can be determined by a method you agree on (La. Civ. Code arts. 2675-2676). The label matters less in Louisiana than in many states, because you can end a lease and evict for the tenant's failure to perform any lease obligation, not just for unpaid rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2719; La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701), and your lessor's privilege on the tenant's belongings secures rent and other lease obligations alike (La. Civ. Code art. 2707). For a default other than unpaid rent, the library's default clause gives the tenant written notice and time to correct it first, and it says an unpaid late fee alone is not grounds to end the lease. The library does not offer an "additional rent" clause for Louisiana: it is not needed to enforce fees, and federal housing programs restrict it.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Louisiana has no statewide rental registration or licensing fee, and no statute that says whether you may pass a local government fee on to your tenant. Unless the lease says otherwise, you as lessor pay the taxes, assessments and other charges on the property, except those that arise from the tenant's own use (La. Civ. Code art. 2689). If a parish or city charges a rental registration, licensing or inspection fee, you may agree in the lease that the tenant reimburses all or part of it; the library offers an optional clause for that, which excludes property taxes, fines and emergency response fees. Louisiana bars parishes and cities from penalizing you because a tenant calls police or emergency help for a crime or domestic abuse at the property (La. R.S. 33:9701), so do not try to recover any such charge from the tenant. Parish or city ordinances set any local rental fees.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to offer the same rent or terms to month-to-month tenants as to tenants with a fixed-term lease, and it does not cap the difference, so you may price and write them differently. What changes with the lease type is how it ends. A fixed-term lease ends on its end date without notice, unless the tenant stays on for a week without either of you objecting, which turns it into a month-to-month lease on the same terms (La. Civ. Code arts. 2720-2724). A month-to-month lease, including one with no agreed term, ends by written notice given at least ten calendar days before the end of a month (La. Civ. Code arts. 2680, 2727-2729).

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute on rent concessions such as a free month, a move-in discount or a rent credit. If you give one, write it into the lease: which rental periods it covers, its amount and that the stated Monthly Rent applies after it ends; the library's rent-concession clause does that. You and the tenant set the rent, and the tenant owes it on the agreed terms (La. Civ. Code arts. 2676, 2683).

The library does not offer a clause that makes the tenant repay the whole concession if the tenant defaults. In Louisiana that is a stipulated-damages term, and a court may reduce it in proportion to the rent the tenant has already paid, or cut it if it is manifestly unreasonable (La. Civ. Code arts. 2005, 2011, 2012). If you want some protection, spread the concession over the term, for example a monthly credit, rather than giving it all up front.

Also say what happens to the concession if the tenant stays on after the term ends and the lease continues month to month (La. Civ. Code art. 2724).

title: No Rent Control
bodyText: Louisiana has no statewide rent control and no limit on how much or how often you may raise the rent; you and the tenant agree the rent in the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2676). No statute expressly bars cities or parishes from adopting rent control, but state law declares that a lessor's rights under the Civil Code may not be altered, abridged or diminished except by state law, subject to the reasonable exercise of the police power (La. R.S. 9:3258). Rent increases are limited in practice by the lease itself: during a fixed term you may not raise rent unless the lease provides for it, and for a month-to-month lease you change the rent by ending the current lease with proper notice and offering new terms (see the rent increase notes). Public housing authorities set rents for their own housing under their own rules. Louisiana's statutes do not set up or limit local rental registration or inspection programs, so check parish and city rules where your property is.

title: No Rent-Demand Bar
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that forbids you from asking for or collecting rent because the unit has code violations or defects, and no rule that suspends rent under a repair order. Unrepaired conditions still cut into what you can collect. You must keep the home suitable for living in and make necessary repairs other than those the tenant caused (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691), and you warrant it is free of defects that prevent its use (art. 2696). If you don't repair within a reasonable time after the tenant asks, the tenant may make the repair and deduct a reasonable cost from the rent (art. 2694). If the home is partly destroyed or its use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may get a reduced rent or end the lease (art. 2715), and an urgent repair you make can also entitle the tenant to a rent reduction (art. 2693). If the home becomes uninhabitable and the tenant is forced out, you must mitigate your damages (La. R.S. 9:3260).

title: Rent Increases During the Term
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute on rent-escalation clauses. During a fixed-term lease the rent is what the lease says: you may raise it only if the lease itself provides for the change, or if the tenant agrees to an amendment (La. Civ. Code arts. 1983, 2676, 2726). The library offers an optional clause that sets the increases in advance, either as a schedule of amounts and dates or as a formula tied to a published price index, with notice of each adjusted amount; a separate optional clause passes through increases in property taxes and insurance.

The library does not offer a clause letting you raise the rent mid-lease to whatever you consider market rent. Louisiana requires the rent to be a sum that is certain or determinable by a method the parties agreed on, and a rent that one side alone can reset is open to challenge. Louisiana has no residential retaliation statute, so no protection depends on having an escalation clause, though fair-housing law still bars increases that discriminate.

For a month-to-month lease you change the rent by giving the termination notice the Civil Code requires and offering new terms.

title: Raising the Rent
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that sets a notice period for raising rent. You change the rent through the lease's term rules. For a month-to-month lease, give the tenant written notice ending the lease at least ten calendar days before the end of a month, and offer a new lease at the new rent; the tenant must agree to it (La. Civ. Code arts. 2676, 2728-2729). For a fixed-term lease, the rent stays as written until the term ends unless the lease itself provides for increases. The lease ends on its end date, but if the tenant stays on for a week without either of you objecting, it continues month to month at the old rent and terms (La. Civ. Code arts. 2720-2724). So give written notice of the new rent or of non-renewal before the term ends; a notice to vacate may be given no more than 30 days before the end of the term (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701). Giving more notice than the minimum is good practice. During a declared state of emergency, Louisiana's price-gouging law bars charging more than ordinary prices for goods and services in the emergency area, for up to 30 days unless renewed (La. R.S. 29:732). It is not settled whether rent counts, so avoid emergency-period increases that aren't based on your costs.

title: When and Where Rent Is Paid
bodyText:
Unless your lease says otherwise, Louisiana law makes rent due at the start of the lease, or at the start of each rental period when rent is paid monthly or by another period, and payable at the address you give the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 2703). State the due date and payment address in the lease. The library's rent clause requires payment without deduction or setoff except as the law allows.

Two Louisiana rules let a tenant reduce what he pays. First, if you don't make a necessary repair within a reasonable time after the tenant asks, the tenant may make it and deduct the reasonable cost from the rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). Second, when you and the tenant owe each other fixed sums of money that are presently due, the debts can cancel each other out automatically to the extent of the smaller one (La. Civ. Code art. 1893). A clear no-setoff term in the lease is your agreement that the tenant pays the rent in full and claims what you owe separately, but it does not take away the repair-and-deduct right.

This applies the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Rent Receipt Duty
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give a tenant a receipt for rent, even rent paid in cash, and a missing receipt is not a defense to eviction under any statute. (The only receipt rule in Louisiana's statutes and codes applies to rent-to-own agreements for furniture and other personal property, not homes.) Give a dated written receipt for every cash payment anyway, showing the amount and what it was applied to. It is your best proof of payment, and under the Civil Code a tenant who accepts a receipt applying a payment to a particular debt generally cannot later ask you to apply it elsewhere (La. Civ. Code art. 1867).

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no law requiring you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, no state rent-reporting program, and no rule on whether you may report rent payments or require a tenant to enroll in a reporting service. If you report rent payments, or use a service that does, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act's accuracy and dispute rules apply; Louisiana's own credit reporting statute regulates the credit bureaus (La. R.S. 9:3571.1). If a reporting service charges the tenant a fee, state the fee and whether enrollment is optional in the lease.

title: Taxes on Rent
bodyText: Louisiana does not charge sales tax on ordinary residential rent. State and local sales tax applies to rooms and other accommodations furnished to transient guests, including houses and apartments rented as short stays, and the law expressly excludes anyone leasing apartments or single-family homes month to month (La. R.S. 47:301(4), 47:301(6), 47:301.3(1)). If you rent short stays, sales tax and any local hotel or short-term rental occupancy tax, such as New Orleans's, may apply, and booking platforms may collect them. Sales tax also applies to parking services, including the use of parking spaces (La. R.S. 47:301.3(3)); if you charge a separate parking fee, ask the Department of Revenue or a tax adviser whether it is taxable.

title: Put Every Fee in the Lease
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that requires your lease to list every fee with its purpose, or that sets a notice period for adding a fee later. In practice the lease is still the only safe place for your fees. A lease has the effect of law between you and the tenant, so the tenant owes the charges it provides for and not others (La. Civ. Code art. 1983). Adding a new fee during a fixed term is an amendment that needs the tenant's agreement (art. 2726), and an unclear fee term in a lease you wrote is read in the tenant's favor (art. 2056). For a month-to-month lease, you add a fee by giving the required termination notice and offering new terms. List each fee, its amount, what it is for and when it is due.

title: No Government Shutdown Protection
bodyText: Louisiana has no law that delays rent, bars late fees or limits eviction for federal or state employees during a government shutdown. Your ordinary lease terms and Louisiana's usual rules on rent and default apply. You may choose to agree a payment plan or waive a late fee for an affected tenant; put any such agreement in writing. Servicemembers have separate rights to end a lease (La. R.S. 9:3261).

title: Louisiana Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Louisiana sets few dollar limits for residential leases; most money rules come from the Civil Code. At a glance: Security deposit: no cap, but you must return it, less what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, within one month after the lease ends (this rule does not apply if the tenant abandons the home without the required notice or before the lease ends), and a willful failure costs you the amount wrongly kept plus $300 or twice that amount, whichever is greater (La. R.S. 9:3251-3252). Late fees: no cap, but a court can cut one that is manifestly unreasonable (La. Civ. Code art. 2012). Application fees: no cap, but give the written notice first when the home will be the applicant's primary residence, unless the home is in an owner-occupied building of no more than four units (La. R.S. 9:3258.1). Bounced checks: a service charge of up to $25 or 5% of the check, whichever is greater, with a posted notice and written demand; after a certified-mail demand and 15 working days, twice the amount owed (at least $100) plus attorney fees (La. R.S. 9:2782). Interest you agree in writing: no more than 12% a year (La. R.S. 9:3500). Attorney fees: by contract only if the written lease sets a fixed or determinable amount (La. Civ. Code art. 2000); for an oral lease, reasonable fees for collecting unpaid rent after a 20-day written demand (La. R.S. 9:3259); and a court may award fees to the winner in deposit suits (La. R.S. 9:3253) and in actions under the eviction article, which by its words covers eviction rules as well as abandonment, so assume an eviction suit can carry fees either way (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)(3)). Servicemembers who end a lease under the military statute owe at most one month's rent (less than six months into the lease) or half a month's rent (six months or more) (La. R.S. 9:3261). Failing to give the foreclosure notices costs $200 (La. R.S. 9:3260.1), and wrongly treating a home as abandoned can cost $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater; the penalty sits in the paragraph on federally declared disaster parishes, so assume it can apply anywhere (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731). There is no cap on rent or rent increases. This summary did not cover local ordinances, case law or federal housing program limits.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no special rule for reducing rent on a subsidized unit when part of it becomes unusable, and nothing says how a reduction is split between the tenant's share and the housing subsidy. The general Civil Code rule applies: if the home is partly destroyed or its use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may get a reduced rent or end the lease, depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2715), and an urgent repair can also justify a rent reduction (art. 2693). For a voucher or other subsidized tenancy, your housing assistance contract and the program's rules decide how the subsidy payment changes, so check them and the housing authority before adjusting either share.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on late fees when a housing subsidy pays part of the rent. The general late-fee rules apply: no cap, but a court can cut a fee that is manifestly unreasonable, and a tenant whose lateness has a valid excuse is not liable for stipulated damages such as a late fee (La. Civ. Code arts. 2008, 2012). Charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share, and not when the delay is the housing agency's; federal program rules and your housing assistance contract may forbid a late fee on the agency's share in any event. Louisiana law also says a pending or received rent subsidy is not payment of rent and is not a defense to eviction (La. R.S. 9:3259.2).

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on passing property-tax or insurance increases on to a residential tenant. Unless the lease says otherwise, you as lessor pay the taxes and other charges on the property, except those that arise from the tenant's own use (La. Civ. Code art. 2689). The library offers an optional clause that has the tenant pay a stated percentage of any increase in property taxes, and if you choose, property insurance premiums, over a base year. It requires you to show the bill and your calculation, and to refund the same share of any later reduction or refund. Use it only with a fixed percentage you can explain, such as the unit's share of the building. If a tenant does not pay an agreed share, it is a default you may deduct from the security deposit like any other default (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)).

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: In Louisiana, when a tenant pays money late, your damages for the delay are interest on the amount: at the rate the lease sets, or if the lease sets none, at the legal rate, which is the judicial interest rate published each year (La. Civ. Code art. 2000; La. R.S. 9:3500; La. R.S. 13:4202). A rate you agree with the tenant must be in writing and may not exceed 12% a year (La. R.S. 9:3500). Interest runs from when the tenant is in default: for rent, from the due date; for amounts with no set due date, such as repair charges, from your written demand (La. Civ. Code arts. 1989-1991). The library offers an optional clause charging interest on unpaid amounts other than rent, from your written demand, at a rate you choose up to 12%. Rent is left out because the late fee already compensates you for late rent, and charging both for the same delay invites a court challenge.

title: No Move-In Inspection Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require a move-in or move-out inspection, a written condition report or inventory, or a signed checklist. Do one anyway. At the end of the lease the tenant must return the home in the same condition as when it was delivered, except for normal wear and tear (La. Civ. Code art. 2683), and you may keep from the deposit only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, with an itemized statement (La. R.S. 9:3251). A dated, signed condition report with photos at move-in, compared with one at move-out, is your best evidence if the tenant disputes a deduction. Offer the tenant a joint walk-through at both ends and give a copy of each report.

title: No Inspection Notice Penalty
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell a tenant about move-in or move-out inspection rights, so there is no penalty for not doing so, and skipping an inspection does not by itself cost you the right to deduct from the deposit. The deposit penalties Louisiana does impose are for willfully failing to return the deposit or send the itemized statement within the deadline: the amount wrongly kept plus $300 or twice that amount, whichever is greater (La. R.S. 9:3252). Without a condition record you may have trouble proving a deduction was reasonably necessary.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If a former tenant never claims or cashes a deposit refund, you may not keep it. Louisiana's unclaimed property law lists security deposits and refunds as property a business holds for its owner (La. R.S. 9:153). No period names deposits. The general five-year period most likely applies, though the three-year period for money owed to a customer from a retail transaction could be argued; the cautious course is to report once three years have passed, because a holder that turns property over to the state in good faith is relieved of later liability (La. R.S. 9:154, 9:162). You then report it to the state treasurer by November 1 for the year ending July 1 and turn it over (La. R.S. 9:159-160). If you have an address and the amount is $50 or more, first send the former tenant written notice 60 to 120 days before you file. Late reports carry interest and daily penalties of up to $5,000, or up to $25,000 plus 25% if willful (La. R.S. 9:176). A lease clause that lets you keep an unclaimed refund, or that charges a fee for not claiming it, is not offered. Waivers of a tenant's deposit rights are void (La. R.S. 9:3254), and a dormancy charge is allowed only under strict conditions (La. R.S. 9:157). Keep a record of each refund you send and any that come back undelivered.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: No Louisiana statute lets a lease fix in advance what you will take from the security deposit for cleaning, carpets, painting or repairs. You may keep only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, and you must send an itemized statement of what you kept and why (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)); these two rules do not apply when the tenant abandons the home without giving the required notice or before the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251(C)). A lease term that waives the tenant's deposit rights is void (La. R.S. 9:3254), and the tenant is not responsible for normal wear and tear (La. Civ. Code art. 2683). So a flat move-out charge taken whether or not the work is needed is not offered for Louisiana. The Civil Code does let parties stipulate damages (La. Civ. Code arts. 2005-2012), but whether a stipulated charge can be kept from the deposit beyond what is reasonably necessary is a question for the courts. Instead, charge the actual, reasonable cost of the cleaning or repair the condition requires, and keep the invoices and photos. You may tell tenants in the lease what you typically charge for common items, as long as you deduct only what is actually needed.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: Louisiana gives tenants no right to pay the security deposit in installments, so you may require the full deposit at signing or before move-in. You may also agree to let a tenant pay it in installments; if you do, write the amounts and due dates into the lease and say what happens if an installment is missed. Every installment you receive is part of the security deposit and must be returned or accounted for within one month after the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251).

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on last month's rent paid in advance. You may collect it, since there is no cap on what you collect up front. How you describe it matters. Louisiana treats any advance or deposit a tenant gives you to secure performance of the lease as a security deposit, refundable within one month after the lease ends with an itemized statement of anything kept (La. R.S. 9:3251). If the lease says the money is rent for a named month, the last month, and you apply it only to that month, it is rent paid in advance. If you reserve the right to use it for damage or other charges, treat it as part of the security deposit. A tenant has no statutory right to skip the last month's rent and tell you to keep the deposit instead: the tenant owes rent on the agreed terms (La. Civ. Code art. 2683), and the deposit is not due back until after the lease ends. Say this in the lease, and say how prepaid last month's rent is credited if the lease ends early or continues month to month.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit
bodyText:
Louisiana's one-month deadline for returning the deposit and sending the itemized statement does not apply if the tenant abandons the home without giving the notice required, or before the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251(C)). The tenant must also give you a forwarding address at the end of the lease (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)). For a month-to-month lease, the law already requires written notice at least ten calendar days before the end of a month (La. Civ. Code arts. 2728-2729). For a fixed-term lease, no notice is needed to leave at the end of the term (art. 2720), so the library offers an optional clause requiring the tenant to give written move-out notice and a forwarding address; that makes the notice "required" for this rule.

This rule does not let you simply keep the deposit. Even when the tenant abandons the home, apply the deposit only to rent and damages the tenant actually owes, keep records, and return or account for any balance, because a court may treat the deposit as still subject to the deposit statute.

title: Deposit After a Victim Early Termination
bodyText: When a tenant ends a lease early under Louisiana's domestic abuse, stalking and cyberstalking statute or its sexual assault statute, the normal deposit rules apply, with no special timeline. You may keep the deposit only for reasons the deposit statute allows, meaning to remedy the tenant's default (such as rent owed through the early termination date) or unreasonable wear, and you must return the rest, with an itemized statement of anything kept, within one month after the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251; 9:3261.1(F); 9:3261.2(C)). The lease ends on the agreed termination date, which must fall within 30 days of the tenant's written request, so your one-month clock runs from that date. If there are other tenants on the lease, the whole lease ends then too. The domestic abuse statute applies only to buildings with six or more dwellings, and not to a building of ten or fewer units where the owner or lessor lives in one; the sexual assault statute has no unit threshold and cannot be waived. Federal rules for federally assisted housing may add requirements.

title: No Expedited Deposit Procedure
bodyText: Louisiana has no special procedure for returning a deposit early, and no fee for doing so. You may return the deposit as soon as you can assess the home; the law sets only the outer limit of one month after the lease ends for the refund, with the itemized statement of anything kept due within that month or, since August 1, 2026, within 15 days after it (La. R.S. 9:3251). Do not charge a fee to process or speed up a refund: you may keep only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, and a lease term waiving the tenant's deposit rights is void (La. R.S. 9:3254). After an eviction the same rules apply. If the tenant abandons the home without the required notice or before the lease ends, the one-month deadline does not apply (La. R.S. 9:3251(C)), but you should still account for the deposit.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on fees, surety bonds or insurance products a tenant pays instead of a security deposit, and no rule requiring you to offer one, to let a tenant switch back to a deposit, or to give notice before a claim under such a program is reported to a credit bureau. Be careful how such a program works. Any money you hold or keep to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit under Louisiana law, whatever you call it, and must be returned or accounted for within one month after the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251); the tenant cannot waive those rights (La. R.S. 9:3254). A premium for a third-party product the tenant chooses is different, but make it optional, describe it in writing, and don't describe it as a deposit.

title: No Furnished Rental Rules
bodyText: Louisiana has no special rules for furnished rentals: no list of required furnishings, no inventory requirement, and no separate rule or limit for a furniture deposit. Furniture you provide is part of what you lease, so the tenant must return it in the same condition, except for normal wear and tear, and is liable for damage caused by the tenant or the tenant's guests (La. Civ. Code arts. 2683, 2687). Any money you hold as security for the furniture is part of the security deposit and follows the one-month return and itemization rule (La. R.S. 9:3251). List the furniture and its condition in the lease or a signed inventory; the library offers an optional furnished-unit clause for that.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on holding deposits or other money taken to reserve a unit before the lease is signed. Treat such money as a contract and put the terms in writing: how much, how long you will hold the unit, what happens if you approve the applicant and they sign, if they back out, or if you decline them. A signed agreement on the unit and the rent can itself be an enforceable contract to lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2670), so say whether it is binding before a full lease is signed. If you want to keep the money when an approved applicant backs out, say so expressly; otherwise refund it. Once the lease is signed, apply the holding money to the first rent or the security deposit; any part you keep as security is a security deposit with the one-month return rule (La. R.S. 9:3251). An application fee is separate and, for a primary residence, needs the written notice described in the application-fee note unless you live in a building of no more than four units (La. R.S. 9:3258.1). If a real estate licensee takes the money, the Louisiana Real Estate Commission's escrow rules also apply.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: Louisiana has no such thing as a nonrefundable security deposit. Any advance or deposit a tenant gives you to secure performance of the lease, including a pet, cleaning, damage or move-in "deposit", must be returned within one month after the lease ends, less only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, with an itemized statement of anything you keep (La. R.S. 9:3251). Calling it nonrefundable in the lease does not change that, because a tenant's waiver of these rights is void (La. R.S. 9:3254). If you want to charge for a service, such as a one-time pet-processing or move-in cleaning service you actually perform, state it as a separate fee for that service, not as a deposit, and don't hold it as security against damage. Whether a court would treat a given fee as a disguised deposit is not settled.

title: No Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule requiring a separate notice that part of a deposit is nonrefundable, because no part of a security deposit can be made nonrefundable in Louisiana (La. R.S. 9:3251, 9:3254). See the note on nonrefundable deposits. If you charge a separate fee for a service you provide, describe it clearly in the lease as a fee, not a deposit.

title: No Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Louisiana does not cap security deposits. You may set the deposit at any amount, including separate pet or other deposits, and the law has no special limits by type of tenancy or for furnished units. All money you hold as security, however labeled, is one security deposit under Louisiana law: return it within one month after the lease ends, less only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, with an itemized statement of anything kept (La. R.S. 9:3251). During a fixed-term lease you may raise the deposit only if the tenant agrees. Federal housing programs and fair-housing rules (for example, no pet deposit for an assistance animal) may still limit what you charge.

title: Holding Security Deposits
bodyText: Louisiana does not tell you how to hold a tenant's security deposit. There is no requirement to use a separate, escrow or interest-bearing account, to tell the tenant where it is held, or to post a bond, and no rule on who keeps any interest. Keeping deposits in a separate account is still good practice, because you must be able to return the deposit within one month after the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251), and if you sell the property you must transfer the deposits to the buyer. If a licensed real estate broker or property manager holds the deposits for you, different rules apply: the Louisiana Real Estate Commission may require client money to be kept in a separate bank account, not mixed with the licensee's own funds, and a licensee can be disciplined for commingling or failing to account for it (La. R.S. 37:1435, 37:1455). An owner managing its own property is outside the license law.

title: No Deposit Interest Requirement
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit, and the deposit may be held in a non-interest-bearing account. If you return the deposit late, the tenant may recover interest on it as damages for the delay at the legal rate (La. Civ. Code art. 2000), and a willful failure to return it also triggers the statutory penalty of the amount wrongly kept plus $300 or twice that amount, whichever is greater (La. R.S. 9:3252). You may agree in the lease to pay interest if you choose.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease cannot make a tenant give up any right under Louisiana's security deposit law; any such waiver is void (La. R.S. 9:3254). That covers the right to have the deposit returned within one month after the lease ends, the limit on what you may keep (only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear), the itemized statement, the transfer of the deposit to a buyer, and the tenant's right to recover the amount wrongly kept plus $300 or twice that amount, whichever is greater, with possible attorney fees (La. R.S. 9:3251-3253). So lease terms making a deposit nonrefundable, presetting deductions regardless of actual damage, or forfeiting an unclaimed refund will not hold up. One limit is written into the statute, not waived by the lease: the one-month return rule does not apply when a tenant abandons the home without the required notice or before the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251(C)).

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: If you sell or otherwise transfer a rented property during a lease, you must transfer each tenant's security deposit to the buyer; once you do, you are relieved of liability for it, and the buyer becomes responsible for returning it at the end of the lease (La. R.S. 9:3251(B)). If you keep the deposit instead, expect to remain liable to the tenant. A tenant can recover the statutory penalty for willful failure from the original lessor or the lessor's successor (La. R.S. 9:3252). If you are buying a rented property, get the deposits (and a list of them) at closing. Under the Civil Code a buyer is not automatically bound by the seller's other lease obligations unless it assumes them, and an unrecorded lease does not bind third persons (La. Civ. Code arts. 2681.1, 2712), but the deposit statute makes the buyer responsible for the deposit. A sale does not end the lease (art. 2711). Tell tenants in writing who now holds their deposit and where to pay rent.

title: No Fee Transparency Law
bodyText: Louisiana has no rental fee-transparency or all-in pricing law. Nothing requires you to advertise a single total price that includes mandatory fees, to state rent in the lease as one all-in figure, or to list fees on the lease's first page. Two general rules still make clear fee disclosure the safe practice. A tenant owes only what the lease provides: a lease has the effect of law between you and the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 1983), so a fee the lease does not state is not owed under it. And a doubtful term in a lease you wrote is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). Louisiana's Unfair Trade Practices Act also bars deceptive practices in trade or commerce (La. R.S. 51:1405). So list every fee, its amount and when it is due in the lease. Separate Louisiana rules cover the application-fee notice for a primary residence, which owner-occupied buildings of no more than four units are exempt from (La. R.S. 9:3258.1), and automatic-renewal disclosures (see the automatic-renewal notes).

title: Accepting Late or Partial Rent
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on what happens when you accept late or partial rent. Under the Civil Code you may refuse a partial payment, with one exception: if the tenant disputes part of what you claim and offers to pay the part not in dispute, you may not refuse that part, and you keep your right to claim the rest (La. Civ. Code art. 1861). Because a late fee compensates you for delay, you may collect both the rent and the late fee (La. Civ. Code art. 2007). The library's late-fee clause says that accepting a late payment does not waive your other rights; no Louisiana statute conflicts with that. Courts may still find that you gave up the right to end the lease for a particular late payment if you accept rent while knowing of the default, so if you intend to end the lease or evict, say so in writing when you accept any money.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to post or give tenants the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits, and has no building-size trigger for such a rule. Louisiana's deposit statute also sets no cap on the amount; it governs return of the deposit, what you may keep, the itemized statement and penalties (La. R.S. 9:3251-3254). Two limits still apply when you set deposits. First, fair housing law bars different deposit terms because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, military status, or natural, protective, or cultural hairstyle (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(2), (6)(b)); the state act has exemptions (La. R.S. 51:2604(B), 2605), and federal fair housing law applies separately. Second, whatever you call it, money you hold to secure the lease is a deposit you must return under the deposit statute.

title: Utility Deposits Held by a Landlord
bodyText: Louisiana has no separate rule for a utility deposit that a landlord holds. If you collect money to secure the tenant's payment of utility charges owed to you under the lease, it is part of the security deposit, because the deposit statute covers any advance or deposit of money that secures the performance of any part of a lease: you must return it within one month after the lease ends, may keep only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default (such as unpaid utility charges) or unreasonable wear, and must itemize what you keep (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)); the deposit penalties apply (La. R.S. 9:3252). One caution: a separate statute says that any person engaged in furnishing gas, electricity or water who demands a cash security from patrons must pay 5% interest a year on it, and must return the balance with interest on demand when service is discontinued, or pay 10% a year on the amount kept after demand (La. R.S. 45:848). It plainly covers utility companies (except municipal and other publicly owned systems, La. R.S. 45:850). Whether it reaches a landlord who sells utilities to tenants by meter is a question for the courts; if you bill tenants for metered utilities and take a separate utility deposit, get advice first or fold the money into the security deposit. Deposits that utility companies themselves charge tenants are governed by the utility's regulator.

title: Tenant Improvements at Lease End
bodyText:
Louisiana has a default rule for attachments, additions and other improvements a tenant makes, and your lease may change it. Unless the lease says otherwise, when the lease ends: the tenant may remove any improvement it made, as long as it restores the property to its former condition; if the tenant leaves it, you may either keep it by paying the tenant the lesser of its cost or the increase in the property's value, or demand that the tenant remove it and restore the property within a reasonable time. If the tenant does not, you may remove it and restore the property at the tenant's expense, or keep it without paying, but to keep it you must send the tenant an additional notice by certified mail after the removal deadline passes. Until you take ownership, the improvement stays the tenant's property and the tenant alone is responsible for harm it causes (La. Civ. Code art. 2695).

Because this is only a default, a lease may say who owns improvements and whether anything is paid; the optional Tenant Improvements clause does that. A lease may also require your consent before any alteration; using the property in a way that may cause damage, or for another purpose, lets you seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2686). You yourself may not make alterations to the property during the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2690).

A tenant with a disability has a separate right to make reasonable modifications (see the Disability Modifications note). Louisiana has no statute giving tenants a right to install items such as solar collectors or vehicle chargers without your consent; the solar-collector statute protects property owners, not tenants (La. R.S. 9:1255).

title: Disability Modifications
bodyText:
Your lease may require your written consent before a tenant alters the property, but Louisiana's fair housing law makes it discrimination to refuse to let a person with a disability make reasonable modifications of the premises, at that person's expense, if the modifications may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises. In a rental, where it is reasonable to do so, you may condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(6)(c)(i)). Louisiana does not shift the cost of these modifications to owners of larger or publicly assisted buildings; the statute puts the cost on the person with the disability.

The state act does not reach a single-family house rented by a private owner of no more than three such houses without a broker or advertising that indicates a discriminatory preference, or rooms or units in a building of up to four units where the owner lives in one of them (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)); federal fair housing law applies separately.

title: No Bed Bug or Pest Statute
bodyText:
Louisiana's statutes and codes contain no rule on bed bugs or other pests in rental housing: nothing sets inspection or treatment deadlines, assigns treatment costs, or lists tenant preparation duties.

The Civil Code's general lease rules decide it. You must deliver the property in good condition and keep it suitable for its purpose, making necessary repairs except those the tenant is responsible for (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684, 2691), and you warrant it against vices or defects that prevent its use, including ones that arise after move-in without the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2696). The tenant must tell you without delay when the property needs repair, and owes you the damages caused by failing to (La. Civ. Code art. 2688). The tenant is liable for, and must repair, damage caused by the tenant's fault or that of people on the property with the tenant's consent (La. Civ. Code arts. 2687, 2692).

Louisiana has no statute giving you a right to enter for pest treatment, so the optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause supplies one by agreement. Some cities' code-enforcement statutes treat vermin-infested buildings as nuisances, and the state sanitary code is an agency rule.

title: No Professional Carpet Cleaning Rule
bodyText:
Louisiana's statutes and codes contain no rule on professional carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing lets you require it as a matter of law, and nothing forbids a lease term requiring it. The default rule is that the tenant must return the property in the same condition as when it was delivered, except for normal wear and tear (La. Civ. Code art. 2683). From the deposit you may keep only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, with an itemized statement (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)), and a lease term waiving those rights is void (La. R.S. 9:3254).

So you may not keep a flat carpet-cleaning charge regardless of condition or cost. You may make professional carpet cleaning a tenant obligation in the lease (the optional Professional Carpet Cleaning clause); if the tenant does not do it, the reasonable cost of having it done is a default you may remedy from the deposit. Use that clause only if the carpets were professionally cleaned before the tenancy began, so the tenant is returning them in the condition received.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacancy Notice Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the property empty in cold weather, or to keep the heat on or protect pipes from freezing while away. The general lease rules apply: the tenant must use the property as a prudent administrator (La. Civ. Code art. 2683), must tell you without delay when the property has been damaged or needs repair (La. Civ. Code art. 2688), and is liable for damage caused by the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2687). If you want advance notice of an absence, put it in the lease; the library's Notice of Extended Absence clause does this, and it applies the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Under Louisiana's Private Works Act, a tenant who hires a contractor for work on the property is treated as an owner of the property for that work. Contractors, workers, suppliers and others who are not paid get claims and a privilege (Louisiana's term for a lien) on the property (La. R.S. 9:4801, 9:4802).

The statute protects your interest in three ways.
- First, claims run only against the owner who contracted for the work, and against another owner only if that owner agreed in writing to the price and work and expressly agreed in writing to be liable for the claims (La. R.S. 9:4806(B)).
- Second, the privilege reaches only the interest of the owner who contracted, so for work your tenant ordered it reaches only the tenant's lease rights, and it ranks below all your rights as lessor, including your right to dissolve the lease for the tenant's nonperformance (La. R.S. 9:4806(C), (D)).
- Third, naming you in a recorded claim does not make you liable or create a privilege on your interest if you are not responsible under those rules (La. R.S. 9:4806(E)).

The practical risk is a writing you sign: do not sign the tenant's contract or anything agreeing to its price and work and to be liable for claims. Giving consent to an alteration under the lease is not, by itself, that kind of agreement, and the optional No Liens for Tenant Work clause says so expressly and makes the tenant clear any claim filed.

These rules apply the same way to fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Disturbances Between Tenants
bodyText:
The lease's No Disturbance clause states the tenant's duty not to disturb neighbors, on top of the tenant's Civil Code duty to use the property as a prudent administrator and for its agreed purpose (La. Civ. Code art. 2683).

Louisiana adds a duty on your side that matters when one of your tenants disturbs another. In a residential lease, your warranty of peaceful possession covers disturbance caused by a person who has access to the property with your consent, or who occupies adjacent property that belongs to you, such as another of your tenants (La. Civ. Code art. 2700). Once you are told of such a disturbance, you must take all steps necessary to protect the disturbed tenant's possession; if you do not, that tenant may sue the person causing it, without losing its rights against you (La. Civ. Code art. 2701). For disturbance by strangers who claim no right in the property, you owe no such protection (La. Civ. Code art. 2702).

Your tools against the tenant causing the disturbance are the lease and the Civil Code: if a tenant uses the property for another purpose or in a way that may damage it, you may seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2686), and you may seek dissolution for failure to perform lease obligations (La. Civ. Code art. 2719). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike; in a month-to-month lease you may also end the lease with the required notice.

title: Move-In Condition Acknowledgments
bodyText:
A lease clause in which the tenant acknowledges that the property is in good, satisfactory condition is useful evidence of its condition at move-in, which matters because the tenant must return the property in the same condition it was delivered, except for normal wear and tear (La. Civ. Code art. 2683), and you may keep from the deposit what is reasonably necessary to remedy unreasonable wear (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)).

In Louisiana it is not a waiver of your warranty. You must deliver the property in good condition suitable for its purpose (La. Civ. Code art. 2684), and you warrant it against vices or defects, including ones you did not know about and ones that arise later without the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code arts. 2696, 2697). A waiver of that warranty works only if it uses clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention, and never for defects you knew or should have known of and the tenant did not, or, in a residential lease, for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); see the library's warranty waiver notes. If the tenant knows of a defect and fails to tell you, the tenant's recovery may be reduced (La. Civ. Code art. 2697).

Louisiana has no statute requiring a move-in inspection, condition checklist or inventory; a written, signed list of existing damage, with photos, is still the best evidence.

title: Tenant Absences and Abandonment
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, and no statute letting a lease require it on particular terms. A lease may still require it as an ordinary contract term, which the library's Notice of Extended Absence clause does (notice no later than the first day of any absence of more than 7 days); a tenant who fails to perform a lease obligation owes the damages caused by the failure (La. Civ. Code art. 1994).

The notice matters most for abandonment. After the required notice has been given, you may take possession without going to court if you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned the property; signs of abandonment include ceasing to live there, returning the keys and removing furnishings and belongings (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(B)). In a parish under a federal disaster declaration, a tenant's ceasing to live there is not evidence of abandonment for 30 days after the initial declaration, and a residential tenant may recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, if you do not follow these rules (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)). An absence notice from the tenant is strong evidence that an empty unit has not been abandoned, so do not treat a noticed absence as abandonment.

The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in your rental, and sets no lease conditions (such as insurance or liability terms) for one. Louisiana's child care law regulates the provider, not the landlord: a family child care provider (one caregiver caring for six or fewer children in a private residence) must register with the state only if the provider receives state or federal funds for the care, and registered providers are inspected by the state fire marshal (La. R.S. 17:407.62, 407.63, 407.64); nothing in it requires your consent or bars you from refusing. The lease decides. A tenant must use the property for the purpose for which it was leased, and using it for another purpose lets you seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code arts. 2683, 2686). If you are willing to allow child care, say so in writing and set your own conditions, such as proof of registration where required and liability insurance naming you; the library offers no standard clause for this. Fair housing law protects familial status, so the issue is the business use, not the presence of children (La. R.S. 51:2606).

title: No Home Business Right
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute making a home-based business a permitted use of a rental home, so the lease decides whether a tenant may work from home or run a business there. The tenant must use the property for the purpose for which it was leased, and if the tenant uses it for another purpose you may seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code arts. 2683, 2686).

If you allow some business use, keep it secondary: when property is leased for more than one purpose, the dominant or more substantial purpose decides what kind of lease it is (La. Civ. Code art. 2671), and rules written for residential leases, such as the limits on waiving the warranty against defects that seriously affect health or safety, apply to residential leases (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). Local zoning may also limit home businesses.

The library's Residential Use Only clause bars commercial use; if you want to allow quiet home offices or remote work, say so in the lease.

title: Yard and Upkeep Duties in the Lease
bodyText:
Louisiana does not require tenant chores such as lawn mowing, leaf raking or watering, or tenant repair duties, to be in a separate signed writing or supported by separate consideration, and has no rule that turns on whether the property is a single-family home. You may put them in the lease. The Civil Code leaves room for this: you must make the repairs needed to keep the property suitable for its purpose, except those for which the tenant is responsible (La. Civ. Code art. 2691), and the tenant must use the property as a prudent administrator (La. Civ. Code art. 2683).

Two limits apply. Shifting duties to the tenant does not, by itself, waive your warranty against vices or defects; a waiver needs clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention and cannot reach, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699; see the library's warranty waiver notes). And if you want the special protection from injury claims that applies when a tenant assumes responsibility for the property's condition (La. R.S. 9:3221), use the library's separate optional assumption clause.

The library's Landscaping and Irrigation clause works in Louisiana as an ordinary lease term, for fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Utility Charges and Liens on Your Property
bodyText: Louisiana has no general statute making a tenant's unpaid water, sewer or other utility bill a lien on your property, and no affidavit or lease-filing procedure to avoid one. Two statutes do create privileges (Louisiana's term for a lien) for local service charges. First, a parish or municipality may adopt an ordinance letting it record a notice of nonpayment of a garbage and trash service charge; the notice is a privilege on the property of the person who failed to pay, ranks ahead of mortgages and all other privileges except tax privileges, and can be filed only after a certified-mail warning and 30 more days of nonpayment (La. R.S. 33:4169.1(C)). If the garbage account is in the tenant's name, the statute reaches the tenant's property; if the charge is billed to you as owner, it can reach yours. Second, a municipality (since 2025) and, from August 1, 2026, a parish, sewerage district or waterworks district has a privilege on multifamily residential property (more than four dwelling units occupied by people other than the owner) that uses a master meter for water or sewer, for the owner's unpaid charges, after a written demand and 30 days (La. R.S. 33:4887). The same garbage statute also lets a local government contract with a water company to shut off water to premises delinquent on garbage charges, after a certified-mail notice and 30 days (La. R.S. 33:4169.1(B)). To protect yourself, have the tenant open utility and garbage accounts in the tenant's own name where the provider allows it, and check your local ordinances. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Occupancy Limits Are Local
bodyText:
Louisiana's statutes set no statewide limit on the number of people per bedroom or per square foot in a private rental, and give neighbors no special right to enforce one. Occupancy standards, where they exist, come from local housing and building codes; public housing authorities set their own occupancy standards for their units.

Louisiana's fair housing law does not limit reasonable local, state or federal restrictions on the maximum number of occupants (La. R.S. 51:2605(C)), but it does bar refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of familial status, which includes children under 18 living with a parent or custodian and a person who is pregnant (La. R.S. 51:2603(8), 51:2606(A)(1)-(2)), so an occupancy limit stricter than the local code that keeps out families with children carries fair housing risk; federal law applies separately. The library's Permitted Occupants clause lists who may live at the property.

title: No Statutory List of Prohibited Tenant Acts
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute listing acts a residential tenant must not commit, such as damaging the property, disturbing neighbors or refusing entry. The Civil Code's general lease duties do the work, whether or not the lease repeats them: the tenant must use the property as a prudent administrator and for its agreed purpose and return it in the condition received, except normal wear and tear (La. Civ. Code art. 2683); is liable for, and must repair, damage caused by the tenant's fault or that of people on the property with the tenant's consent (La. Civ. Code arts. 2687, 2692); and must tell you without delay of damage, needed repairs or disturbance by third persons (La. Civ. Code art. 2688). If the tenant uses the property for another purpose or in a way that may damage it, you may seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2686).
