Specific conduct, such as noise, alterations and access, is covered by the library's lease clauses. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Illegal Use: Lease Remedies and Nuisance Abatement
bodyText: No Louisiana statute automatically voids or annuls a lease when the tenant uses the property for an illegal purpose; you must act under the lease and the Civil Code. If a tenant uses the property for a purpose other than the one it was leased for, you may seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2686), and you may seek dissolution for failure to perform lease obligations (La. Civ. Code art. 2719); see also the library's criminal activity clause. Acting matters because Louisiana's public nuisance law can reach you as owner. Crimes of violence, illegal weapons offenses, felony theft, drug dealing, prostitution and obscenity on the premises are prohibited activities. Public officials, or any seven residents of the election precinct, may sue to enjoin anyone who conducts or knowingly permits them on the premises, including owners and tenants (La. R.S. 13:4711, 13:4712). A written notice of violation from the attorney general, district attorney, sheriff or city or parish attorney creates a presumption that you knowingly permitted the nuisance (La. R.S. 13:4713(A)(1)). The court may award abatement expenses and attorney fees, a civil penalty of up to $10,000 and damages (La. R.S. 13:4713(C)(2)), and if you knew of the nuisance it may order the premises closed for five years unless released on bond (La. R.S. 13:4715, 13:4716). Renting a place to someone you know or have good reason to believe intends to use it for prostitution is itself a crime (La. R.S. 14:282(A)). If you receive a notice of violation, act on the lease promptly.

title: Enforcing a Residential-Use Clause
bodyText:
Louisiana gives you a specific Civil Code remedy when a tenant uses the property for a purpose other than the one it was leased for, or in a way that may damage it: you may ask a court for an injunction, dissolution of the lease and any damages you suffered (La. Civ. Code art. 2686). The tenant's basic duty is to use the property as a prudent administrator and for its agreed purpose (La. Civ. Code art. 2683), and the library's Residential Use Only clause states that purpose. Dissolution follows the contract rules for failure to perform (La. Civ. Code art. 2719); to recover possession you still need a court eviction (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701 and following).

For a month-to-month lease you may instead end it with the required written notice (La. Civ. Code arts. 2727-2729). Keep any business use you allow secondary, because a lease's dominant purpose decides whether it is regulated as residential (La. Civ. Code art. 2671).

title: Smoking Rules in Louisiana Rentals
bodyText:
Louisiana leaves smoking inside rental homes to the lease. The Louisiana Smokefree Air Act bans smoking in public buildings, schools, enclosed public places and enclosed areas of places of employment, but expressly does not prohibit smoking in private homes and private residences, unless the home is used for child care or day care (La. R.S. 40:1291.11(A), (B)(1)).

Two points matter for landlords.
- First, a private residence is not a place of employment unless used as a licensed child care, adult day care or healthcare facility, but your leasing office and other enclosed areas your employees normally use are, and as an employer you may not knowingly permit smoking there (La. R.S. 40:1291.3(7), 40:1291.11(A)(3), (5)).
- Second, the act defines smoking as lighted tobacco or any other lighted combustible plant material, so it does not address vaping (La. R.S. 40:1291.3(14)); your lease can.

Louisiana has no statute making smoke drift between units a nuisance, requiring a smoking-policy disclosure in the lease, or protecting a tenant's medical marijuana use in rental housing, so the library's Smoking Policy clause, which bans smoking and vaping of any kind on the property, is lawful. Parishes and cities may adopt stricter smoke-free rules (La. R.S. 40:1291.11(D)).

The policy works the same in fixed-term and month-to-month leases; adding a ban to an existing lease needs the tenant's agreement or, for a month-to-month lease, a new lease after proper termination notice.

title: Subleasing and Assignment
bodyText:
In Louisiana a tenant has the right to sublease and to assign or encumber its rights in the lease unless the lease expressly prohibits it (La. Civ. Code art. 2713). So if you want control, the lease must say so; the library's No Subletting or Assignment clause does, by requiring your prior written consent in your sole discretion.

Three Louisiana rules shape how that clause is read.
- First, a lease provision that prohibits any one of assigning, encumbering or subleasing is deemed to prohibit the others, unless a contrary intent is expressed.
- Second, in every other respect a provision that prohibits a tenant from assigning, encumbering or subleasing is strictly construed against you (La. Civ. Code art. 2713), so write any restriction plainly.
- Third, a subtenant or assignee gets no greater right to use the property than the tenant had (La. Civ. Code art. 2713.1).

Louisiana has no statute requiring you to consent, limiting your reasons for refusing, or treating your silence as approval. If you do consent to an assignment, the original tenant is not released unless you agree to release it: under the general rules on assumption of obligations, an assumption must be in writing to be enforced against the new party, and your consent does not release the original obligor, who stays solidarily bound (La. Civ. Code arts. 1821, 1823).

These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Claims and Lawsuits Against the Property
bodyText:
Louisiana already requires a tenant to notify you without delay when the tenant's possession has been disturbed by a third person, as well as when the property is damaged or needs repair, and you may recover the damages caused by the tenant's failure to do so (La. Civ. Code art. 2688). If a third person sues the tenant claiming a right in the property or contesting the tenant's right to possess it, the tenant may bring you into the suit as a party and be dismissed from it on request (La. Civ. Code art. 2701). Your own duty is to take all steps necessary to protect the tenant's possession against such a claim as soon as you are informed of it (La. Civ. Code arts. 2700, 2701).

Louisiana has no statute on a tenant attorning to (recognizing as landlord, or paying rent to) a stranger who claims the property, and none declaring such an attornment void. The library's Notice of Proceedings clause, which requires the tenant to tell you of any proceeding to recover the property and hand over written notices, restates and sharpens the Civil Code duty. If your property is under foreclosure, you have separate disclosure duties to the tenant (see the foreclosure disclosure notes).

These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Tenant's Insurance and Your Duties
bodyText: No Louisiana statute says whether you may require a tenant to carry renters insurance, to make a claim on the tenant's own policy, or to name you on it, and none governs how a tenant's insurance claim affects the lease. A lease may require renters insurance as an ordinary contract term. Three Civil Code rules limit how far insurance terms can go. First, your repair duty stays with you: you must make the necessary repairs except those the tenant is responsible for, such as damage caused by the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code arts. 2691, 2692), so a lease cannot make the tenant's insurer the first source for repairs that are yours. Second, any clause that excludes or limits in advance your liability for intentional or gross fault, or for causing physical injury, is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). Third, a waiver of your warranty against vices or defects needs clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention and does not reach defects you knew or should have known of, or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). What you can do is have the tenant carry liability and contents coverage and look to the tenant, and the tenant's policy, for damage the tenant causes (La. Civ. Code art. 2687).

title: Wells and Septic Systems
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes do not assign maintenance of a private water well or an individual sewage (septic) system between landlord and tenant. The general lease rules decide it: you must make the repairs needed to keep the property suitable for its purpose, except those the tenant is responsible for (La. Civ. Code art. 2691), and the tenant must repair damage caused by the tenant's fault or by people on the property with the tenant's consent, and deterioration beyond normal or agreed use, such as a septic failure caused by flushing items the tenant was told not to (La. Civ. Code art. 2692). The tenant must tell you without delay when the system needs repair (La. Civ. Code art. 2688). You may assign routine tasks, such as not overloading the system, to the tenant in the lease; shifting the system's repair to the tenant does not waive your warranty against defects that seriously affect health or safety in a residential lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). Permits, design and water-quality rules for wells and septic systems come from state health and water rules and local ordinances.

title: Shifting Repairs to the Tenant
bodyText:
Louisiana lets the lease decide who makes which repairs, with no separate-writing, consideration or good-faith formality and no rule that depends on the type of dwelling. Your Civil Code duty is to make all repairs that become necessary to keep the property suitable for its purpose, except those for which the tenant is responsible (La. Civ. Code art. 2691). The tenant is responsible by law for damage caused by its fault and deterioration beyond normal or agreed use (La. Civ. Code art. 2692), and the lease may add specified repairs; the library's optional Tenant-Performed Repairs clause does this.

Limits: shifting repairs does not by itself waive your warranty against vices or defects, which can be waived only by clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention and never for defects you knew or should have known of and the tenant did not, or, in a residential lease, for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); and a clause excluding liability for intentional or gross fault or for physical injury is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). A separate statute protects you from injury claims only if the lease says the tenant assumes responsibility for the property's condition, and even then not for defects you knew or should have known of or failed to fix within a reasonable time after notice (La. R.S. 9:3221; see the library's optional assumption clause).

For the repairs that stay yours: if you fail to make a necessary repair within a reasonable time after the tenant's demand, the tenant may make it and get reimbursed or deduct the reasonable cost from rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2694); and you may make a repair that cannot wait until the lease ends even if it inconveniences the tenant, who may then get a rent reduction or dissolution depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2693). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Tenant Duties Under Louisiana Law
Utility Money You Collect from Tenants
bodyText:
If your lease has the tenant pay you for water, electricity, gas, heat or sewer service, Louisiana makes it a crime to knowingly fail to apply that money to the utility bill within 60 days after you receive the bill, or to use deception or false promises in failing to apply it (La. R.S. 14:71.5, enacted 2025). Penalties rise with the amount, from up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine for under $1,000 to up to twenty years and a $50,000 fine for $25,000 or more, plus full restitution. It does not apply if you cannot pay because the tenant did not pay you enough on time, or because of the utility company's own billing error or delay.

If instead the tenant pays the provider directly, which the library's Utilities Paid by Tenant clause provides for, this statute does not come into play. Louisiana's statutes do not address a utility refusing service to a new tenant because of a former occupant's unpaid bill, or make a tenant's unpaid utility bill a ground for eviction; utility service rules are set by the Public Service Commission and local utilities.

Liens for unpaid local charges are covered in the library's utility lien note.

title: Submetered Utilities and Shutoffs
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes set no special rules for electricity, gas or water that you submeter or bill to tenants, and no statute lets you interrupt a tenant's utility service for nonpayment. Do not cut off service as a collection or eviction tool, and never for a tenant on active military duty, whom Louisiana protects from utility shutoffs for nonpayment (La. R.S. 29:317-319; see "Utility Shutoff Rules"). You are bound to maintain the property in a condition suitable for its purpose and to protect the tenant's peaceful possession for the whole lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), and the lawful way to remove a tenant is the court eviction process. Three statutes touch submetering. First, if you collect money from tenants under the lease for utility service, you commit a crime if you knowingly fail to pay the utility bill within 60 days after receiving it (La. R.S. 14:71.5). Second, a gas distribution system in an apartment complex, housing project or mobile home park, where the operator buys metered gas and resells it through its own pipes, whether by meter or through the rent, is a master meter system and part of the regulated natural gas distribution systems under the state's gas pipeline law (La. R.S. 30:503(8), (9)). Third, anyone engaged in furnishing gas, electricity or water who demands a cash security deposit must pay 5% interest on it (La. R.S. 45:848); whether that reaches a submetering landlord is unsettled (see the utility deposit note).

title: No Alternate Housing Duty
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to house a tenant elsewhere or pay relocation costs during repairs, after a casualty, or when a unit becomes unfit, whether or not the tenant asks. The Civil Code instead adjusts the rent or ends the lease. If you make a repair that cannot wait until the lease ends, the tenant may get a rent reduction or abatement, or dissolution of the lease, depending on the circumstances, including each side's fault, how long the repair takes and how much use is lost (La. Civ. Code art. 2693). If the property is partly destroyed or its use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may get a rent reduction or dissolution, plus damages if you were at fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2715); total destruction without either party's fault ends the lease with no damages owed (La. Civ. Code art. 2714). If the tenant is constructively evicted and the property is uninhabitable through no fault of the tenant, you must mitigate your damages (La. R.S. 9:3260). Damages for your own breach of the lease may include the tenant's reasonable costs, but no statute fixes them as relocation costs. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Included and Excluded Appliances
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute listing appliances you must supply, presuming that appliances in a unit are yours to maintain, or barring a lease from excluding them. What you lease is what you and the tenant agree on (La. Civ. Code art. 2668). Appliances you include become part of the leased property, so you must deliver them in good condition, keep them suitable for their purpose and repair them, except for damage the tenant causes (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684, 2691, 2692), and your warranty against vices or defects covers them (La. Civ. Code art. 2696); list them in the lease, as the library's Appliances and Equipment clause does.

An item left in the unit that you do not want to maintain should be excluded in writing. Because a tenant may argue that anything left in the unit was leased with it, treat an exclusion that relieves you of the warranty like a waiver: it works only if it is in clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention, never for defects you knew or should have known of and the tenant did not, and, in a residential lease, never for defects that seriously affect health or safety, such as a gas appliance that leaks (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). A clause excluding liability for causing physical injury, or for intentional or gross fault, is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). The library's optional Items Not Included clause follows these limits; simpler still, remove items you will not maintain.

These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Common-Area Lighting Statute
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes do not set lighting requirements for common halls, stairways or entrances in rental buildings, and do not say whether a tenant may be made to pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's own electric meter. The general lease rules apply. You must keep the property suitable for its purpose and protect the tenant's peaceful possession (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), and you warrant it against vices or defects, a warranty that in a residential lease protects everyone living there under the lease and cannot be waived for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code arts. 2696, 2698, 2699); a dark stairway can be such a defect. If common-area lights run through a tenant's meter, say so plainly in the lease and adjust the rent or reimburse the tenant, because the tenant otherwise pays only for its own use under the utility clause. Building, fire and housing codes adopted by the state fire marshal, the state construction code and local governments may set lighting rules.

title: Rent After Condemnation
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that expressly bars you from collecting rent after a unit is condemned, placarded or ordered vacated. Expect to collect little anyway, because the Civil Code ties rent to the tenant's use. If, without the tenant's fault, the property's use is substantially impaired, the tenant may obtain a reduction of the rent or dissolution of the lease, whichever fits the circumstances, and damages too if you were at fault; if the impairment comes from circumstances outside the property, the tenant may dissolve the lease but not reduce the rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2715). If the property is lost, totally destroyed or expropriated without either party's fault, the lease ends and neither side owes damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2714). Your warranty that the property is fit for its purpose and free of defects that prevent its use continues through the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2696), so a condemnation caused by defects you should have repaired exposes you to the tenant's claims. If the tenant is constructively evicted and the property is uninhabitable through no fault of the tenant, you must mitigate your damages (La. R.S. 9:3260). Municipal and parish condemnation and demolition procedures are in separate statutes and local ordinances. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Habitability Rules Louisiana Lacks
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Louisiana counterpart. (1) No right for a tenant to withhold rent or pay it into escrow or the court registry because of needed repairs. The tenant's remedies are in the Civil Code: make a necessary repair you fail to make within a reasonable time after demand and deduct the reasonable cost from rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2694), seek a rent reduction or dissolution when use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2715), seek dissolution for your failure to perform (La. Civ. Code art. 2719), or claim damages under your warranty against vices or defects (La. Civ. Code art. 2696). (2) No fixed repair deadline: the test is a reasonable time after the tenant's demand (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). (3) No statewide minimum indoor temperature and no air-conditioning or cooling duty for rentals; whether heat or cooling equipment you provide must work is governed by your general duties to keep the property suitable for its purpose and free of defects (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691, 2696). (4) No duty to provide substitute housing, and (5) no express bar on collecting rent after condemnation (see the library's notes on each). Local housing codes and state agency rules may add duties, so check them.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that lets, or forbids, a lease naming who must make repairs. You may require repair requests to come to you and use your own contractors for the repairs you make. The question matters for the tenant's Civil Code repair remedy: if you fail to make a necessary repair within a reasonable time after the tenant's demand, the tenant may have it made and get reimbursed or deduct the cost from rent, but only to the extent the repair was necessary and the amount reasonable (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). That article does not say who must do the work. The library does not offer a clause that requires the tenant to use your designated repairer for a repair you failed to make, because a term narrowing the tenant's remedy would be read against you in case of doubt (La. Civ. Code art. 2056), and whether a lease may limit the article 2694 remedy is a question for the courts. Your practical protection is to respond promptly to repair demands, since the remedy opens only after a reasonable time passes. State licensing laws may require licensed trades for some work. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Disability Accommodations and Service Animals
bodyText:
Louisiana's fair housing law makes it discrimination to refuse reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(6)(c)(ii)), for example an exception to a no-pets rule for an assistance animal, or a reserved parking space. Reasonable modifications of the premises are covered in the Disability Modifications note; Louisiana lets you condition a modification only on restoring the interior, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and has no rule requiring an interest-bearing account for a restoration deposit or requiring the lease to state the restoration condition. The state act does not reach a single-family house rented by a private owner of no more than three such houses without a broker, or a building of up to four units where the owner lives in one (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)); federal law applies separately.

Service dogs: a person with a disability who has a trained service dog is entitled to full and equal access to housing offered for rent, may not be charged extra for the dog, but is liable for any damage the dog does to the premises or any person on them (La. R.S. 46:1954(C)); that rule does not cover a single-family home whose occupants rent out no more than one room (La. R.S. 46:1952(1)).

Support animals: since 2024, a healthcare provider may issue documentation of a need for a support animal only after a 30-day therapeutic relationship, two sessions and a clinical evaluation, and the documentation must show its date and the provider's license number and type (La. R.S. 46:1974(A)); misrepresenting a disability-related need for a support animal, or misrepresenting an animal as a service dog to the owner of a residential dwelling, carries fines of up to $500 for a first offense (La. R.S. 46:1974(C), 46:1975, 46:1977).

That act does not restrict fair housing accommodation rights (La. R.S. 46:1978), so evaluate each request under fair housing law.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and no special rent-abatement remedy for it. The Civil Code decides it. You are bound to deliver the property at the agreed time and in good condition (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684), and a binding agreement to lease can exist before the lease starts, once the property and the rent are agreed, unless the parties understood it would not bind them until written or until other terms were agreed (La. Civ. Code art. 2670). If you cannot deliver because you rented the property to someone else, the tenant left out may seek dissolution of the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2719) and the damages your failure caused (La. Civ. Code art. 1994), and an obligor in bad faith owes all direct damages, foreseeable or not (La. Civ. Code art. 1997). Between the two tenants, a lease of an immovable has effect against third persons only from the time it is filed for registry (La. Civ. Code art. 2681.1), so a recorded lease can matter; residential leases are rarely recorded. Do not sign a new lease until the prior tenant's right to occupy has ended. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Employee Background-Check Mandate
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to run background checks on property managers, maintenance workers or other employees who have keys to or enter tenants' units. Screening is still sensible. In a residential lease your warranty of peaceful possession covers disturbance by anyone who has access to the property with your consent (La. Civ. Code art. 2700), and once told of such a disturbance you must take all steps necessary to protect the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 2701); a clause excluding liability for intentional or gross fault, or for physical injury, is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). If you do screen, Louisiana employment law, federal consumer-reporting law and fair housing law govern how.

title: Which Defects Count
bodyText: Louisiana measures defects by their effect on the use of the property, at several levels. Your warranty covers vices or defects that prevent the property's use for the purpose for which it was leased, including ones you did not know about and ones that arise after move-in without the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code arts. 2696, 2697). Your repair duty covers all repairs that become necessary to keep the property suitable for that purpose (La. Civ. Code art. 2691), and the tenant's repair-and-deduct remedy reaches only necessary repairs at a reasonable cost (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). A rent reduction or dissolution without your fault requires that the property's use be substantially impaired (La. Civ. Code art. 2715). The most serious tier is a vice or defect that seriously affects health or safety: in a residential lease no waiver can reach it (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). Cosmetic problems that do not prevent or impair the use of the property generally fall outside these remedies, but the Civil Code's lease articles do not list which conditions qualify; that is decided case by case. If a tenant knew of a defect and did not tell you, the tenant's recovery may be reduced (La. Civ. Code art. 2697).

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: No Louisiana statute presumes that you breached your repair or warranty duties because of a code violation or a missing facility, or that you had notice or took too long to repair. A tenant who claims a breach must prove it under the ordinary rules. The Civil Code does shape the proof in two ways. Your warranty covers vices or defects even if you did not know of them (La. Civ. Code art. 2697), so lack of knowledge is not a defense to the warranty itself, though it matters for whether a waiver works and for how much a tenant who knew and stayed silent can recover (La. Civ. Code arts. 2697, 2699). And the tenant's right to make a repair and deduct the cost arises only after a demand and a reasonable time (La. Civ. Code art. 2694), which the tenant must show. Courts may still allocate burdens in particular cases.

title: No Required Fitness Statement
bodyText: Louisiana does not require your lease to state that you will deliver the property fit for habitation. The duty exists anyway: you must deliver the property at the agreed time and in good condition suitable for the purpose for which it was leased, keep it in that condition for the whole lease and make necessary repairs (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684, 2691), and you warrant that it is free of vices or defects that prevent its use (La. Civ. Code art. 2696). In a residential lease that warranty protects everyone living there under the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2698). The lease-content rules Louisiana does have are narrow, such as the sex-offender database notice in leases a real estate licensee executes (see the library's disclosure notes). This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Health-District Rental Rules Notice
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give tenants health-department or health-district rental rules on request, or to post a notice of occupants' rights, and no statute sets up a tenant referral to a health district. Health and safety in rentals is handled by the state sanitary code and parish and municipal health and housing codes, and by your Civil Code duties to keep the property suitable for its purpose and free of defects (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2696). One state program reaches rentals directly: when the state health officer learns of a case of lead poisoning, the dwelling where the person lives may be inspected if the occupants consent, and a dangerous lead level must be reported to the owner and all affected tenants and a warning posted at the main entrance until the hazard is corrected (La. R.S. 40:1285.4(B), (C)); see the library's lead notes. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Heat and Hot Water
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring you to supply heat or hot water, setting a minimum indoor temperature, or limiting when the cost of heat may be shifted to the tenant. The lease decides who pays for heating fuel and utilities, as the library's Utilities Paid by Tenant clause does. Equipment you provide is part of the leased property, so you must deliver it in good condition, keep it suitable for its purpose and repair it, except for damage the tenant causes (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684, 2691, 2692), and your warranty against vices or defects covers it (La. Civ. Code art. 2696). A failure that seriously affects health or safety, such as a heater that leaks carbon monoxide, is a defect no residential lease can waive (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); see also the library's detector notes. If you fail to make a necessary repair within a reasonable time after the tenant's demand, the tenant may repair and deduct (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). If you collect money from the tenant for gas or electricity billed to you, you must apply it to the bill within 60 days of receiving it (La. R.S. 14:71.5). Local housing codes may set heat rules. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: A Louisiana tenant's remedies against you come mainly from the Civil Code. Repairs: if you fail to make a necessary repair within a reasonable time after the tenant's demand, the tenant may have it made and get immediate reimbursement or deduct the reasonable cost from rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). Rent reduction: if the property's use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may get a reduction of rent or dissolution of the lease, plus damages if you were at fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2715); during a repair that cannot wait, the tenant may get a reduction, abatement or dissolution depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2693). Dissolution: when you fail to perform your obligations, the tenant may ask a court to dissolve the lease, or in some circumstances treat it as dissolved, and recover damages (La. Civ. Code arts. 2719, 2013); a court may give you extra time to perform, and a lease will not be dissolved if you have substantially performed and what is missing does not substantially impair the tenant's interest (La. Civ. Code arts. 2013, 2014). The tenant may also serve a notice to perform within a reasonable time, warning that the lease will be deemed dissolved if you do not (La. Civ. Code art. 2015). Damages: you owe the damages your failure causes; foreseeable damages if you acted in good faith, all direct damages if in bad faith (La. Civ. Code arts. 1994, 1996, 1997). Disturbance: if you do not act on a covered disturbance, the tenant may sue the person causing it (La. Civ. Code art. 2701). Separate statutes add penalties for specific violations, including the deposit penalty (La. R.S. 9:3252), the abandonment and disaster-parish rules (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)) and the military termination right (La. R.S. 9:3261(F)). Louisiana gives tenants no general right to withhold rent or pay it into court. These remedies apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Your Maintenance and Repair Duties
bodyText:
In Louisiana your maintenance duties come from the Civil Code, not a separate habitability statute, and they apply to written and oral, fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike. You must deliver the property at the agreed time in good condition suitable for the purpose for which it was leased (La. Civ. Code art. 2684), maintain it in a suitable condition and protect the tenant's peaceful possession for the whole lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), and make all repairs that become necessary to keep it suitable, except repairs the tenant is responsible for (La. Civ. Code art. 2691). You also warrant that the property is free of vices or defects that prevent its use, including defects that arise after move-in without the tenant's fault and defects you did not know about (La. Civ. Code arts. 2696, 2697); in a residential lease the warranty protects everyone who lives there under the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2698).

Most of these rules can be adjusted by the lease, but not all: a warranty waiver must be clear, unambiguous and brought to the tenant's attention, and it never covers defects you knew or should have known of and the tenant did not, or defects that seriously affect health or safety in a residential lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2699; see the library's warranty-waiver note). During the lease you may not alter the property (La. Civ. Code art. 2690), but you may make a repair that cannot wait, and the tenant may then get a rent reduction or dissolution depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2693).

The tenant must tell you without delay when the property is damaged or needs repair, and owes you damages for failing to (La. Civ. Code art. 2688). If you fail to make a necessary repair within a reasonable time after the tenant's demand, the tenant may make it and deduct the reasonable cost from rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). There is no statutory repair deadline and no statutory right to end the lease within a set number of days if the home is unfit at move-in; a tenant's remedy for a failure to deliver in good condition is dissolution and damages under the general contract rules (La. Civ. Code art. 2719).

Local codes: a city or town may adopt an ordinance under Louisiana's Slum Clearance Law letting a public officer declare a dwelling unfit for human habitation, inspect it, and issue orders served on the owner and recorded in the mortgage records (La. R.S. 40:580.2, 40:580.3, 40:580.4, 40:580.7). Whether your city has such an ordinance, and what other local housing codes require, depends on the local ordinance; check it.

title: No Required Facilities List
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes and codes do not list specific facilities you must supply in a rental (such as hot water, garbage receptacles, window screens, door locks or kitchen facilities), and they do not separately require you to keep every appliance or facility you supply in working order. Your duties are the general ones: deliver the property in good condition suitable for its purpose, keep it that way with the repairs that become necessary, and answer for vices or defects that prevent its use (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684, 2691, 2696). Anything you supply under the lease (an appliance, a fixture, a gate opener) is part of the leased property, so if it fails without the tenant's fault you must repair it unless the lease makes it the tenant's responsibility (La. Civ. Code art. 2691). Two specific state rules exist nearby: smoke and carbon monoxide detectors in one- and two-family dwellings at the time of lease (see the library's detector note), and, in the City of Monroe only, a statute requiring every building to be kept in a safe and sanitary condition, with required devices and safeguards kept in good working order, as the owner's responsibility (La. R.S. 33:4770.1, 33:4770.8). City and parish housing codes may add facility requirements, so check yours.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule that your promise to clean, repair or improve a unit must be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. A promise you make still binds you: a lease may be oral or written (La. Civ. Code art. 2681), contracts have the effect of law between the parties and must be performed in good faith (La. Civ. Code art. 1983), and you must deliver the property at the agreed time in good condition suitable for its purpose (La. Civ. Code art. 2684). If you do not keep a promise, the tenant may seek dissolution of the lease and damages under the general contract rules (La. Civ. Code art. 2719). Proof is where writing matters: when the lease is written, other evidence generally may not be used to vary it, though a later valid oral agreement may be proved (La. Civ. Code art. 1848), and an unwritten agreement worth more than five hundred dollars must be proved by at least one witness and other corroborating circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 1846). So put any promised work in the lease or a signed addendum with a date, and keep the library's entire-agreement clause in mind: a promise left out of a written lease may be hard for either side to enforce. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Rent-Receipt Anti-Waiver Rule
bodyText: Some states bar any lease, assignment, deed or mortgage from letting a person collect the rent free of the duty to keep the unit habitable. Louisiana has no such statute. The rules that come closest: when you sell the property, the lease continues, but the buyer is not bound by your lease obligations unless the buyer assumes them, and the tenant keeps an action against you for any loss the transfer causes (La. Civ. Code arts. 2711, 2712); the deposit must go to the buyer, who then owes its return (La. R.S. 9:3251(B)). If you pledge your rights in the leases and rents to a lender, the tenant pays the lender only after being notified in writing and told to pay it, and the tenant may raise against the lender any defense arising out of the lease, such as your failure to make repairs, unless the tenant agreed otherwise (La. Civ. Code arts. 3161, 3162, 3169). Because Louisiana's repair rules can be reallocated by the lease within limits (see the library's repair-allocation note), what you cannot shift is limited by the warranty-waiver rules (La. Civ. Code art. 2699) rather than by a rent-receipt rule. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals
bodyText: Louisiana has no statewide rental registration, licensing or periodic inspection program; some cities and parishes run their own under local ordinances, so check locally. Two state laws give officials inspection powers. A city or town that adopts an ordinance under the Slum Clearance Law may authorize its public officer to investigate dwelling conditions and to enter premises to examine them, in a way that causes the least possible inconvenience to the people in possession; orders are served on the owner and posted on the property (La. R.S. 40:580.4, 40:580.7). The Department of Agriculture may enter a dwelling to inspect and treat for Formosan termites upon reasonable notice, during reasonable hours, with the consent of the owner, renter, or the lessee if the property is under lease, and if consent is refused it must get a court order (La. R.S. 3:3391.9). No Louisiana statute lets a lease authorize a government housing inspector to enter so that the tenant must allow entry without giving consent at the time, and the library does not offer such a clause for Louisiana: the termite statute ties entry to the lessee's consent or a court order, and the Louisiana Constitution protects every person's home against unreasonable searches (La. Const. art. I, § 5). Your own entry for inspections is governed by the lease's access terms. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notice
bodyText: How the tenant tells you about a needed repair matters in Louisiana, but no statute requires a particular form. The tenant must notify you without delay when the property is damaged or needs repair, and you may recover the damages its failure to do so causes (La. Civ. Code art. 2688); if the tenant knows of a defect and fails to tell you, its recovery under your warranty may be reduced (La. Civ. Code art. 2697). The tenant's repair-and-deduct right starts only after your failure to repair within a reasonable time after demand by the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). The Civil Code's general rules say an obligor is put in default by a written request, an oral request made before two witnesses, a lawsuit, or a specific provision of the contract (La. Civ. Code art. 1991). You may ask in the lease that repair requests be made in writing or through a portal, and doing so helps you prove when you were told. But a lease term cannot change rules that turn on what you knew rather than on written notice: your warranty waiver is ineffective for defects you knew or should have known of and the tenant did not (La. Civ. Code art. 2699), and the injury-liability protection for a lease in which the tenant assumes responsibility for the property's condition does not apply if you knew or should have known of the defect, or received notice of it and failed to fix it within a reasonable time (La. R.S. 9:3221). Treat any actual notice (a call, text or conversation) as notice. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Lock or Rekey Statute
bodyText:
Louisiana's statutes and codes do not require you to install deadbolts, door viewers or peepholes, window latches or other security hardware in a rental, whatever the building's age, and do not require you to rekey or change the locks between tenants. Your general duties still apply: you must deliver the property in good condition suitable for its purpose and keep it that way (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684), and locks and doors you provide are part of the leased property, so a broken lock is a repair you owe unless the tenant caused it (La. Civ. Code arts. 2691, 2692).

In a residential lease your warranty of peaceful possession also covers disturbance by anyone who has access with your consent (La. Civ. Code art. 2700), which is one reason to rekey at each turnover and control who holds keys. A clause excluding your liability for physical injury, or for intentional or gross fault, is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004).

City and parish building and housing codes may set lock standards, so check yours. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Senior Housing Staff Card Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require work cards, licenses or background checks for maintenance or management staff in housing for people 55 or older, or in any other private rental housing. Louisiana's senior-housing rule is a fair housing exemption: the Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act's familial-status protections do not apply to dwellings under a state or federal program designed to assist elderly persons, or to housing for older persons, meaning housing intended for and at least 80% occupied by at least one person 55 or older per unit, with significant facilities and services for them and published policies showing that intent, or housing intended for and occupied solely by persons 62 or older (La. R.S. 51:2605(C)). Continuing care retirement communities, which sell care contracts with an entrance fee, are regulated separately (La. R.S. 51:2172, 51:2173). If you choose to screen staff who will have keys to residents' homes, see the library's note on employee screening: your warranty of peaceful possession covers disturbance by anyone who has access with your consent (La. Civ. Code art. 2700).

title: No Rule on Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes do not regulate splitting a shared (master-metered) utility bill among tenants: no law bans ratio or formula billing (by square footage, occupants or similar), sets a formula, requires a disclosure, or makes unenforceable a term charging a tenant for a utility that is not separately metered to the unit. If you allocate utility costs, the lease must state the method: the quantity of a contract's object may be undetermined only if it is determinable (La. Civ. Code art. 1973), and rent must be certain or determinable through a method the parties agreed (La. Civ. Code art. 2676), and the lessor otherwise pays charges that burden the property except those arising from the tenant's use (La. Civ. Code art. 2689), a rule the lease may vary. Three related rules: money you collect from tenants for utility service must be applied to the bill within 60 days after you receive it (La. R.S. 14:71.5; see the library's note on utility money you hold); a gas system in an apartment complex that resells metered gas to residents, by meter or through the rent, is a regulated master meter system (La. R.S. 30:503(8)); and if you use a third-party billing company for individually metered units, the tenant may request copies of the original bills (see the library's tenant bill transparency note). Check them and your utility's tariff before allocating. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Learning of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes give you no procedure to authorize a utility, by a separate document or otherwise, to warn you before it shuts off a tenant's own service, and none lets a tenant name you to receive copies of shutoff notices. Utility service and disconnection rules are set by the Public Service Commission, which regulates public utilities (La. Const. art. IV, § 21(B)), and by local utilities and water districts; ask your utilities whether they offer a third-party notice option the tenant can sign up for. The lease can ask the tenant to tell you promptly if a utility serving the home will be shut off, which fits the tenant's duty to use the property as a prudent administrator (La. Civ. Code art. 2683). Do not take over or interrupt the tenant's service yourself (see the library's note on submetered utilities and shutoffs).

title: When the Utility Account Is Yours
bodyText: When a utility account serving your tenants is in your name, Louisiana's statutes give the tenant no special protection if you fall behind: there is no statute letting tenants pay the utility and deduct it from rent, no rent receiver for unpaid utilities, no duty to identify tenants to the utility, and no statutory notice to each unit before a building-wide shutoff. The consequences fall on you through the lease and the Civil Code: if the lease makes you responsible for a utility, failing to pay it is a failure to perform, and the tenant may seek dissolution and damages (La. Civ. Code arts. 2719, 1994), and a loss of service that substantially impairs use of the home without the tenant's fault can support a rent reduction or dissolution (La. Civ. Code art. 2715). If you collect money from tenants for utility service and knowingly fail to pay the bill within 60 days after receiving it, you commit a crime (La. R.S. 14:71.5; see the library's note on utility money you hold). For master-metered water or sewer on a multifamily property, local governments have a privilege on the property for your unpaid charges (see the library's utility lien note). This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Cutoff for Untransferred Utilities
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule letting you shut off a utility still in your name because the tenant did not move the account into the tenant's own name, and the library does not offer an opt-in cutoff clause for Louisiana. Cutting service to a tenant in possession risks breaching your duty to maintain the property and protect the tenant's peaceful possession for the whole lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), and the lawful way to remove a tenant is the court eviction process (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701, 4731). What you can do: require in the lease that the tenant open accounts in the tenant's name by the start date (the library's Utilities Paid by Tenant clause), treat the tenant's failure as a lease default (see the library's default clause), and bill the tenant for service you paid that the lease puts on the tenant; if you then close your own account, do so only in a way that leaves the tenant's service uninterrupted, by coordinating with the utility. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Utility Bill Copies for Tenants (Third-Party Billing)
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes require no lease disclosure for submetered or landlord-billed utilities and set no submeter billing limits or late-fee caps (see the library's note on submetered utilities). One statute does apply to utility billing: Louisiana's Tenant Bill Transparency law. It covers you if you (or your property manager) use third-party billing, meaning an intermediary that handles invoicing and payment between you and the tenant, for a residential unit that has its own meter for water, gas or electricity from a regulated or local-government utility (La. R.S. 51:3271, 51:3272). The tenant may ask in writing for a copy of the utility's original bill for any utility supplied to the unit, naming the utility, the dates (no earlier than the last day of the billing cycle before the request) and whether the tenant wants all future bills too (La. R.S. 51:3273(A), (B)). You must send copies of past bills within thirty days of a proper request, and copies of future bills within thirty days after you receive each one (La. R.S. 51:3273(C), (D)). Requests and responses may be electronic if they meet Louisiana's electronic-transactions law (La. R.S. 51:3273(F)). Your failure to comply does not excuse the tenant from paying the billing service in full (La. R.S. 51:3273(E)), but you may be fined up to $500 per violation, and the tenant or the attorney general may sue to stop violations and recover the penalties (La. R.S. 51:3274). The law has no unit-count or owner-occupancy exception. This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Blight Lists, Receivership and Code Fines
bodyText: Louisiana has no tenant-initiated receivership and no code-enforcement receivership that takes over the rents of an ordinary occupied rental because of repair violations. Two state laws let local governments act against substandard property. First, under the Louisiana Housing Preservation Act, a parish or municipality may keep a list of blighted housing properties (for example, property below federal minimum habitability standards declared unfit, or property vacant for eighteen months and declared a public nuisance), with certified-mail notice to the owner and a right to appeal, and may ask a court to place a listed property in a receivership of up to five years so the local government or a qualified rehabilitation entity can rehabilitate it; that action requires the owner's consent, and the owner may petition to be reinstated by agreeing to finish the plan and honor its financing (La. R.S. 40:600.33, 40:600.34, 40:600.37, 40:600.41, 40:600.42). Second, a parish or municipality may adopt an administrative-adjudication procedure for housing, public-health, fire-code and blight violations by owners, their agents or tenants: after at least fifteen days' notice (thirty days, also to mortgagees, for a blight or abandonment hearing), a hearing officer may fine you, order the violation corrected by a date, have the work done if you do not, record a lien that is added to your property tax bill, and condemn or demolish blighted property; you may appeal to the district court within thirty days (La. R.S. 13:2575). Cities that adopt Slum Clearance Law ordinances may also issue orders against unfit dwellings (see the library's maintenance note). These tools apply whatever the building's size. Check whether your city or parish has adopted them.

title: No Cable or Satellite Access Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute giving tenants a right to cable television, satellite, broadband or other telecommunications access in a rental building, no rule requiring you to let a provider wire the building, no rule on payments from providers for access, and no ban on charging cable subscribers different rent. Louisiana's video-service law regulates providers' state franchises and use of public rights-of-way, and bars a certificated provider from denying service to residential subscribers based on race or income, but it says nothing about access to private rental buildings (La. R.S. 45:1362, 45:1374, 45:1375). Federal rules, govern a tenant's right to install over-the-air reception devices (satellite dishes and antennas) in areas within the tenant's exclusive use and limit exclusive building contracts with cable providers; check them before restricting dishes or signing an exclusive service agreement. Your lease rules on alterations and installations still apply within those limits.

title: Repair and Deduct
bodyText: A Louisiana tenant's main remedy when you fail to repair is repair and deduct, and it has four conditions: the repair must be one you are bound to make (a necessary repair to keep the property suitable for its purpose, not one the tenant owes because it caused the damage); the tenant must first demand the repair; you must have failed to make it within a reasonable time after that demand; and the tenant may recover or deduct only to the extent the repair was necessary and the amount reasonable (La. Civ. Code arts. 2691, 2692, 2694). Once those are met, the tenant may demand immediate reimbursement from you or apply the amount to rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2694). No dollar cap, no fixed waiting period and no limit on how often applies. Other remedies: a rent reduction or abatement, or dissolution, while you make a repair that cannot wait (La. Civ. Code art. 2693); a reduction or dissolution when use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, with damages if you were at fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2715); and dissolution and damages for your failure to perform (La. Civ. Code arts. 2719, 1994). Louisiana has no rent escrow or rent-into-court procedure and no general right to withhold rent outside article 2694 (see the library's notes on tenant remedies and habitability rules Louisiana lacks). Whether a lease may waive or narrow the repair-and-deduct right is not answered by the text: the Civil Code states limits for warranty waivers (La. Civ. Code art. 2699) but none for article 2694, so do not rely on a waiver. A tenant who deducts more than article 2694 allows has underpaid rent, which you may treat as a default. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Entry Is Set by Your Lease
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute giving you a right to enter a residential rental or setting a notice period, permitted hours or purposes for entry. Your right to enter during the lease comes from the lease itself, so put it there: the library's Landlord's Right of Entry clause gives you reasonable access for maintenance, repairs and showings on 24 hours' notice except in emergencies.

The Civil Code frames how you use that right. You must protect the tenant's peaceful possession for the whole lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), and in a residential lease your warranty covers disturbance by anyone who has access with your consent, including your staff and contractors (La. Civ. Code art. 2700). You may make a repair that cannot wait until the lease ends even if it inconveniences the tenant, who may then get a rent reduction or dissolution depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2693), but you may not alter the property during the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2690).

No statute treats a tenant's repair request as consent to entry, lets a separate scheduled-service notice dispense with entry notice, requires showings to be approved in a separate document, or sets a penalty for unlawful or harassing entry; those questions are governed by the lease and general contract law. If the tenant unreasonably refuses entry the lease allows, that is a failure to perform, and you may seek dissolution or damages (La. Civ. Code arts. 2719, 1994); entering without the tenant's agreement or a lease right, or entering to harass, risks breaching your peaceful-possession duty, with damages owed to the tenant.

Rent-to-own laws that bar entry clauses apply to leases of goods, not homes (La. R.S. 9:3304, 9:3356). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Victim Lock-Change Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring you to change the locks, or letting a tenant change them without your consent, because a tenant or household member is a victim of domestic abuse, stalking or sexual assault. The tools Louisiana does provide: a court hearing a domestic abuse petition may grant the petitioner possession of the residence to the exclusion of the abuser, by evicting the abuser or restoring possession to the petitioner, where the home is leased by both of them or solely owned by the petitioner, or leased solely by the abuser who owes the petitioner support, and may restore the petitioner's personal property, including keys (La. R.S. 46:2135(A)(3), (A)(6)). In buildings of six or more dwellings (but not a building of ten or fewer units where the owner or lessor lives in one), you may not end or refuse to renew a lease, or issue a notice to vacate, because domestic abuse occurred on the premises against a tenant or household member, and you are entitled to an immediate eviction of an abuser named in the documentation the victim gives you (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (D), (F), (G)). When a tenant gives you such an order or documentation, changing the locks promptly at the tenant's request, and not giving the excluded person a key, is good practice even though no statute requires it; the library's Keys clause bars tenants from duplicating keys without your consent, so agree on who pays and who gets keys.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute aimed at smart locks, keypads, key fobs, app-based or biometric entry systems in residential rentals: nothing requires you to offer a physical key as an alternative, limits the entry data such a system collects, or sets rules for sharing it. The general rules apply whatever the technology. Your entry rights come from the lease (see the library's note on entry), and an entry log does not create a right to enter that the lease does not give. You must protect the tenant's peaceful possession (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), and in a residential lease your warranty covers disturbance by anyone who has access with your consent, which includes people to whom you issue codes (La. Civ. Code art. 2700). A system that fails and locks the tenant out is a repair you owe unless the tenant caused it (La. Civ. Code arts. 2691, 2692). If the system collects personal information, Louisiana's general data-security and breach-notice laws may apply.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: Louisiana does not require apartment owners, at any size of complex, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a key log, restrict master keys, or run background checks on employees who can enter units. The only master-key statute in Louisiana's statutes and codes concerns a single master elevator key for fire emergencies in buildings of six or more stories and in other buildings (except one- and two-family dwellings) where a new elevator was installed after January 1, 2013 (La. R.S. 40:1582), and locksmith licensing rules govern locksmiths, not owners (La. R.S. 40:1664.3). Key control still matters: in a residential lease your warranty of peaceful possession covers disturbance by anyone who has access with your consent (La. Civ. Code art. 2700), and once told of such a disturbance you must take all steps necessary to protect the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 2701); a clause excluding liability for intentional or gross fault or for physical injury is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). See the library's notes on employee screening and on locks.

title: Belongings Left Behind
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute telling you how to store, sell or dispose of belongings a residential tenant leaves behind: no notice form, storage period or value threshold. Specific procedures exist only for other settings: a rented lot for a factory-built (mobile) home worth $5,000 or less, with notice, newspaper advertisement and court approval before sale (La. R.S. 9:3259.3), and self-service storage units, where property left fifteen days after the rental agreement expires following a nonrenewal notice is deemed abandoned (La. R.S. 9:4759.2).

For a home, three sets of general rules apply.
- (1) Possession. You may retake the home without a court order only after the required notice to vacate has been given (or waived in the lease) and only on a reasonable belief that the tenant has abandoned it; ceasing to live there, returning the keys and removing furnishings are signs of abandonment, but in a parish under a federal disaster declaration ceasing to live there is not evidence of abandonment for thirty days after the initial declaration, and a residential tenant may recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, from a lessor who fails to comply (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(B), (C)). Otherwise you need a judgment of eviction; the sheriff, constable or marshal executing the warrant clears the premises of any property in them (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4734).
- (2) Ownership. The tenant's belongings remain the tenant's until abandoned: a thing is abandoned only when its owner gives up possession intending to give up ownership (La. Civ. Code art. 3418). Leaving items behind is evidence of that intent, not proof of it.
- (3) Your privilege. Your privilege on the tenant's belongings for rent is enforced only through the court by sequestration, and many household items are exempt (see the library's lessor's privilege note); you may not take or sell belongings yourself to pay rent.

A lease may fill the gap. Louisiana law does not forbid a lease term in which the tenant agrees how property left behind will be handled, so the library offers an optional Property Left Behind clause. It is lawful because it applies only after the lease has ended and you have lawfully regained possession, gives the tenant written notice and a stated time to claim the property, has you store it with reasonable care meanwhile, does not let you sell it to pay rent, and does not excuse your intentional or gross fault, which no clause may do (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). Do not use a clause that deems a home abandoned after a few days' absence or lets you dispose of belongings at once without responsibility: it conflicts with the reasonable-belief, notice and disaster rules above.

This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Attorney Fees in Louisiana Leases
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute that caps attorney fees in a residential lease, voids a fee clause, or makes a one-way fee clause run both ways.

What the law says:
- (1) For money the tenant owes (rent and other sums), if a written lease expressly says the tenant will also pay your attorney fees in a fixed or determinable amount, you are entitled to that amount (La. Civ. Code art. 2000). A fixed figure (such as a percentage of the amount owed) or a stated method is enough; the library's default clause uses reasonable fees for the prevailing party, and the library offers an optional fixed-fee clause for unpaid sums. Keep the figure modest.
- (2) For other lease obligations, including possession in an eviction, fees come from the lease's terms as an ordinary contract; no statute awards them (La. Civ. Code art. 1983).
- (3) Oral leases only: a tenant who fails to pay rent within twenty days after a written demand stating the correct amount, delivered by certified mail, personal delivery or posting on the door, owes reasonable attorney fees when you win judgment (La. R.S. 9:3259).
- (4) Statutes award fees in particular disputes whatever the lease says: in a deposit suit, the court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party, tenant or landlord (La. R.S. 9:3253); in an action under the eviction article (its words reach eviction rules as well as abandonment and the disaster-parish rules), the court may award costs and fees to the prevailing party, so assume an eviction suit can carry fees either way (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)(3)); and bad-check claims carry fees after the statutory demand (La. R.S. 9:2782).

Fee clauses do not change the military, domestic-abuse or sexual-assault termination limits, which no lease may waive. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Condominium Conversions
bodyText: Louisiana gives tenants no notice period, right to stay, or right of first refusal when a rental building is converted to condominiums, and requires no special lease statement about a planned conversion. The Condominium Act's only conversion rule is a buyer disclosure: the public offering statement for a condominium containing any building with more than ten units that was occupied, wholly or partly, by people other than purchasers before the declaration was recorded must include an architect's or engineer's report on the building's structural components, roof and mechanical and electrical installations, the declarant's estimate of their remaining useful life (or a statement that none is made), and any outstanding building-code violation notices with estimated cure costs; this applies only to units that may be used as residences (La. R.S. 9:1124.104). Existing leases survive the conversion and sale of units: a transfer of the leased property does not end the lease, the tenant has an action against you for any loss the transfer causes, a buyer is not bound by your lease obligations unless it assumes them, and a lease of an immovable binds third persons only from the time it is filed for registry (La. Civ. Code arts. 2711, 2712, 2681.1); the deposit passes to the buyer (La. R.S. 9:3251(B)). City or parish ordinances may add rules.

title: After a Hurricane, Flood or Other Disaster
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute that ends a tenancy or suspends rent because of a declared disaster, but several rules decide what happens after a hurricane, flood or fire.

The lease: if the home is lost or totally destroyed without either party's fault, the lease ends and neither owes damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2714); if it is partly destroyed or its use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may get a rent reduction or dissolution, plus damages if you were at fault, but if the impairment comes from circumstances outside the property (for example, an evacuation order or a closed access road), the tenant may dissolve the lease but is not entitled to a rent reduction (La. Civ. Code art. 2715). You may make repairs that cannot wait, with a reduction or dissolution available to the tenant depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2693); see the library's casualty termination clause for your own option to end the lease.

Possession: in a parish under a federal disaster declaration, a tenant's absence is not evidence of abandonment for thirty days after the initial declaration; a residential tenant may recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, if you do not comply (the penalty sits in the disaster paragraph, but assume it can apply anywhere), may get a restraining order without posting the usual security during those thirty days, and the court may award fees to the prevailing party (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)). If the tenant is constructively evicted because the home is rendered uninhabitable without the tenant's fault, you must mitigate your damages (La. R.S. 9:3260).

Pricing: during a state of emergency declared by the governor or a parish president, prices for goods and services in the emergency area may not exceed those ordinarily charged just before the emergency, except for listed cost-based reasons, initially for up to thirty days (La. R.S. 29:732(A), (B)); the statute does not mention rent, so avoid raising rent in an emergency area during the declared period.

Applicants: your application-fee notice must tell applicants they may submit a hardship statement about a declared disaster (La. R.S. 9:3258.1; applies to primary residences, not owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units).

These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Early Termination for Victims of Abuse, Stalking or Sexual Assault
bodyText: The domestic abuse statute applies only to a lease of a dwelling in a building or structure with six or more separate residential dwellings, and not to a structure of ten or fewer units where the owner or lessor lives in one (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A)); the sexual assault statute has no unit threshold (La. R.S. 9:3261.2). Domestic abuse, stalking and cyberstalking (La. R.S. 9:3261.1): a tenant may end the lease early if the tenant or a household member is a domestic abuse victim and the tenant (1) asserts in writing that the tenant or household member is a victim and asks for early termination, (2) gives you reasonable documentation of an act of domestic abuse on the leased premises within the past thirty days (for stalking or cyberstalking that did not occur on the premises, with a written declaration of why living there may threaten the victim's safety), (3) asserts in writing that the tenant will not knowingly and voluntarily let the abuser have further access to, visit or occupy the unit, acknowledging that a violation may lead to eviction, (4) otherwise meets or agrees to meet the lease requirements, and (5) if you ask, gives you in writing the abuser's name and address. You must then terminate the lease as a matter of law on a mutually agreed date within thirty days of the written request; the tenant must move out by then to avoid future rent and owes only rent through that date and obligations already outstanding, paid on or before move-out (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(E), (F)). Sexual assault (La. R.S. 9:3261.2): a tenant who is a victim of a sexual assault in Louisiana within the past sixty days, occurring after the lease was signed, may end the lease on the same pattern (written assertion, reasonable documentation, with a declaration if the assault was not on the premises, a written promise not to let the offender have access, and meeting lease requirements); the same thirty-day termination and rent rules apply, and this right cannot be waived or modified by the lease under any circumstances (La. R.S. 9:3261.2(B), (C), (E)). Under both statutes: when there are several tenants on the lease, the entire lease ends on the agreed date and you are entitled to an immediate eviction of all lessees on presenting the documentation to the court; you are also entitled to an immediate eviction of a lessee or co-lessee named as the abuser or offender in the documentation; and you may keep the deposit only for reasons the deposit statute allows (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(F)(2)-(3), 9:3261.2(C)(2)-(3); see the library's note on deposit timing). The abuser or offender need not be a co-tenant. These rights apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Proof for Abuse and Sexual Assault Protections
bodyText: The domestic abuse statute applies only to a lease of a dwelling in a building or structure with six or more separate residential dwellings, and not to a structure of ten or fewer units where the owner or lessor lives in one (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A)); the sexual assault statute has no unit threshold (La. R.S. 9:3261.2). For the domestic abuse protections, "reasonable documentation" means only (a) a completed Certification of Domestic Abuse in the statutory form, signed under oath by a qualified third party, or (b) a Uniform Abuse Prevention Order (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(B)(7)). A qualified third party is the executive director, program director or another employee of a community-based shelter under contract with the Department of Children and Family Services, provided the employee is a licensed clinical social worker; or a licensed professional counselor, prosecuting attorney or investigating law enforcement officer personally involved in the case (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(B)(6)). The statute's punctuation leaves unclear whether the license condition reaches the shelter's directors and whether the counselor must work at a shelter, so the cautious course is to accept a certification from any of these people. The certification form, which must read substantially as set out in the statute, has the victim describe the incident, dates and places, explain any off-premises stalking risk, and name the perpetrator if known, under penalty of perjury, with the third party's verification, license or tax number and address (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(H)). For the sexual assault termination right, the documentation is likewise only a certification of sexual assault in the statutory form signed under oath by a qualified third party, or a Uniform Abuse Prevention Order; qualified third parties are a sexual assault center program director, a sexual assault advocate who is a licensed clinical social worker or licensed professional counselor, a healthcare provider who did a forensic medical examination, or a prosecuting attorney or investigating officer involved in the case (La. R.S. 9:3261.2(A)(1)-(2), (D)). You may not require other proof, such as a police report, as a condition of the statutory rights. On a domestic abuse termination you may ask for the abuser's name and address in writing (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(E)(5)). The statutes set no confidentiality rule for these documents; treat them as confidential and share them only as needed, for example with the court in an eviction of the abuser.

title: Eviction Protections for Domestic Abuse Victims
bodyText: The domestic abuse statute applies only to a lease of a dwelling in a building or structure with six or more separate residential dwellings, and not to a structure of ten or fewer units where the owner or lessor lives in one (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A)); the sexual assault statute has no unit threshold (La. R.S. 9:3261.2). In covered buildings you may not: refuse to lease solely because an applicant or household member is or was a victim of domestic abuse, or (except as below) because of activity directly related to it, if the applicant provides reasonable documentation and otherwise qualifies (this does not apply to an applicant you previously evicted for any reason); or terminate, fail to renew, or issue an eviction notice or notice to vacate because domestic abuse or directly related activity occurred on the premises and the victim is a tenant or household member. Exception: if the abuser's continued presence in or near the unit leads to one or more additional violent disturbances or altercations that threaten the safety or peaceable possession of the tenant or other residents, you may evict, even if the abuser's presence is uninvited, and you may at your discretion offer the tenant a different available unit (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(D)(1)). The victim must give you reasonable documentation on or before the application, termination or nonrenewal date or before the eviction judgment, or loses any claim; a notice you issued for another lease reason before receiving documentation is not penalized, but if the only reason was a single act of domestic abuse, no breach is alleged and you receive documentation before judgment, you must rescind it (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(D)(2)-(3)). No lease may limit anyone's right to call police or emergency help after domestic abuse or penalize the tenant for such a call; such a provision is null (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(C)), and in any rental, a parish or city may not adopt an ordinance that penalizes you, or authorizes eviction or lease termination, because a tenant called police or emergency help about domestic abuse or another crime (La. R.S. 33:9701(E), (F)). Enforcement is limited: a victim may sue in district court within one year for injunctive relief only; frivolous suits draw sanctions; no suit lies if the victim later knowingly let the abuser back in; and you are immune from suits by the abuser over evicting the abuser under the statute (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(I)-(K), (M)). Nothing limits your right to refuse, end or not renew a lease, or evict, for reasons unrelated to the abuse (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(G)). The sexual assault statute gives an early-termination right but no eviction protection.

title: When the Property Is Expropriated
bodyText: If the government takes your rental property by expropriation (eminent domain), the Civil Code decides what happens to the lease, and the lease may vary these rules. A total taking ends the lease, and neither you nor the tenant owes the other damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2714). A partial taking, or one that otherwise substantially impairs the tenant's use without the tenant's fault, lets the tenant obtain a rent reduction or dissolution, whichever fits the circumstances; if the impairment comes from circumstances outside the leased property, the tenant may dissolve the lease but not reduce the rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2715). Timing: when there is a building on the property, the court in the expropriation case may postpone the expropriating authority's right to enter for up to thirty days after the last defendant is served, and may fix a reasonable daily rental to be paid by a defendant who stays in possession after compensation is withdrawn (La. R.S. 19:148, 48:448). The Constitution requires just compensation paid to the owner, including relocation costs and other damages the owner actually incurs (La. Const. art. I, § 4(B)); whether and how a tenant shares in the award is a question for the expropriation proceeding and case law. The rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes set no general rules for when a gas, electric or water utility may shut off a home: no statutory notice period, no winter, heat or holiday ban, and no medical-certificate protection appear in the statutes. Those rules come from the Public Service Commission, which regulates public utilities (La. Const. art. IV, § 21(B)), and from city, parish and district utilities.
