Statutes that do touch shutoffs: during an energy emergency declared by the Commission, utilities must offer a deferred-billing program to eligible customers (low-income seniors, people receiving food stamps or TANF, people whose only income is Social Security, and people who need electrically powered life-sustaining equipment), and an enrolled customer who keeps up the program payments may not be shut off (La. R.S. 45:1221, 45:1222); a parish or municipality may contract with a water company to shut off water to premises delinquent on garbage charges, but only after certified-mail notice and 30 more days of nonpayment (La. R.S. 33:4169.1(B)); a water cooperative may discontinue service to a customer who fails to pay (La. R.S. 45:1604); and no provider of natural gas, electricity, or water or sewerage service may stop service to the home of a residential consumer on active military duty for nonpayment, must offer at least as long as the period of service to repay arrears on return, and may not charge late fees or interest for that time (La. R.S. 29:317, 29:318, 29:319). These rules bind utilities and other providers. If you yourself supply gas, electricity or water to tenants through your own system, do not cut service to a service member in any case. You may not cut off a tenant's utilities yourself as a collection or eviction tool (see the library's notes on submetered utilities and peaceful possession). This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Who May Represent an Entity Landlord
bodyText: If you own rentals personally, you may handle your own eviction: the unauthorized-practice law does not stop anyone from attending to his own business, claims or demands (La. R.S. 37:212(B)). If the owner is a corporation, LLC, partnership or other entity, the general rule is that only a licensed attorney may appear for it or prepare pleadings for it in court (La. R.S. 37:212(A)(1), 37:213(A)), with one exception: an entity may assert or defend a claim not exceeding $5,000 on its own behalf in courts of limited jurisdiction through a duly authorized partner, shareholder, officer, employee or authorized agent or representative, but not a claim of another entity or an assigned claim (La. R.S. 37:212(C)). Whether an eviction, which seeks possession rather than money, counts as a claim not exceeding $5,000 is not answered by the statute; check the practice of your local court and get advice before a non-lawyer appears for an entity. The eviction articles themselves let the lessor's agent deliver the notice to vacate and cause the tenant to be cited (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701, 4731(A)), but that does not settle who may appear and argue at the hearing. Violations carry criminal fines for the entity and anyone who assists it (La. R.S. 37:213(C)-(D)). This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination Statute
bodyText: Louisiana gives neither you nor the tenant a statutory right to end a lease because of a sudden environmental or public-health event, such as contamination, a chemical release, smoke or a government health order. The Civil Code's general rules apply: if the home is destroyed or lost without either party's fault, the lease ends (La. Civ. Code art. 2714); if its use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may obtain a rent reduction or dissolution, but when the cause is outside the property (for example, a nearby release or an area-wide order) the tenant may dissolve but not reduce the rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2715); and if the home is made uninhabitable without the tenant's fault and the tenant is forced out (constructively evicted), you must mitigate your damages (La. R.S. 9:3260). You may make repairs or remediation that cannot wait, with a rent reduction or dissolution available to the tenant depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2693). A landlord's own option to end the lease after such an event exists only if the lease reserves it, and then you must give the longer of the lease's notice and the Civil Code's periodic-lease notice, which cannot be waived in advance (La. Civ. Code art. 2718); the library's casualty termination clause ("Landlord Termination After Fire or Casualty" clause) covers damage to the home by fire or other casualty; whether contamination of the home counts as a casualty is unsettled, and the clause does not reach an area-wide order that leaves the home undamaged. The library does not add a separate environmental-event clause for Louisiana; a landlord who wants a broader termination right should add its own clause and take advice first. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Delays After an Eviction Judgment
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute letting a court delay an eviction because moving would be a hardship for the tenant (for example because of age, illness, children or weather). The eviction timeline is short and fixed: the hearing on the rule to show cause can be held as early as the third day after service; if you win, the court renders the judgment of eviction immediately, and it stays effective for at least ninety days; if the tenant does not leave within twenty-four hours, the court issues a warrant for the sheriff, constable or marshal to put you in possession (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4732, 4733). An appeal suspends the eviction only if the tenant answered the rule under oath with an affirmative defense and applied for the appeal and filed a bond within twenty-four hours of the judgment (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4735). The stays that do exist: for a tenant on active military duty (or whose immediate family member is) under a rental agreement made on or after June 29, 2005, whose ability to pay is materially affected by the service, the court may on its own and must on the tenant's motion stay the case for ninety days (or another period justice requires) or adjust the rent obligation, and may grant you equitable relief; this does not apply to landlords operating fewer than four residential premises (La. R.S. 29:311, 29:315). In a parish under a federal disaster declaration, the abandonment rules give the tenant thirty days' protection, and a tenant may get a restraining order without posting security during that time (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)). Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) adds its own stay, not covered here.

title: No Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute sealing, shielding or expunging eviction court records, removing them from public indexes after a period, or automatically clearing dismissed cases, and none limits your use of eviction records in screening beyond general fair-housing and consumer-reporting law. One related rule: if you charge an application fee, your written notice must say whether you consider eviction records in deciding whether to rent, and must tell the applicant that he or she may submit a statement of up to two hundred words about financial hardship from a declared disaster or emergency and how it affected the applicant's credit, employment or rental history (La. R.S. 9:3258.1(A)); this applies to lessors of property to be used as the tenant's primary residence, except owner-occupied buildings of no more than four units, and gives no one a right to sue (La. R.S. 9:3258.1(C), (D)).

title: Serving Eviction Papers
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute providing for a lease to name a person who will accept eviction papers for the tenant, and the library does not offer such a clause. The rules: the notice to vacate must be written and delivered to the tenant (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701), and it cannot be sent only electronically, because Louisiana's electronic-transactions law does not apply to notices of eviction under a rental agreement for an individual's primary residence (La. R.S. 9:2603(B)(4)(b)(ii)). The rule to show cause is served by a proper officer, either personally on the tenant or at the tenant's home on a person of suitable age and discretion who lives there (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 1231, 1232, 1234). If the premises are abandoned or closed, or the tenant's whereabouts are unknown, notices, process, pleadings and orders may be attached to a door of the premises with the same effect as personal service (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4703). Service may be made on a representative appointed by mandate (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 1235), but a tenant may generally revoke a mandate at any time (a mandate can be made irrevocable only if it also serves another's interest and the parties so agree), it ends at the tenant's death, and a person you choose for the tenant would not be the tenant's own representative (La. Civ. Code arts. 2989, 3024, 3025); relying on a lease-named agent risks defective service and a delayed eviction.

title: Peaceful Possession
bodyText: Louisiana writes the tenant's right to quiet possession into the Civil Code. You must protect the tenant's peaceful possession for the whole lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), and you warrant it against anyone who claims ownership of, a right to possess, or any other right in the property (La. Civ. Code art. 2700). In a residential lease the warranty also covers disturbance by a person who has access to the property with your consent (your employees, contractors or agents, for example) or who occupies adjacent property that belongs to you, such as another of your tenants (La. Civ. Code art. 2700). As soon as you are told of a covered disturbance you must take all steps necessary to protect the tenant's possession; if you do not, the tenant may sue the person causing it without losing its rights against you (La. Civ. Code art. 2701). You are not bound to protect against strangers who claim no right in the property (La. Civ. Code art. 2702). You may not alter the property during the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2690), though you may make a repair that cannot wait (La. Civ. Code art. 2693). Your own conduct: no Louisiana statute specifically forbids a residential lockout or sets a penalty for one, but the only way the eviction articles let you retake possession without a court order is when you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned the premises after the required notice to vacate has been given (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(B)); otherwise possession is recovered by a court judgment and a warrant executed by the sheriff, constable or marshal (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4731-4734). In a parish under a federal disaster declaration, a tenant's stopping living there is not evidence of abandonment for thirty days after the initial declaration, and the same paragraph lets a residential tenant recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, from a lessor who fails to comply with the article (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)); because that penalty sits in the disaster-parish paragraph, whether it reaches a lockout outside a disaster parish is unsettled, so assume it can. Changing the locks, removing doors or cutting services to force a tenant out risks a breach of your peaceful-possession duty, damages, and that penalty. The rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: When a Tenant Leaves Early or Disappears
bodyText: When a tenant moves out early or disappears, Louisiana's rules come from the Civil Code and the eviction articles, not from an abandonment statute. Leaving does not end a fixed-term lease, which ends only when the term expires (La. Civ. Code art. 2720); for a month-to-month or other periodic lease, the tenant's surrender of possession at the time a termination notice would be due counts as the tenant's notice of termination (La. Civ. Code art. 2729). Retaking the home: you may take possession without going to court only after the required notice to vacate has been given (or waived in the lease) and only on a reasonable belief that the tenant has abandoned it; in a parish under a federal disaster declaration, ceasing to live there is not evidence of abandonment for thirty days after the initial declaration, and a residential tenant may recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, if you do not follow these rules (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(B), (C)). Do not rely on a lease term that conclusively presumes abandonment after a few days' absence. Rent and re-renting: the tenant who abandons remains liable under the lease. If you dissolve the lease, you recover your loss, but you must make reasonable efforts to reduce it, chiefly by trying to re-rent, and the tenant may have the damages reduced if you do not (La. Civ. Code arts. 1995, 2002); see the library's remedies note for the choice between dissolving and keeping the lease in force (and the optional rent acceleration clause). If the tenant left because the home was made uninhabitable without the tenant's fault or the tenant was constructively evicted, you must mitigate your damages by statute as well (La. R.S. 9:3260). The deposit: when a tenant abandons without the required notice or before the lease ends, the one-month return and itemization deadline does not apply (La. R.S. 9:3251(C)), but you may still keep only what covers the tenant's actual default. The library does not offer a clause forfeiting the whole deposit when a tenant leaves early: a forfeiture is stipulated damages, which cannot be collected on top of the rent it stands for and may be reduced for the tenant's partial performance (La. Civ. Code arts. 2005, 2007, 2011), and any waiver of the deposit statute's protections is null (La. R.S. 9:3254). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases as stated.

title: Ending a Lease Early in Louisiana
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute giving a tenant a general right to end a fixed-term lease early or capping an early-termination fee; the library's Early Termination clause supplies a contractual option.

Louisiana adds these rules.
- (1) Notice: when a lease reserves a right to end it before the end of the term, the party ending it must give the longer of the notice the lease specifies and the notice the Civil Code requires to end a periodic lease (for a month-to-month lease, written notice at least ten calendar days before the end of a month), and the right to that notice cannot be given up in advance (La. Civ. Code arts. 2718, 2728, 2729). The library's 30-day written notice satisfies this for monthly rent periods; do not shorten it.
- (2) The fee: an early-termination fee works like stipulated damages, which a court may change only if so manifestly unreasonable as to be contrary to public policy (La. Civ. Code arts. 2005, 2012; see the library's stipulated-damages note).
- (3) Statutory exits override the lease: an active or reserve service member (or spouse) with qualifying orders, discharge, government quarters, a service injury requiring more than fifteen days' hospitalization, or death in service may end the lease on at least thirty days' written notice, owes at most one month's rent (half a month after six months of the lease), gets the full deposit back if otherwise compliant, and cannot be made to waive these rights (La. R.S. 9:3261); victims of domestic abuse, stalking or cyberstalking (buildings of six or more dwellings, not a building of ten or fewer units where the owner or lessor lives) and of sexual assault (no unit threshold) may end the lease within thirty days on documentation, owing rent only to the termination date (La. R.S. 9:3261.1, 9:3261.2; see the library's note). No early-termination fee may be charged on top of those limits.
- (4) Other endings: a tenant may seek dissolution if the home becomes substantially unusable without the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2715); the lease does not end at the death of either party (La. Civ. Code art. 2717). A tenant who simply leaves stays liable for the rent, subject to your duty to mitigate (see the library's abandonment note).

Month-to-month leases end on the ordinary notice, so early-termination fees do not fit them.

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units opt out of a tenant's rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. Louisiana has no rent escrow program and no such exemption or notice. The tenant's repair remedies come from the Civil Code and apply to every lessor regardless of how many units you own or whether you live in the building: repair and deduct after your failure to make a necessary repair within a reasonable time after demand (La. Civ. Code art. 2694), a rent reduction or dissolution when the property's use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2715), and dissolution for your failure to perform (La. Civ. Code art. 2719). Louisiana's unit-count and owner-occupancy exceptions appear only in other statutes, such as the application-fee notice (only for property to be used as the tenant's primary residence, and not for owner-occupied buildings of no more than four units, La. R.S. 9:3258.1(C)) and the domestic-abuse protections (buildings of six or more dwellings, not ten-or-fewer-unit buildings where the owner or lessor lives, La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A)). Because the Civil Code repair rules can be reallocated by the lease within limits, see the library's repair-allocation and warranty-waiver notes for what you can and cannot change.

title: Evictions for Criminal Activity
bodyText:
Louisiana has no separate fast-track eviction for drug or violent crime, because every eviction already uses the same summary procedure: a notice to vacate of at least five days, not counting weekends and legal holidays (unless the tenant waived it by a written waiver contained in the lease), a hearing as early as the third day after service, a judgment rendered immediately, and a warrant if the tenant has not left within twenty-four hours (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701, 4731-4733). What speeds a criminal-activity case is the lease: the library's optional Criminal Activity clause makes such conduct a default you may act on without giving time to correct it, and the lease may waive the notice to vacate (see the library's waiver clause).

Two statutes add tools.
- Under the domestic abuse statute (buildings of six or more dwellings, not a building of ten or fewer units where the owner or lessor lives in one), you are entitled to an immediate eviction of the abuser on presenting the court with reasonable documentation of the abuse (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (G)).
- Under the street-gang nuisance law, anyone may ask a court to order an owner or lessee to remove or evict persons using premises for a pattern of criminal gang activity, but no injunction or penalty issues against you unless you knew or should have known or were notified, and the suit may be filed only thirty days after notice to you (La. R.S. 15:1405(B), (D), (E)).

The drug and violent-crime nuisance statutes can also reach owners who knowingly permit such activity (see the library's illegal-use note). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Tenants When Your Rental Is Seized and Sold
bodyText: When your rental is seized and sold for your mortgage debt, Louisiana law decides the tenant's fate mainly by recordation. A lease recorded in the parish conveyance records before the mortgage binds the buyer at the sheriff's sale for all its terms (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 2372; La. R.S. 9:2721(B)). An unrecorded lease, or one recorded after the mortgage, has no statutory protection against the buyer (La. Civ. Code arts. 2681.1, 2712); whether it is cut off entirely is a question for the courts. Once the property is seized, the sheriff (or a keeper named in your mortgage) collects the rents, and a keeper must keep providing the services you owe under recorded leases (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 327; La. R.S. 9:5138(B)). For a residential property the sheriff must also serve the occupants a written notice that the property has been seized (or, above ten units, the lender may post a sign instead); without it the buyer cannot use the quick writ of possession against tenants and must evict through the ordinary court process (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 2293(B)(2)-(4); La. R.S. 13:4346). Separately, you must disclose a pending foreclosure before and during the lease and notify tenants within seven days of being served (see the foreclosure-disclosure note). Federal law may give tenants additional protection after a foreclosure. For a month-to-month tenant the buyer may end the tenancy with the ordinary termination notice; a fixed-term tenant under a lease recorded before the mortgage keeps the full term.

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute written for lease guarantors (co-signers). A guarantor is a "surety" under the Civil Code, and the guaranty must be express and in a writing (La. Civ. Code art. 3038). A guarantor who is a private individual, such as a parent, is usually an ordinary surety, and the guaranty is read strictly in the guarantor's favor (La. Civ. Code arts. 3042, 3044). That matters at renewal. When a fixed-term lease reconducts to month to month or is extended, the lease terms continue (La. Civ. Code arts. 2724, 2725), but no Louisiana law says the guarantor's promise continues with it; if the guaranty speaks only of the original lease, assume it does not reach a renewal. If you change the lease in a material way (for example, raise the rent or extend the term) without the guarantor's consent, an ordinary guaranty is extinguished (La. Civ. Code art. 3062). A guarantor may also end the guaranty by notice to you, but stays liable for what the tenant already owed and for obligations you were already bound to let the tenant incur when the notice arrived (La. Civ. Code art. 3061). So: have the guarantor sign a written guaranty that names the lease, says whether it covers renewals, extensions, reconduction and amendments, and states any maximum; get the guarantor's written consent to any renewal or change. A guarantor is liable for the full amount without your first suing the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 3045). Louisiana sets no cap on deposits, from tenants or guarantors.

title: No Homestead or Exemption Waivers in the Lease
bodyText: Some states' lease forms have the tenant waive homestead or property exemptions. Do not put such a waiver in a Louisiana lease. Louisiana's homestead exemption protects up to $35,000 of a home the debtor owns and lives in, so it never covers your rental (La. R.S. 20:1(A)). A homestead waiver is valid only if the owner signs a written waiver, the owner's spouse also signs it if they are married and not legally separated, a copy goes to the homeowner, and it is recorded in the parish mortgage records (La. R.S. 20:1(D)); a sentence in a lease does not meet that. The tenant's household goods, clothing, furniture, appliances, pets and other listed belongings are exempt from seizure under any writ (La. R.S. 13:3881(A)), and the statute gives no way to waive those exemptions in a lease. Your lessor's privilege lets you seize nonexempt belongings in the unit through the court (see the lessor's privilege note). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Early Termination for Illness or Care Moves
bodyText: Louisiana gives tenants no right to end a lease early because of age, illness or disability, or because they must move to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility. Unless the lease gives an exit, a tenant who leaves early stays bound for the rent, subject to your duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent and reduce the loss. A month-to-month tenant may simply give the ordinary termination notice (ten calendar days before the end of a month, in writing). A tenant's death does not end the lease either (La. Civ. Code art. 2717). Louisiana's statutory early-exit rights are narrower: active and reserve service members (including a member hospitalized more than 15 days for a service injury, or killed in service) (La. R.S. 9:3261), victims of domestic abuse, stalking or cyberstalking in buildings of six or more units, except owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer (La. R.S. 9:3261.1), and victims of sexual assault (La. R.S. 9:3261.2). If you choose to give a tenant an early exit in the lease, the tenant still must give at least the notice the Civil Code requires for a periodic lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2718). A tenant with a disability may ask for a reasonable accommodation, such as an early release, under fair housing law.

title: Your Remedies When a Tenant Defaults
bodyText:
When a tenant fails to pay rent or breaks another lease obligation, Louisiana gives you two main paths.
- 1. End the lease and take the property back. You dissolve the lease (by the notice your lease provides, or a notice to perform for defaults other than rent) and then evict through the court (La. Civ. Code arts. 2704, 2013-2017; La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701-4735). You may recover unpaid rent up to dissolution, plus damages for the rent you lose afterward, but you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent and reduce that loss (La. Civ. Code arts. 1995, 2002). For a month-to-month lease that loss cannot run past the date the lease could have been ended by notice.
- 2. Keep the lease in force and collect the rent. You may sue for rent as it comes due and, if your fixed-term lease has an acceleration clause, for all rent for the rest of the term (see the optional Rent Acceleration clause). If you accelerate, the tenant keeps the right to stay; do not also evict for the same unpaid rent.

Louisiana's courts decide how strictly these two paths are kept apart. Either way, unpaid rent bears interest, a written lease may provide for attorney fees in a fixed or determinable amount (La. Civ. Code art. 2000), and an oral lease gives attorney fees only after a 20-day written demand (La. R.S. 9:3259, oral leases only). You also have a privilege on the tenant's nonexempt belongings in the unit, enforced through the court. A suit for back rent must be filed within three years (La. Civ. Code art. 3494).

title: No Statutory Right to Pay and Stay Before Judgment
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that lets a tenant who is behind on rent undo the end of the lease, or stop your eviction case, by paying what is owed before the court rules. If rent is not paid when due you may dissolve the lease and recover possession through the eviction procedure (La. Civ. Code art. 2704), and you may refuse a partial payment (La. Civ. Code art. 1861). Two Civil Code rules can still help a tenant: when a court is asked to dissolve a contract it may give the tenant more time to perform, and a contract may not be dissolved for a minor shortfall when most of the performance has been rendered (La. Civ. Code arts. 2013, 2014). The eviction judge hears any defense the tenant raises (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4732). If the tenant offers the full rent before you have ended the lease and you refuse it without a good reason, the tenant can deposit the money with the court and, if the court finds the offer valid, it counts as paid from the day it was offered (La. Civ. Code arts. 1869-1871). If you accept full payment after giving notice, you may have trouble showing the lease ended; decide before you take the money. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Right to Redeem After an Eviction Judgment
bodyText: Louisiana gives a tenant no statutory right to keep the home by paying what is owed after you win an eviction judgment. If the tenant does not leave within 24 hours of the judgment, the court issues a warrant for the sheriff, constable or marshal to put you in possession (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4733); an appeal stops the eviction only if the tenant answered under oath with a defense and files the appeal and bond within 24 hours (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4735). The judgment stays effective for at least 90 days (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4732(B)). You may refuse a partial payment (La. Civ. Code art. 1861). The tenant may pay money owed into the court registry if you refuse it without good reason (La. Civ. Code arts. 1869-1871), but that settles the debt, not the right to stay after a judgment of eviction. A charity or other third person may pay rent the tenant owes, even over your objection (La. Civ. Code art. 1855), but a rent subsidy application or award is not payment and is not a defense to eviction (La. R.S. 9:3259.2). If you accept full payment after judgment and still intend to evict, say so in writing; whether accepting the money gives up the judgment is a question for the courts. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Agreed (Stipulated) Damages in a Lease
bodyText:
Louisiana allows a lease to fix in advance the damages a tenant owes for a breach or for paying late ("stipulated damages"), and a court may change the agreed amount only if it is so manifestly unreasonable as to be contrary to public policy (La. Civ. Code arts. 2005, 2012). You do not have to prove your actual loss to collect it (La. Civ. Code art. 2009).

Three limits matter:
- 1. No double recovery. You may collect either the agreed damages or the performance they stand for (such as the rent), not both, unless the damages are only for delay, like a late fee (La. Civ. Code art. 2007).
- 2. Damages for delay need the tenant to be in default, which happens automatically when rent is not paid on its fixed due date (La. Civ. Code art. 2010). Agreed damages for nonperformance may be reduced for the part of the lease the tenant did perform (La. Civ. Code art. 2011).
- 3. Statutory exits override the lease. A service member who ends a lease under La. R.S. 9:3261 owes at most one month's rent (half a month after six months), and a victim who ends a lease under the domestic abuse statute (buildings of six or more units, but not owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer) or the sexual assault statute owes rent only through the termination date (La. R.S. 9:3261.1, 9:3261.2).

You may not turn the security deposit into a forfeit; it must be returned less what is reasonably needed to cover the tenant's actual default (La. R.S. 9:3251(A), 9:3254). The one-month return rule does not apply when the tenant abandons the property without the required notice or before the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251(C)); even then, keeping the whole deposit as a penalty is not offered.

The library's late fee and early-termination fee are stipulated damages; a separate fixed sum for every default is not offered.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix and Bill
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute that lets you fix a problem the tenant caused and charge the tenant for it, or add the cost to the rent. The tenant must repair damage caused by the tenant's fault (or that of people the tenant lets in) and wear beyond normal use (La. Civ. Code arts. 2687, 2692). If the tenant does not, your statutory remedies are a court order, damages or ending the lease (La. Civ. Code arts. 1986, 2686), and you may make any repair that cannot wait until the lease ends, even if it inconveniences the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 2693).

Louisiana has no entry statute, so your right to come in to do the work comes from the lease. A lease may give you a contractual right to make the tenant's repairs after notice and bill the reasonable cost; the library's optional Landlord's Right to Correct clause does this and keeps the charge separate from rent. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Self-Help Evictions
bodyText: In Louisiana you may take back a rental home only through the court eviction process: a written notice to vacate (at least five days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, unless the lease contains the tenant's written waiver), a rule to show cause, a judgment of eviction, and a warrant carried out by the sheriff, constable or marshal (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701-4734). Do not change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out. During the lease you must protect the tenant's peaceful possession (La. Civ. Code art. 2682(3)), and in a residential lease you answer for disturbance by people you let onto the property (La. Civ. Code art. 2700); a tenant you lock out can end the lease and sue for damages. The only exception: after giving the required notice, you may take possession without further court process if you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned the property, for example keys returned and belongings removed (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(B)). In a parish under a federal disaster declaration, a tenant's absence is not evidence of abandonment for 30 days after the declaration, and failing to follow the article lets a residential tenant recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, plus an injunction and possibly attorney fees (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)); whether that penalty also applies outside a disaster parish is unsettled, so assume it can. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases. Louisiana has no statute that names lockouts or utility shutoffs (see the lockout note).

title: No Notice Fees
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on charging a tenant a fee for preparing or delivering a notice, such as a notice to vacate. You or your agent deliver the notice yourselves, so there is no officer's fee to pass on before you file (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701). If you file an eviction and win, the court ordinarily makes the losing party pay the court costs (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 1920). The library does not offer a notice-fee clause for Louisiana. For late rent, the Civil Code limits your damages for the delay to interest on the amount owed, plus attorney fees if a written lease sets a fixed or determinable amount (La. Civ. Code art. 2000) or, under an oral lease, reasonable attorney fees if you win after the rent stays unpaid 20 days past a written demand (La. R.S. 9:3259); a separate notice fee is not recoverable on top of that. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Nuisance Suits Against Your Rental
bodyText: Two Louisiana laws let public officials or neighbors sue over criminal activity at your rental, and both can reach you as owner. First, if the property is used for drug dealing, prostitution, obscenity, crimes of violence, illegal weapons offenses or felony theft, public officials or any seven residents of the precinct may sue to stop it. A written notice of violation from the attorney general, district attorney, sheriff or city or parish attorney is treated as proof that you knew; if you knew, the court may order the property closed for five years unless you post a bond (La. R.S. 13:4711-4716; see the illegal-use note). Second, if members of a criminal street gang use the property for a pattern of gang activity, anyone may sue to have them evicted or the property closed, and the court can order you to remove them, seal the property, and later order demolition or sale and a civil penalty of up to $5,000 if you do not comply. A suit cannot be filed until 30 days after you (or your tenant) receive notice of the activity, and you are exposed only if you knew, should have known or were notified (La. R.S. 15:1405). Neither law diverts your rent to the court or ends the lease for you. When you get a notice, act promptly under the lease: misuse and criminal activity let you seek an injunction or dissolve the lease and evict (La. Civ. Code arts. 2686, 2719). Do not end a lease because a tenant or household member was the victim of domestic abuse in a building of six or more units (unless it is owner-occupied with ten or fewer units) (La. R.S. 9:3261.1). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Tenant's Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes say almost nothing about a tenant's belongings after an eviction. When the sheriff, constable or marshal executes the eviction warrant, the officer clears the premises "of any property therein" in front of two witnesses to put you in possession (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4734). No statute sets a storage period, inventory, notice, sale or disposal procedure for what is removed or left behind, and none protects you from liability for it. Because of that, treat belongings as still the tenant's. Property is abandoned only when the owner gives it up intending to give up ownership (La. Civ. Code art. 3418), and pets and other domestic animals cannot be claimed by taking them (La. Civ. Code art. 3417); arrange for animals promptly with the tenant or animal control. If rent is owed, your lessor's privilege lets you seize the tenant's nonexempt movables through the court while they are on the property and for 15 days after removal if they are still the tenant's and can be identified, but not household essentials or pets, which are exempt from seizure (La. Civ. Code arts. 2707, 2710; La. R.S. 13:3881). The careful course is to photograph and list what remains, notify the tenant in writing at the last known and forwarding addresses, and hold the items for a reasonable time before disposing of them. A person who is not a lessee and stays more than five days after a written notice to vacate commits criminal trespass (La. R.S. 14:63(C)). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: Louisiana does not require a tenant to pay rent into court to defend an eviction or to bring a counterclaim, and has no rent-escrow procedure. The eviction rule is heard no earlier than the third day after service, and the judge hears any defense the tenant raises (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4732). To stay in the unit during an appeal, the tenant must have answered under oath with a defense and file the appeal and a bond set by the court within 24 hours of the judgment (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4735). A tenant who has claims against you arising from the same lease may be required to raise them in your case rather than in a later suit (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 1061); whether that applies in a summary eviction is unsettled. If you refuse a tenant's full rent payment without good reason, the tenant can deposit it with the court and, if the court finds the offer valid, it counts as paid from the day it was offered (La. Civ. Code arts. 1869-1871). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Termination Over Repair Costs
bodyText: Louisiana gives neither you nor the tenant a right to end a lease because a repair would be too expensive. Your duty to make necessary repairs during the lease has no cost ceiling (La. Civ. Code art. 2691). What ends or changes a lease is the extent of the damage: if the property is totally destroyed or expropriated without anyone's fault, the lease ends and no one owes damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2714); if it is partly destroyed or its use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may get a rent reduction or end the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2715); and during an urgent repair the tenant may get a rent reduction or dissolution depending on the circumstances (La. Civ. Code art. 2693). If you want the right to end the lease after a serious casualty, the lease must give it to you (see the optional casualty termination clause). A month-to-month lease may be ended by either party with the ordinary notice.

title: No Anti-Retaliation Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no general law against retaliating against a tenant. No statute stops you from ending or not renewing a lease, raising the rent or evicting because the tenant complained to you or to a government agency, asked for repairs, used the tenant's repair-and-deduct right or joined a tenants' group, and there is no presumption of retaliation. During a fixed term you may end the lease only for the tenant's breach or under a right the lease reserves; a month-to-month lease may be ended by either side with the required notice. Some specific rules do apply. Fair housing law makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising fair housing rights (La. R.S. 51:2609). In buildings of six or more units (except owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units), you may not end, refuse to renew or issue a notice to vacate because domestic abuse occurred on the property against a tenant or household member (with a narrow exception where the abuser's continued presence leads to further violence that threatens the property's safety), and the lease may not limit or penalize calling the police or emergency help (La. R.S. 9:3261.1). Parishes and cities may not penalize you, or authorize an eviction, because a tenant called for emergency help (La. R.S. 33:9701). Even without a statute, acting in bad faith can expose you to claims; avoid timing a termination or rent increase right after a complaint.

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals
bodyText: Louisiana has no special rules for seasonal residential leases. A seasonal lease is an ordinary fixed-term lease: write in the start and end dates, and it ends on the end date without notice (La. Civ. Code arts. 2678, 2720). If the tenant stays a week past the end date (one day, if the term was a week or less) and neither you nor the tenant has given notice to vacate or terminate or otherwise objected, the lease is reconducted: month to month if the term was a month or longer, day to day if it was shorter (La. Civ. Code arts. 2721, 2723), so give written notice before the season ends if you need the unit back. If you rent a former one- or two-family home to guests for 29 days or less, Louisiana's short-term rental camera law applies: no hidden or disguised cameras except in common areas (never bedrooms or bathrooms), and only after you post the statute's exact surveillance notice; guests recorded in violation can recover damages, punitive damages and attorney fees (La. R.S. 21:61). Short-term rentals may also need local permits and occupancy-tax registration.

title: Service Members: Early Termination and Eviction Stays
bodyText: Louisiana gives service members two protections on top of federal law. 1. Ending the lease early (La. R.S. 9:3261). An active or reserve member of the U.S. armed forces, including the National Guard and Coast Guard, or the member's spouse, may end a residential lease when the member gets permanent change-of-station orders, or temporary duty orders of more than three months, to go 35 miles or more away; is discharged, released or retires; is ordered into government housing; is offered government housing that was unavailable at signing (if the member told you in writing at signing about a pending request); is hospitalized more than 15 days for a service injury; or is killed in service. The tenant gives written notice with a termination date at least 30 days out (no more than 60 days before departure for orders) and gives you a copy of the orders or other proof before that date. The tenant owes at most one month's rent if fewer than six months of the lease were completed, or half a month's rent after six months, and gets the full deposit back if the lease was otherwise followed. This right cannot be waived in the lease; a violation costs $200 plus other damages. 2. Eviction stays (La. R.S. 29:315). If you operate four or more residential premises and the rental agreement was signed on or after June 29, 2005, a court may (and on the tenant's motion must) stay an eviction for 90 days or adjust the rent when a tenant, or a member of the tenant's immediate family, is on active duty (federal or Louisiana state orders) and that service materially affects the ability to pay. Federal law (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) may give more; this note covers Louisiana law only.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Louisiana has no law that delays an eviction or excuses late rent because a tenant's Social Security, public assistance, voucher or other government payment arrived late. A tenant's application for, or receipt of, rent subsidy is not payment of rent and is not a defense to eviction (La. R.S. 9:3259.2). The eviction judge does hear any defense the tenant raises, and in a case to dissolve a contract a court may give extra time to perform (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4732; La. Civ. Code art. 2013). The one statutory stay is for tenants on active military duty, and only for landlords with four or more rental premises (La. R.S. 29:315). If you take housing vouchers, federal program rules may impose their own requirements. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: When a Tenant May End the Lease Early
bodyText: A Louisiana tenant may end a lease early, whatever the lease says, in these cases: (1) Military: an active or reserve service member (or spouse) with qualifying orders, discharge or retirement, government housing, a service injury with more than 15 days in hospital, or death in service, on at least 30 days' written notice; rent owed is capped at one month (half a month after six months) (La. R.S. 9:3261). (2) Domestic abuse, stalking or cyberstalking: in buildings of six or more units (but not owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units), a victim who gives the required written statements and documentation of abuse within the past 30 days gets an early termination on an agreed date within 30 days (La. R.S. 9:3261.1). (3) Sexual assault: a victim of a sexual assault within the past 60 days, occurring after the lease was signed, who gives the required statements and documentation gets an early termination on an agreed date within 30 days; this applies to every residential lease (La. R.S. 9:3261.2). (4) Destruction or loss of use: the lease ends if the property is totally destroyed or expropriated, and a tenant may get a rent reduction or end the lease after partial destruction or a substantial loss of use that is not the tenant's fault (La. Civ. Code arts. 2714, 2715). (5) Your breach or fraud: a tenant may seek dissolution if you fail to perform your lease obligations (La. Civ. Code art. 2719), or annulment plus damages and attorney fees if you obtained the lease by fraud, including by staying silent about something you had to disclose (La. Civ. Code arts. 1948, 1953, 1958). Leaving a required statement out of the lease does not wipe out rent already owed in Louisiana, though some statutes charge a fixed $200 penalty. A month-to-month tenant may also simply give the ordinary notice.

title: No Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Louisiana has no "tenancy at will." Every lease has a term. If you and the tenant agree on none, including under an oral lease, a lease of a home is month to month (La. Civ. Code arts. 2678-2681), and either side ends it by written notice at least ten calendar days before the end of a month (La. Civ. Code arts. 2728-2729). Someone you let live in the property without any lease (for example, a relative or a caretaker) is an occupant, not a tenant: when the purpose of the stay ends, you give a written notice to vacate with five days to leave (not counting weekends and legal holidays) and then use the eviction procedure if needed (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4702, 4704).

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: Louisiana has no law of its own on what happens to a lease when a tenant files for bankruptcy. Federal bankruptcy law controls: once a case is filed, an automatic stay generally stops eviction filings and collection efforts until the court allows them, and the tenant's lease and deposit are handled under federal rules. Get advice before acting against a tenant in bankruptcy. Louisiana's own exemptions decide what property the tenant keeps (La. R.S. 13:3881(B)(1)), and a guarantor stays liable even if the tenant's debt is discharged in bankruptcy (La. Civ. Code art. 3046). The library does not offer a clause making a tenant's bankruptcy a default. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText:
In Louisiana a lease does not end when a tenant dies (La. Civ. Code art. 2717). The tenant's heirs (or the succession representative, once one is appointed) step into the tenant's place, and rent keeps accruing as a debt of the estate until the lease ends (La. Civ. Code arts. 935, 1415).

A month-to-month lease can be ended by the heirs, the representative or you with the usual written notice ten calendar days before the end of a month; a fixed-term lease runs to its end date unless the lease gives an early-termination right (see the optional Death of Sole Tenant clause). Any authority the tenant gave someone, such as an emergency contact or agent, ends at death (La. Civ. Code art. 3024). Deal only with the succession representative or the heirs.

For estates of $200,000 or less (Louisiana residents), the heirs may use a small succession affidavit, and paying the deposit or handing over belongings to the persons named in it gives you a full release (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 3421, 3431-3434). Return the deposit within one month after the lease ends, less lawful deductions, to the representative or the persons named in the affidavit; the one-month rule does not apply if the tenant abandoned the property without required notice or before the lease ended (La. R.S. 9:3251). Do not dispose of a deceased tenant's belongings yourself; arrange removal with the heirs or representative.

title: Removing Squatters and Other Occupants
bodyText: Louisiana gives you two ways to remove someone living in your property who is not your tenant. Civil: a person who lives there only by permission (for example a former tenant's guest, a relative or a caretaker) is an "occupant." When the reason for the stay has ended, deliver a written notice to vacate giving five days to leave, not counting weekends and legal holidays; if the person stays, file a rule to show cause and get a judgment and warrant as in any eviction (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4702-4704, 4731-4734). A tenant can use the same procedure against someone the tenant let in. Criminal: it is criminal trespass for an occupant to stay more than five days after being served that notice, or for a squatter (someone with no right of possession, ownership, occupancy or lease) to stay after you tell them to leave orally, in writing, or by posting a conspicuous "private property, no trespassing" sign; the police can enforce it (La. R.S. 14:63(C)). A person with real authority to be there has a defense, so do not use the trespass law against a tenant or anyone claiming under a lease; a tenant must be evicted through the court.

title: Accepting Rent After a Default or Notice
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute that makes you give up a default, a notice to vacate or an eviction by accepting rent, and none that forbids a lease clause saying acceptance is not a waiver. The library's late-fee clause has such a sentence, and the optional Acceptance of Payments clause extends it to payments taken after a notice or during an eviction.

But Louisiana courts can still find that you gave up a right by your conduct (the Civil Code recognizes tacit remission of a debt, La. Civ. Code art. 1888), so be careful:
- (1) If you intend to end the lease or evict, put it in writing before or when you accept any money, and say the payment is accepted without waiving the notice or the eviction. A written notice to vacate or other objection also keeps a fixed-term lease from renewing month to month when the tenant stays past the end date (La. Civ. Code art. 2721).
- (2) You may refuse a partial payment, except that if the tenant disputes part of what you claim and offers the undisputed part, you must take that part, keeping your claim to the rest (La. Civ. Code art. 1861).
- (3) The tenant may choose which debt a payment covers; otherwise the Civil Code's order applies, starting with debts already due (La. Civ. Code arts. 1864-1868).
- (4) A rent subsidy application or award is not payment and is no defense to eviction (La. R.S. 9:3259.2).

The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Minors in Leases and Evictions
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on naming minors in an eviction. Name every adult tenant who signed the lease (and any other adult occupant) as a defendant; the eviction is brought against the lessee or occupant, and when the sheriff, constable or marshal executes the warrant the premises are cleared so you get possession (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4731, 4734). A minor cannot be sued in his own name: a claim against an unemancipated minor is brought against the parent or tutor (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 732). Renting to a minor: majority is 18 (La. Civ. Code art. 29). A lease signed by an unemancipated minor can be undone by the minor, unless it was for something necessary for the minor's support or education, or the minor's business, or you reasonably relied on the minor's claim to be an adult (La. Civ. Code arts. 1918, 1923, 1924). A fully emancipated minor can contract like an adult (La. Civ. Code art. 1922). If you rent to someone under 18, have a parent or other adult sign as a co-tenant or guarantor. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: How Notices Must Be Given
bodyText: Louisiana has no "actual notice" rule that lets you and the tenant add your own way of giving legal notices, such as text messages, beyond the electronic-delivery rules below. A notice ending a lease of a home must be in writing (La. Civ. Code art. 2729); a tenant who moves out and hands back possession by the date notice is due has given notice by doing so. A notice to vacate must be written and delivered to the tenant, or attached to a door if the unit is abandoned or closed or you cannot find the tenant (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701, 4703). You may agree with the tenant to use e-mail or other electronic messages; between parties who have agreed, an electronic record the recipient can keep satisfies a rule requiring a writing (so a tenant's e-mailed termination notice can count), but either side may later refuse to continue electronically, a message the recipient cannot save or print does not bind the recipient, and Louisiana's electronic transactions law does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a tenant's primary residence, so deliver those on paper (La. R.S. 9:2603, 9:2605, 9:2607, 9:2608). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Automatic Renewal and Reconduction
bodyText:
A Louisiana fixed-term lease ends on its end date without notice. If the tenant stays a week past that date and neither of you has given notice or objected, the lease renews month to month on the same terms (La. Civ. Code arts. 2720-2724). A lease may instead renew itself for a longer period, or give the tenant an option to extend (La. Civ. Code art. 2725), but then two consumer laws may apply.

Now: if a contract with a consumer renews automatically unless the consumer cancels, you must disclose the automatic renewal clearly and conspicuously in the contract and say clearly how to cancel; if you do not, the renewal shrinks to a 30-day renewal on the same terms (La. R.S. 9:2716). The law does not apply when the tenant can cancel by written notice within 30 days or one month after the initial term ends (for example, a lease that converts to month to month). Whether this law reaches home leases is not settled, so comply.

From January 1, 2027: Louisiana's Click-to-Cancel Act (2026 Act 830) adds rules for businesses with both 50 or more employees and $5 million or more in annual revenue (counting affiliates): conspicuous renewal terms next to the signature, the tenant's affirmative consent, a copy of the terms the tenant can keep, an easy way to cancel online, by e-mail or by phone, and a notice at least 3 days before a renewal of 12 months or more or a renewal at a higher price. The Act defines merchandise to include real estate, but whether it reaches residential leases is not settled.

The library's optional Automatic Renewal clause is drafted to meet both laws.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Leases
bodyText:
Louisiana has no law written for arbitration clauses in residential leases. Its general Binding Arbitration Law makes a written agreement to arbitrate future disputes valid and enforceable, except on the grounds that would undo any contract, and a court must pause a lawsuit on an arbitrable issue if a party asks (La. R.S. 9:4201, 9:4202).

No statute says whether an eviction must stay in court despite an arbitration clause, and courts may scrutinize an arbitration clause a tenant had no real chance to negotiate. An arbitration clause that reached possession could delay your own fast summary eviction, so keep eviction out of any clause. If you use one anyway, exclude eviction and possession actions and small money claims, and have a lawyer review it.

The library now offers an optional clause, "Binding Arbitration of Money Claims" clause, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: Domestic Abuse Law Citations Check
bodyText: Louisiana's lease protections for survivors of domestic abuse, stalking, cyberstalking and sexual assault (La. R.S. 9:3261.1, for buildings of six or more units other than owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units; and La. R.S. 9:3261.2, for all residential leases) borrow definitions from the criminal code and the victims' and protective-order laws. Those laws have not been moved or renumbered: domestic abuse battery and "household member" are still in La. R.S. 14:35.3, stalking and cyberstalking in La. R.S. 14:40.2 and 14:40.3, and the protective order a tenant may show you is still the court's "Uniform Abuse Prevention Order" (La. R.S. 46:2136.2). The sexual-assault statute's references (sexual assault centers and advocates, forensic medical examinations, sex offenses and victims) also still point to the right sections. Some of those sections were amended in 2026, which does not change how you apply the lease statutes; one victim-definition section in Title 46 was amended by 2026 acts not yet reflected in the published code. Accept the documents the statutes list (a completed certification form signed by a qualified third party, or a Uniform Abuse Prevention Order). This check did not cover court forms or case law.

title: No Emergency Contact Law
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour phone number, to post a contact, or to put the owner's or manager's name and address in the lease. The tenant must tell you without delay when the property is damaged or needs repair (La. Civ. Code art. 2688), and you may make urgent repairs (La. Civ. Code art. 2693), so give the tenant a reliable way to reach you, including after hours, and an address for notices and rent; if you give no address, rent is payable at the tenant's address (La. Civ. Code art. 2703). Some cities or parishes may have their own posting or registration rules. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring building energy benchmarking or governing the release of a tenant's energy usage data to you, and none that lets a lease clause authorize it. Whether a utility will give you a tenant's usage data is up to the utility's rules and the Louisiana Public Service Commission; if you need it, ask the tenant to sign the utility's own consent form. Check whether your city has a benchmarking program.

title: No Informal Dispute Resolution Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no law on lease clauses that require informal talks or mediation before going to court. A court may refer a civil case to mediation on a party's motion, but any party can cancel the referral by objecting within 15 days (La. R.S. 9:4103). The library does not offer an informal-resolution clause for Louisiana because it would add a step before your summary eviction; you can still offer to talk or mediate in any dispute. The Civil Code already builds in some pre-suit steps: the tenant must tell you promptly about needed repairs, and must ask you to repair before making a repair and deducting it from rent (La. Civ. Code arts. 2688, 2694). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Statewide Landlord Registration
bodyText: Louisiana has no statewide landlord registration or rental licensing law. No landlord-tenant statute requires you to register with the state, the parish or the assessor, makes registration a condition of evicting, gives tenants a right to leave if you are unregistered, or requires an out-of-state owner to hire a Louisiana broker. Two general business rules can still apply. An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business here must first get a certificate of authority from the secretary of state, and until it is authorized it may not present any judicial demand, an eviction included, in a Louisiana court; its leases stay valid (La. R.S. 12:301, 12:314, 12:1342, 12:1354). Acquiring property not as part of a regular business activity is not transacting business, so whether renting out property counts depends on the facts (La. R.S. 12:302(J), 12:1343(10)). And if you, as an individual, rent under a name other than your own real name, you must first file an assumed-name certificate with the clerk of court of each parish where you do business (in New Orleans, the register of conveyances); a violation is a misdemeanor, and each day is a separate offense (La. R.S. 51:281, 51:284). If you lease or manage your own property, directly or through your employees, you do not need a real estate license (La. R.S. 37:1438(A)(1), (A)(5)); a company that manages other people's rentals for them generally does (La. R.S. 37:1437). Some Louisiana cities and parishes have their own rental registration, licensing or inspection programs; check local ordinances.

title: No Lockouts or Utility Shutoffs for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that lets you lock out a tenant, change the locks, remove doors or shut off utilities because rent is late, and a lease clause cannot give you that right. When rent is unpaid you may end the lease, but you regain possession only "in the manner provided by law": a written notice to vacate (unless the tenant waived it in a written waiver contained in the lease) and a court eviction (La. Civ. Code art. 2704; La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701-4734). Until then you must keep protecting the tenant's peaceful possession and keep the property suitable for living (La. Civ. Code art. 2682). The only time you may retake the unit without court is after the required notice, when you reasonably believe the tenant has abandoned it (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(B)); in a parish under a federal disaster declaration, absence alone is not abandonment for 30 days. A lessor who fails to comply with that article owes a residential tenant $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater; the penalty sits in the disaster paragraph, but its words are not limited to disasters, so assume it can apply anywhere (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)). Louisiana allows lock-outs only in other settings, such as self-storage units and abandoned factory-built homes on rented lots; those statutes do not apply to a home you rent out. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Louisiana has no end-of-term possession bond: nothing lets a tenant post a bond at move-in, backed by an agreed (confessed) judgment, so that you can retake the unit without an eviction case. To recover possession you use the written notice to vacate (which the tenant may waive only by a written waiver contained in the lease) and the court's summary eviction procedure (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701, 4731-4734). The only bond in that process is the tenant's: a tenant who wants to appeal and stay in the unit must answer under oath with a defense and file the appeal and bond within 24 hours of the judgment (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4735). Louisiana's confession of judgment works only for enforcing mortgages and privileges by seizure and sale, not for getting a rental back (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 2631-2632). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Blank-Space Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in before signing, and no rule that a blank is a breach by you. Fill in or strike every blank anyway, because Louisiana law decides what a blank means, and usually against you. The rent must be a sum certain or determinable by an agreed method; if it is neither, there is no lease (La. Civ. Code arts. 2668, 2676). If the length of the lease is left blank, the law makes it month to month (La. Civ. Code art. 2680). Any doubt about a term in your own standard form is resolved in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). Required disclosures, such as a pending foreclosure (La. R.S. 9:3260.1) or, in a written lease a real estate licensee executes (entered on or after January 1, 2002), the sex offender database notice (La. R.S. 37:1469), must actually appear in the lease.

title: No Lease Copy Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and no rule that failing to give one keeps you from enforcing the lease or evicting. A lease may even be oral (La. Civ. Code art. 2681). Give every tenant a fully signed copy anyway: it is your best proof of the terms, any doubt in your own form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056), and an electronic lease sent in a way that keeps the tenant from storing or printing it is not enforceable against the tenant (La. R.S. 9:2608(C)). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Louisiana statute requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term, including a notice period longer than the law's, for it to bind the tenant; the signatures on the lease are enough as far as the statutes go. Two terms still need special care. A waiver of your warranty against defects works only if its language is clear and unambiguous and is brought to the tenant's attention (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); having the tenant initial it beside the clause is good evidence of that, though the law does not require initials. If the lease lets either side end it early, the notice is the longer of the lease's period or the Civil Code's (ten calendar days before the end of a month for a month-to-month lease), and the right to that notice cannot be given up in advance (La. Civ. Code arts. 2718, 2728). Louisiana's only lease-initials rule is for self-service storage units, not homes (La. R.S. 9:4758.1).

title: Lease Length Limits
bodyText: Louisiana sets no minimum length for a residential lease and a maximum of 99 years; a longer term, or an option that could extend it past 99 years, is cut back to 99 years (La. Civ. Code art. 2679). A term is fixed when the lease ends on a set date or on a stated event (La. Civ. Code art. 2678). If the length is left blank, or depends only on your will or only on the tenant's with no agreed maximum, the lease is month to month (La. Civ. Code arts. 2679, 2680). An oral lease can be for any length, but a lease of a home binds a buyer or other third person only once it is filed in the parish conveyance records (La. Civ. Code art. 2681.1).

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Louisiana sets no minimum type size for a residential lease, and no statute makes small print in a lease unenforceable. Two terms still have to stand out. A waiver of your warranty against defects works only if its language is clear and unambiguous and brought to the tenant's attention (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). If your lease renews automatically, the renewal clause and how to cancel must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously (La. R.S. 9:2716). Print the whole lease in a readable size and put waivers and renewal terms in bold or capitals; any doubt about your own form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056).

title: No Agent Rule for Out-of-State Individual Owners
bodyText: Louisiana does not require an individual owner who lives out of state to name a Louisiana agent in the lease or with any state office before renting or suing, and no state statute requires a tenant or manager to withhold Louisiana income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. Owning rental property here is enough for Louisiana courts to hear claims arising from it (La. R.S. 13:3201(A)(5)). If a tenant sues you and cannot serve you or an agent for service of process, the court appoints an attorney to represent you and the case goes forward against that attorney (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 5091), so it is in your interest to give tenants a reliable address and the name of your local manager. An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation is different: one transacting business in Louisiana must first get a certificate of authority from the secretary of state, an authorized foreign corporation must keep a registered agent here, and until it is authorized it may not present any judicial demand, an eviction included, in a Louisiana court, though its leases stay valid (La. R.S. 12:301, 12:308(A), 12:314, 12:1342, 12:1354). Acquiring property not as part of a regular business activity does not count as transacting business (La. R.S. 12:302(J), 12:1343(10)), so whether renting out property does depends on the facts; get the certificate before you need to file. If the parish or city condemns an unsafe building, its notice may go to your agent, the occupants or an attorney appointed for an absent owner (La. R.S. 33:4765).

title: How to Deliver Notices
bodyText:
Louisiana lets you or your agent deliver a notice to vacate yourself; it must be in writing and delivered to the tenant, and no sheriff or process server is needed for the notice (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701). If the unit is abandoned or closed, or you cannot find the tenant, you may attach notices to a door of the unit instead (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4703). A notice ending a lease of a home must be in writing (La. Civ. Code art. 2729).

E-mail and other electronic notices work only if you and the tenant agreed to deal electronically, the tenant can stop at any time, and a message the tenant cannot save or print does not bind the tenant (La. R.S. 9:2605, 9:2608). The electronic transactions law does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a tenant's primary residence, or notices of utility shutoff, so deliver those on paper (La. R.S. 9:2603). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Move-Out Form Rules
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule about the move-out or notice-to-vacate form you may ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep the form to what the tenant's notice needs: the move-out date and a forwarding address, which the tenant must give you for the deposit statement (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)). A tenant's notice ending a lease of a home must be in writing, and a tenant who hands back possession on time has given notice by doing so (La. Civ. Code art. 2729). A new term slipped into a move-out form binds the tenant only if the tenant actually agreed to it (La. Civ. Code arts. 1927, 2726), and any doubt in your form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056), so put any new deal, such as an early-release charge, in a separate signed amendment. The same applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Where Louisiana Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Most Louisiana lease rules are defaults: your lease may choose differently, and a silent lease takes the default, often against you. The lease decides: when and where rent is due (otherwise at the start of each rental period, at the address you give) (La. Civ. Code art. 2703); how long the lease lasts (otherwise month to month) (La. Civ. Code art. 2680); who pays taxes and charges on the property (otherwise you, except charges from the tenant's use) (La. Civ. Code art. 2689); which repairs the tenant makes, and whether the tenant takes responsibility for the condition of the premises (La. Civ. Code art. 2691; La. R.S. 9:3221); what happens to tenant improvements at the end (La. Civ. Code art. 2695); whether the tenant may sublease or assign (allowed unless the lease expressly forbids it) (La. Civ. Code art. 2713); whether co-tenants are each liable for the whole rent (only if the lease clearly says so) (La. Civ. Code art. 1796); interest and attorney fees (fees only if the written lease fixes them or a way to compute them) (La. Civ. Code art. 2000); whether the lease ends automatically on a stated default (La. Civ. Code art. 2017); whether the tenant waives the five-day notice to vacate (only by a written waiver in the lease) (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701); whether you limit your warranty against defects (clear language brought to the tenant's attention, never for defects that seriously affect health or safety) (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); and whether either side may end the lease early (La. Civ. Code art. 2718). A lease cannot override a law that protects the public interest (La. Civ. Code art. 7).

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Louisiana has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases, no readability test, and no required statement listing the rights a tenant gives up under the lease. Plain wording still protects you, because Louisiana reads unclear terms against the landlord: any doubt about your own standard form is resolved in the tenant's favor, and doubt caused by an explanation you should have given is resolved against you (La. Civ. Code arts. 2056, 2057). A waiver of your warranty against defects works only in clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention (La. Civ. Code art. 2699).

title: No Renter's Insurance Rules
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute on renter's insurance in residential leases. You may require the tenant to carry renter's insurance as an ordinary lease term, and no state rule lets the tenant pick the carrier, sets a proof deadline, governs coverage you buy when the tenant does not, caps an administrative fee, or requires a written statement that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings or a flood-risk notice before signing. Say plainly in the lease that your insurance does not cover the tenant's property.

Insurance terms cannot be used to excuse you in advance for intentional or gross fault, or for physical injury you cause; those clauses are null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). The tenant answers for damage the tenant or the tenant's guests cause, and the tenant's policy is the usual source for it (La. Civ. Code art. 2687).

The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Tenant's Insurance Does Not Shift Your Repairs
bodyText:
You may require renter's insurance (see the shared tenant's-property-insurance clause), but a tenant's policy does not shift your repair duty: you must make the repairs needed to keep the home suitable, except damage the tenant or the tenant's guests caused (La. Civ. Code arts. 2691, 2692). Nothing in Louisiana law lets you send those repairs to the tenant's insurer first.

The library does not offer a clause releasing you from all liability for the tenant's belongings: Louisiana voids any advance release for intentional or gross fault or for physical injury (La. Civ. Code art. 2004), and a waiver of your warranty against defects does not cover defects you knew or should have known of, or defects that seriously affect health or safety in a residential lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). The limited warranty waiver the library offers separately is the lawful way to narrow that warranty. See also the row on tenant insurance claims.

The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: Selling a rented home does not end the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2711). The buyer is not bound by your lease obligations unless it assumes them (La. Civ. Code art. 2712), but a buyer takes subject to a lease recorded in the parish conveyance records before the buyer's own rights (La. Civ. Code art. 2681.1; La. R.S. 9:2721(B)); if the buyer does not take over the lease, you stay liable to the tenant for any loss the transfer causes (La. Civ. Code art. 2711). The usual approach is to assign your rights in the lease to the buyer, which you may do (La. Civ. Code art. 2713). Tell the tenant in writing, because an assignment binds the tenant only once the tenant knows of it, and rent paid to you before then counts (La. Civ. Code arts. 2643, 2644). Transfer the security deposits to the buyer; that releases you and makes the buyer responsible for returning them (La. R.S. 9:3251(B)). No statute requires a notice when you change property managers, but tell tenants where to pay rent and send notices. The library does not offer a clause letting you end the lease because you sell: a lease may reserve a right to end it early (La. Civ. Code art. 2718), but in 2026 the Legislature removed the words in art. 2711 that let the parties agree otherwise, so whether a sale-termination clause works is unsettled. If you want one, add your own clause and take advice first. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases, except that a buyer who takes over a month-to-month lease may end it with the usual notice (ten calendar days before the end of a month).

title: Building and Business Size Thresholds
bodyText: A few Louisiana rules depend on the size of your building, portfolio or business, and each exemption needs every condition it lists. (1) The domestic abuse and stalking protections apply only in buildings of six or more units, and not in a building of ten or fewer units where you or the lessor live in one of them; a seven- to ten-unit building with no owner in residence is covered (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A)). (2) The application-fee notice applies to every rental of a tenant's primary residence except an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units (La. R.S. 9:3258.1(C)). (3) Louisiana's fair housing law exempts an individual who owns no more than three single-family houses and rents one without a broker or discriminatory advertising, and an owner who lives in a building of four or fewer units; anyone who owns a building for five or more families is treated as in the rental business, and the ban on discriminatory advertising always applies (La. R.S. 51:2604). (4) From January 1, 2027, Louisiana's Click-to-Cancel Act (2026 Act 830, adding automatic-renewal and cancellation rules) does not apply to a business with fewer than 50 employees or less than $5 million in annual revenue, counting affiliates, so it reaches only businesses over both lines. (5) The court-ordered eviction stay for a tenant on active military duty applies only to landlords and park operators operating four or more residential premises, and only to rental agreements made on or after June 29, 2005 (La. R.S. 29:315). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Oral Leases and Recording
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute of frauds for leases: a residential lease may be oral or written, for any length up to 99 years (La. Civ. Code arts. 2679, 2681). Writing matters in three ways.
