First, a lease binds a buyer, mortgage lender or other third person only after it, or a signed notice of lease giving the parties, property, date, term and any renewal or purchase options, is filed in the parish conveyance records (La. Civ. Code arts. 2681.1, 3338; La. R.S. 9:2742). This is a recording rule; an unrecorded lease still binds you and the tenant. Second, some terms work only in writing: the tenant's waiver of the five-day notice to vacate must be a written waiver in the lease (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701), and contractual attorney fees need a written contract (La. Civ. Code art. 2000). Third, a promise to sign a lease later is enforceable once you agree on the property and the rent, unless you both understood nothing was binding until it was in writing, so say so in any pre-lease paperwork if that is your intent (La. Civ. Code art. 2670). The same applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: State-Prescribed Wording
bodyText: Louisiana has no statutory lease form you must use. It prescribes wording only for three side documents. (1) If your rental is seized in a foreclosure, your written notice to tenants (due within seven days of service) must name the court, case name and docket number and include the statute's statement that it is not a notice to vacate and that rent is still owed (La. R.S. 9:3260.1). (2) A tenant claiming domestic abuse, stalking or cyberstalking protection may use the Certification of Domestic Abuse form set out in the statute; this law applies only in buildings of six or more units, and not in owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer (La. R.S. 9:3261.1). (3) A tenant ending a lease after a sexual assault may use the certification form set out in that statute (La. R.S. 9:3261.2). Other notices have required contents but no set wording: the sex offender database notice in written leases a real estate licensee executes (entered on or after January 1, 2002) (La. R.S. 37:1469) and the application-fee notice (La. R.S. 9:3258.1), which applies to rentals of a tenant's primary residence except owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Tenant Portal Law
bodyText: Louisiana has no law on tenant portals. You may make an online portal the agreed way to pay rent (no statute requires you to take cash, checks or another paper option) and may sign the lease electronically if the tenant agrees to do business electronically (La. R.S. 9:2605). Three limits apply. A tenant who agreed to use electronic records may refuse to handle later transactions, such as a renewal or amendment, electronically, and a lease cannot take that right away (La. R.S. 9:2605(C)). A document the tenant cannot save or print does not bind the tenant (La. R.S. 9:2608). Notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a tenant's primary residence are outside the electronic transactions law, so deliver them on paper even if the portal also posts them (La. R.S. 9:2603). Do not add a fee for paying by debit card through the portal (see the debit-card surcharge note). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Rent Ledger Duty
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring you to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a payment history on request, or attach one to a nonpayment notice or eviction filing. Keep one anyway: in an eviction for nonpayment you must prove what is owed. Two record duties do exist. If you keep any part of a deposit, you must send an itemized statement of what you kept and why within one month after the tenancy ends, or within fifteen days after that month (La. R.S. 9:3251(A)). Under an oral lease, attorney fees for unpaid rent are recoverable only after a written demand that correctly states the rent owed (La. R.S. 9:3259). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Protecting Applicant and Tenant Data
bodyText: If you keep applicants' or tenants' Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers or bank and card account numbers electronically, Louisiana's data breach law applies to you. You must use reasonable security procedures to protect that information, destroy records you no longer keep by shredding or erasing them so they cannot be read, and, after a breach, notify each affected Louisiana resident within 60 days of discovering it, unless a reasonable investigation shows no reasonable likelihood of harm, in which case keep your written finding for five years (La. R.S. 51:3073, 51:3074). A violation is an unfair trade practice, and a person harmed by late notice may sue for actual damages (La. R.S. 51:3074(J), 51:3075). The law says it takes effect only once the attorney general issues rules (La. R.S. 51:3077); check those rules for added details such as notice to the attorney general. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Changing Lease Terms Mid-Tenancy
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute letting you change a lease term by notice, and no special notice for raising a fee the lease already sets or for new house rules. A change binds the tenant only if the tenant agrees to it; an agreed amendment does not create a new lease (La. Civ. Code arts. 1927, 2726). For a month-to-month lease, if the tenant will not agree, you may end the lease with written notice at least ten calendar days before the end of a month and offer a new lease on the new terms, for any term, not just rent (La. Civ. Code arts. 2728, 2729). For a fixed-term lease, the terms stay as written until the term ends unless the lease itself provides for the change, such as a stated rent schedule or a rule-change clause. See the note on raising rent for timing at the end of a fixed term.

title: No Sunset on Tenant Laws
bodyText: None of Louisiana's core residential lease laws is set to expire. The Civil Code lease articles, the lease statutes in Title 9 (deposits, application-fee notice, foreclosure notice, military and abuse-victim protections) and the eviction articles of the Code of Civil Procedure have no sunset dates. They change only when the legislature amends them, as it did in 2026 for deposit statements, domestic abuse protections and several lease articles, so check for amendments each year.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Louisiana has no law requiring you to provide a lease, or a translation of it, in a language other than English, even if you advertise or negotiate in another language. If you negotiate in a tenant's language, consider giving a translation for reference, because Louisiana reads doubtful terms in your own form in the tenant's favor, and doubt caused by an explanation you should have given is resolved against you (La. Civ. Code arts. 2056, 2057); and a tenant who misunderstood a term may in some cases claim that error vitiated his consent, if the misunderstanding concerned something without which he would not have agreed and you knew or should have known it (La. Civ. Code arts. 1948, 1949). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Several Louisiana notices must be in writing, and your lease should not suggest that a spoken notice will do. In writing: a notice ending a lease of a home, from you or the tenant (although a tenant who hands back possession on time has given notice) (La. Civ. Code art. 2729); your notice to vacate (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701); your itemized statement of deposit deductions, a right the lease cannot waive (La. R.S. 9:3251, 9:3254); the tenant's demand for the deposit (La. R.S. 9:3252); your foreclosure disclosure and seizure notice (La. R.S. 9:3260.1); the application-fee notice for rentals of a tenant's primary residence, except owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units (La. R.S. 9:3258.1); your rent demand under an oral lease (La. R.S. 9:3259); a service member's termination notice (La. R.S. 9:3261); a domestic abuse or stalking victim's request in buildings of six or more units, except owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer (La. R.S. 9:3261.1), and a sexual assault victim's request (La. R.S. 9:3261.2); and your certified-mail notice before keeping a tenant's improvements (La. Civ. Code art. 2695). The tenant's report of damage or needed repairs is not required to be written, but ask for it in writing (La. Civ. Code art. 2688). The only written notice a lease may give up is the five-day notice to vacate, through a written waiver in the lease (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Animals Left in a Rental
bodyText: Louisiana gives you no special right to enter a rental to check on, feed or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. Your entry right comes from the lease. Abandoning an animal without arranging its care, or failing to give an animal in one's charge proper food, water, shelter or care, is criminal cruelty (La. R.S. 14:102, 14:102.1), so if you find an animal left without care, call local animal control rather than keeping or disposing of it yourself. To plan ahead, use the optional clause in which the tenant names someone you may let in to care for or remove the animal if the tenant cannot. That authority ends if the tenant dies (La. Civ. Code art. 3024); then deal with the tenant's heirs or succession representative. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give a tenant with a dog or cat a state fact sheet on pets and eviction, or any other pet disclosure. Two rules still matter if a tenancy with pets ends badly. Pets are exempt from seizure, so you cannot take a tenant's dog, cat or other household pet under your lessor's privilege for unpaid rent (La. R.S. 13:3881(A)(4)(f)). And abandoning an animal is a crime, so if a tenant leaves or is evicted and a pet is left behind, contact the tenant and local animal control rather than keeping or disposing of the animal yourself (La. R.S. 14:102.1). These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute on pet fees, so the general rules decide. A refundable pet deposit is a security deposit: hold it with the rest of the deposit, return it within one month after the lease ends less only what is reasonably needed to fix the tenant's default or unreasonable wear, and send an itemized statement of anything you keep; the lease cannot waive these rules (La. R.S. 9:3251, 9:3254). There is no cap on deposits.

Monthly pet rent is simply part of the rent, so state it as a fixed amount (La. Civ. Code arts. 2675, 2676). You cannot make a pet deposit nonrefundable; if you charge a one-time fee, tie it to a service you actually provide and do not hold it as security (whether a court would treat a flat pet fee as a disguised deposit is unsettled).

Never charge pet rent, a pet deposit or other extra charge for a service dog; the tenant is still liable for damage the dog causes (La. R.S. 46:1954(C)), and fair housing law treats other assistance animals the same way. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Pet Rules Are Set by Your Lease
bodyText: Louisiana has no pet law for rentals: your lease decides whether pets are allowed, which ones, and on what terms, and a violation is a lease default you handle like any other. Louisiana law gives tenants no right to keep pets, including in senior housing (federal rules for some assisted housing are separate). Do not remove or hold a tenant's pet yourself: household pets are exempt from seizure, so even your lessor's privilege for unpaid rent cannot reach them (La. R.S. 13:3881(A)(4)(f)), and you must protect the tenant's peaceful possession during the lease and regain the unit only through the court eviction process (La. Civ. Code art. 2682; La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701-4734). Service dogs and other assistance animals are not pets. These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Penalty for Refusing a Service Dog
bodyText: Refusing a tenant or applicant with a disability the use of a trained service dog in housing is a crime in Louisiana. A person with a disability who has a service dog (including one in training) is entitled to full and equal access to housing offered for rent, may not be charged extra for the dog, and is liable for any damage the dog does to the premises or to people there (La. R.S. 46:1954(C)); the only exception is a single-family home whose occupants rent out no more than one room (La. R.S. 46:1952(1)). If you or your agent deny, threaten, punish or otherwise interfere with that right, you face a fine of $100 to $500, up to six months in jail, or both, plus the tenant's actual economic losses and possibly attorney fees (La. R.S. 46:1956). Fair housing law separately covers emotional-support and other assistance animals. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Service and Support Animal Misrepresentation
bodyText: Louisiana penalizes service and support animal misrepresentation in housing. It is unlawful to misrepresent an animal as a service dog or service dog in training to the owner or operator of a residential dwelling, or to claim a disability-related need for a support animal that one does not have (La. R.S. 46:1974(C), 46:1975). A healthcare provider may write a support-animal letter only after a therapeutic relationship of at least 30 days, at least two sessions and a clinical evaluation, and the letter must show its effective date and the provider's license number and type (La. R.S. 46:1974(A)), so you may look for those items when you review a letter. Violations carry fines of up to $500 for a first offense, $1,000 for a second and $2,500 after that (La. R.S. 46:1977). The law does not reduce a tenant's fair housing right to a reasonable accommodation (La. R.S. 46:1978), so handle every request under fair housing rules, and do not treat a letter's missing details alone as grounds to deny without reviewing the request; the statute gives you no lawsuit of your own and no immunity for injuries. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Towing From Your Property
bodyText:
Louisiana's private-property towing law covers apartment and housing complexes. Before you have any vehicle towed:
- (1) post signs at every entrance and exit warning that unauthorized vehicles may be towed, naming the towing company with its address and phone number in letters at least two inches tall, and also mark any reserved or restricted spaces where towing applies; from August 1, 2026, the signs must be ones approved by the Louisiana State Police Towing and Recovery Unit under its rules;
- (2) sign a written contract with the towing company that states your parking rules and the reasons for towing, keep a copy at your business office, and renew it every year, because from August 1, 2026 these contracts expire each June 13 (La. R.S. 32:1736; 2026 La. Acts No. 440).

If you meet those requirements, you need not tag the vehicle or sign the tow bill before the tow; otherwise a tow needs police authorization or a dated removal tag signed by you or your manager. Towing fees are set by the Public Service Commission, and in parishes of 300,000 or more people they cannot exceed the local government's own towing fee (La. R.S. 32:1733).

Write your lease's parking rules to match your towing contract, because the law lets you tow only unauthorized vehicles, and a tenant's own car is unauthorized only as your posted rules and contract define. Booting is regulated separately (La. R.S. 32:1741). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Vehicle Damage and Theft
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute on parking in residential leases, so your lease and parking rules control where tenants park (see the shared parking clause and the towing note).

Be careful about promising or disclaiming security. You are generally not responsible for theft or vandalism of a tenant's vehicle by strangers who claim no right in the property (La. Civ. Code art. 2702), but in a residential lease you do answer for disturbance by people you let onto the property, such as staff and contractors, or by occupants of your adjacent property (La. Civ. Code art. 2700). A lease clause cannot excuse you in advance for intentional or gross fault, or for physical injury (La. Civ. Code art. 2004), and a waiver of your warranty against defects (for example a collapsing carport) does not cover defects you knew or should have known of, or defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). For that reason the library does not offer a broad release of liability for vehicle damage.

These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Storage Space Leased With the Home
bodyText:
A storage space you lease with the home is part of the leased property; Louisiana's self-storage law, with its lien-and-sale procedure, applies only to facilities designed and used to rent storage space, and does not allow residential use (La. R.S. 9:4757). So you cannot sell a tenant's stored goods under the self-storage procedure.

Your security for unpaid rent is the ordinary lessor's privilege on the tenant's belongings in the leased property, including the storage space, which you enforce only through the court, and exempt items such as household furniture and clothing cannot be seized (La. Civ. Code arts. 2707, 2710; La. R.S. 13:3881). A lease clause cannot excuse you in advance for intentional or gross fault or physical injury, and a warranty waiver does not cover defects you knew or should have known of (La. Civ. Code arts. 2004, 2699), so the library does not offer a broad release for damage to stored items.

These rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right
bodyText: Louisiana gives tenants no right to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental, and no law limits your choice to refuse or to set conditions. If you allow one, put the terms in writing: the optional EV charger clause covers your consent, licensed installation and permits, insurance, who pays for the electricity, and what happens to the charger when the lease ends. Without such terms, the Civil Code's default rules on tenant improvements apply at the end of the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2695). If you resell electricity to a tenant for charging, check the Public Service Commission's rules first. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: EV Chargers When the Lease Ends
bodyText: Louisiana has no special rule for a tenant's electric vehicle charger at the end of a lease; the general rules for tenant improvements apply unless your lease says otherwise. The tenant may remove the charger and must restore the property; if the tenant leaves it, you may keep it by paying the lesser of its cost or the value it adds, or demand that the tenant remove it and restore the property within a reasonable time, and if the tenant does not, remove it at the tenant's expense or keep it without payment after a further certified-mail notice (La. Civ. Code art. 2695). The optional EV charger clause lets you settle this in advance. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No EV Charger Installation Rules
bodyText: Louisiana sets no rules on the conditions you may require for a tenant's electric vehicle charger, such as registration, insurance, licensed installation, permits or paying for electricity. Because tenants have no statutory right to install one, the conditions are whatever you and the tenant agree to in writing; the optional EV charger clause lists the usual ones. Building, electrical and permit requirements come from local codes. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rules
bodyText: Louisiana has no law on tenant electric vehicle charging in shared parking areas: no right to a charger in a common area, no rules on reserving or charging a fee for a charging space, and no rules for condominium or association-managed parking. Any shared-area charger is a matter for written agreement with you (and with any association that controls the parking). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Parking Rules Notice Law
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule on how you give tenants parking or towing rules: no required delivery before signing, no required heading, no limit on what vehicle information you may ask for, and no rule tying a parking permit to the lease term. Attach your parking rules to the lease so they bind the tenant, and make them match the parking rules and towing reasons in your written contract with the towing company, which the towing law requires (La. R.S. 32:1736). Changing the rules mid-lease binds the tenant only if the tenant agrees or the lease reserves your right to adopt reasonable rule changes. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no unbundled-parking law: you may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately, as you and the tenant agree. If parking is separate, put the space, the charge and what happens to the parking if the lease ends in writing, and state the charge as a fixed amount. A separate parking charge may raise a sales tax question, because Louisiana's sales and use tax reaches the use of parking spaces (La. R.S. 47:301.3(3)); ask the Department of Revenue or a tax adviser before you start charging separately. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: Louisiana has no recreational cannabis law, and no law protects medical marijuana patients in rental housing or limits what your lease may say about cannabis. Patients may obtain medical marijuana, including smokable raw or crude forms, on an authorized clinician's recommendation (La. R.S. 40:1046), but nothing requires you to allow smoking, vaping or growing it in your property, so the library's smoking policy, which bans smoking and vaping of any kind, may cover cannabis too. Possession without a recommendation is still a crime, though fourteen grams or less carries only a fine of up to $100 by summons (La. R.S. 40:966(C)). Growing, selling or distributing marijuana is illegal drug activity your criminal-activity clause can treat as a default. If you take federal housing assistance, federal rules may require you to bar it altogether. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no law letting a tenant take in friends or family displaced by a hurricane, flood or fire despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting such stays or deciding when a displaced guest becomes a tenant. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply, subject to fair housing law, local occupancy codes and any emergency orders. After a disaster, consider giving written, time-limited consent to displaced guests rather than treating their stay as a default. If a guest will not leave after the purpose of the stay has ended, the removal route is a written notice to vacate of five days (not counting weekends and legal holidays) and the court eviction process, not self-help (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4702). See the disaster note for how a hurricane or flood affects the lease itself. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Firearms at Rental Property
bodyText:
Louisiana has one firearm rule aimed at property owners: you may not forbid anyone who lawfully possesses a firearm from keeping it in a locked, privately owned vehicle in your parking lot, garage or designated parking area, and in exchange you are not civilly liable for incidents involving a firearm stored that way (La. R.S. 32:292.1). If you operate as a business, you may require that it be kept out of sight or in a locked case or container in the vehicle. Exceptions include property where state or federal law bans firearms.

No Louisiana statute stops a lease from restricting firearms inside the home or protects a concealed-carry permit holder's right to keep one there, but the Louisiana Constitution treats the right to keep and bear arms as fundamental, so the library offers only an optional clause barring unlawful discharge and requiring lawful storage ("Firearm Discharge and Storage" clause). If you want a broader restriction, add your own clause and take advice first. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Guest Rights Statute
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute giving your tenant's guests, visitors, caregivers, tradespeople or delivery people a right of access to a rental, no statute limiting how long a guest may stay, and no ban on guest fees. Guest rules are lease terms, so put them in the lease.

Several general rules frame them. Your tenant is liable for damage to the property caused by anyone who is on the premises or uses it with the tenant's consent (La. Civ. Code art. 2687). In a residential lease, your warranty against vices and defects protects everyone who lives in the premises in accordance with the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2698).

A person who stays only by permission, such as a guest who has outstayed the lease's limit, is an "occupant" whom you (or the tenant) can remove with a written notice to vacate of five days (not counting weekends and legal holidays) and a court eviction if needed (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4702, 4704); see the occupant-removal guidance in the library. In a building of six or more dwellings (except an owner-occupied building of ten or fewer units), a lease may not limit the right of the tenant or any other person, including a guest, to call the police or emergency help in an emergency or after domestic abuse on the premises, or penalize anyone for doing so (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)).

Public housing authorities have their own rules: they may end a tenancy for drug-related or criminal activity by a household member's guest and may limit access to their developments to residents and their permitted guests, among others (La. R.S. 40:506, 40:508).

title: Police Cooperation and Calls for Help
bodyText: Louisiana has no crime-free lease statute and no law requiring you to join a crime-free housing program or to give police or child-protection investigators information about your tenants, or access to a unit, without legal process. One specific duty exists: when a court has ordered a wiretap, pen register, trap and trace device or cellular tracking device, a landlord must, at the request of the authorized law enforcement agency, furnish the information, facilities and technical assistance needed to install it unobtrusively. You are compensated for reasonable expenses and cannot be sued in a Louisiana court for helping under the court order (La. R.S. 15:1312.1, 15:1316). Two rules protect tenants who call for help. In a building of six or more dwellings (except an owner-occupied building of ten or fewer units), a lease may not limit the right of a tenant or anyone else to call the police or emergency help in an emergency or after domestic abuse on the premises, or penalize anyone for the call; such a provision is null (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)). And no parish or city may fine you or authorize an eviction because a tenant, or someone acting for the tenant, called the police or emergency officials about domestic abuse or another crime (La. R.S. 33:9701). If you want a term on criminal activity, use the library's optional criminal-activity clause, which keeps victims and emergency calls out of its reach; officials and neighbors can also sue an owner over drug, violence and gang nuisances (see the nuisance guidance in the library). Three reporting duties bind you as they bind anyone. Any person who has cause to believe that an adult (as the statute defines it: someone who, because of a physical, mental or developmental disability or the infirmities of aging, cannot manage his own resources, carry out daily activities or protect himself) has been or may be further harmed by abuse, neglect or exploitation must report it to an adult protection agency or to police, and knowingly and willfully failing to is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to six months in jail, or both (La. R.S. 15:1503, 15:1504(A), 15:1505(A), 14:403.2(A)). Any person 18 or older who witnesses the sexual abuse of a child and knowingly and willfully fails to report it to law enforcement or the Department of Children and Family Services faces a fine of up to $10,000, up to five years in prison, or both (La. R.S. 14:403(A)(4)); the general child-abuse reporting duty binds the mandatory reporters the Children's Code lists, and anyone else may report (La. Ch.C. art. 609). And any person having knowledge of a death under sudden, accidental, violent or suspicious circumstances, or without medical attendance in the 24 hours before death, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately notify the coroner, and no one may move the body without first notifying the coroner and receiving permission; failing to comply is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $5,000 (La. R.S. 13:5712). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building, gated community or other multi-unit property to reach tenants' doors, and no duty to set aside an area for campaign or voter literature. Whether outsiders may enter common areas is up to you and your lease rules, applied evenly. The only election rule touching rentals runs the other way: the ban on campaign signs and petitioning near a polling place during early voting and on election day does not apply to political signs that the owner, the lessee or a lawful occupant places on private property not being used as a polling place, or that others place there with their consent (La. R.S. 18:1462). A tenant's right to display a removable, portable United States flag is covered in the display-rights guidance in the library.

title: No Tenant Solar Device Right
bodyText: Louisiana gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, portable or balcony solar device, or any other solar equipment, at a rental. Louisiana's solar-access law says no person or entity may unreasonably restrict a property owner's right to install or use a solar collector, subject to zoning, servitudes, building restrictions and historic-district rules (La. R.S. 9:1255). It protects the owner, which is you, not your tenant, so it does not stop you from limiting or banning tenant solar devices in the lease. Your lease decides: a consent-before-alterations term covers solar equipment, and the improvements terms (or, absent them, the Civil Code's default rule on removal at the end of the lease) govern anything you allow (La. Civ. Code art. 2695). Louisiana's renewable-energy lease statutes concern leases of land for commercial solar, wind or hydroelectric production, not homes.

title: No Recycling Notice Requirement
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, to provide recycling containers or service at a rental, or to include recycling information in the lease, whatever the building's size. Louisiana's Solid Waste Recycling and Reduction Law sets state goals, has the state assist and fund local recycling programs, and leaves it to parishes and municipalities to choose their own programs (La. R.S. 30:2411, 30:2413); it places no duty on residential landlords. Check your parish or city: local solid-waste ordinances, may require recycling service or set container rules for apartment buildings. If you offer recycling, a short note in the lease or the property rules on where the containers are and what goes in them is good practice.

title: Tenant United States Flag
bodyText:
Whatever your lease says, you may not adopt or enforce a lease term that forbids or restricts a person from displaying a removable, portable flag of the United States. You may set reasonable rules on the flag's size, and the time, place and manner of display, and a court may stop a violation by injunction, and when it does, court costs and reasonable attorney fees are also available (La. R.S. 9:1114, enacted in 2025). The same rule binds condominium associations and planned communities, and a planned community's flag rule must be consistent with federal law (La. R.S. 9:1114, 9:1141.37(D)).

No other Louisiana statute protects a tenant's flags, banners or political signs against your lease rules, and none limits association rules on political signs, so a lease term requiring your consent before posting signs or banners visible from outside is lawful. The only election rule touching signs on private property exempts signs that the owner, lessee or occupant puts up from the polling-place electioneering ban (La. R.S. 18:1462(B)). Religious displays are covered in the religious-display guidance in the library.

If you want flag rules, put them in the lease; the optional flag-display clause does this. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Religious Display Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on a door frame, a cross or a holiday decoration, against your lease rules, and none barring you from limiting them. Louisiana's fair housing law still applies: you may not discriminate against a tenant because of religion in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or in services or facilities (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(2)), so apply any display rule evenly, without singling out one faith, and consider allowing small door-frame items. The state act does not reach a single-family house rented by a private owner of no more than three such houses without a broker or discriminatory advertising, or rooms or units in a building of up to four units where the owner lives in one of them, though the advertising ban still applies (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)); federal fair housing law applies separately. The library's shared rules on fastenings and signs save any display the law entitles a tenant to make. A removable, portable United States flag is protected by statute; see the flag-display guidance in the library.

title: Property Rules Are Lease Terms
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute on landlord rules or house rules: nothing sets when rules are enforceable, requires you to give them to applicants before signing, or limits how far a rule may change the tenant's bargain. Rules bind a tenant as lease terms, because a contract has the effect of law for the parties and must be performed in good faith (La. Civ. Code art. 1983). So attach the rules to the lease, or have the lease refer to rules the tenant receives before signing.

The tenant must use the property as a prudent administrator and for the purpose for which it was leased (La. Civ. Code art. 2683), and a use for another purpose or one that may damage the property lets you seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2686). A rule you adopt during the lease is an amendment, which binds the tenant once the tenant agrees to it; an amendment made without intent to create a new contract does not create a new lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2726). The library's Rules and Regulations clause takes that route: a new or changed rule binds the tenant during the term only if the tenant agrees in writing or it is part of a renewal.

A lease clause letting you change rules on your own, by notice, is not offered for Louisiana: no statute authorizes it, ambiguous terms in a lease you drafted are read against you (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). A month-to-month tenancy can be ended, and new rules offered for the next lease, on the ordinary termination notice (ten calendar days before the end of the month, in writing).

Separate laws limit particular rules, such as the flag-display, emergency-call and fair housing rules described elsewhere in the library.

title: Smoke From Other Units
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on tobacco smoke drifting between units and none authorizing a lease clause in which the tenant gives up claims over drifting smoke, so a smoke-drift waiver is not offered for Louisiana. Civil Code limits make such a waiver unreliable. In a residential lease, your warranty of peaceful possession covers disturbance by a person who has access to the property with your consent or who occupies adjacent property you own, such as a neighboring tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 2700). A waiver of your warranty against vices or defects must be clear, unambiguous and brought to the tenant's attention, and in a residential lease it cannot waive defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). And any clause excluding liability in advance for causing physical injury, or for intentional or gross fault, is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). The better tool is a smoking policy: the library's Smoking Policy clause bans smoking and vaping on the property, which you can adopt for every unit you control. Enclosed common areas can also be covered by state law: the Smokefree Air Act bans smoking in any enclosed area within a place of employment, which includes hallways and other areas under an employer's control that employees normally frequent, and forbids an employer to knowingly permit smoking there, though a private residence is not a place of employment (La. R.S. 40:1291.3(5), (7), 40:1291.11(A)(3), (5), (B)(1)). Whether a particular apartment hallway qualifies depends on whether your staff normally work there. See the smoking-law guidance in the library.

title: No Tenant Security-Camera Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute giving a tenant a right to install security cameras or a video doorbell, and none limiting your lease rules on them, so your lease controls: a term requiring your written consent before the tenant fastens anything to the property or makes alterations covers cameras and doorbells. General criminal laws apply to anyone who records. It is a crime to use a camera or other image recording device to observe or record a person without consent for a lewd purpose, or to record certain intimate images where the person has a reasonable expectation of privacy (La. R.S. 14:283). Louisiana's wiretap law makes it a crime to intercept an oral or electronic communication, but not where the person recording is a party to the conversation or one party has consented, unless the recording is for a criminal, tortious or other injurious purpose (La. R.S. 15:1303(A), (C)(4)); a camera that records sound in a hallway or at a neighbor's door can raise this issue. A separate rule binds owners of short-term rentals (a building that may have been a one- or two-family dwelling, rented for 29 days or less): the owner may use hidden or disguised cameras only in common areas, never bedrooms or bathrooms, and only after conspicuously posting the statutory surveillance notice; guests recorded in violation may recover actual and punitive damages and attorney fees (La. R.S. 21:61). That rule does not apply to ordinary residential leases of 30 days or more. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals: nothing requires you to allow them, bars you from banning them, or sets insurance or installation rules. Your lease decides. The library's shared rule on fastenings and heavy items requires your written consent before a tenant keeps a waterbed or other water-filled furniture, and you may condition consent on proof of insurance, a frame or liner, or placement on a ground floor. The Civil Code backs this up: the tenant is liable for damage caused by the tenant's fault or that of people on the premises with the tenant's consent, and must repair it (La. Civ. Code arts. 2687, 2692), and if the tenant uses the property in a manner that may cause damage, you may seek an injunction, dissolution of the lease and damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2686). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Condominium and HOA Rules for Rentals
bodyText:
If your rental is a condominium unit or a lot in a planned community (a homeowners association), the association's documents can reach your tenant, and Louisiana law adds some rules.

Condominiums: the declaration and bylaws have the force of law between unit owners, and the declaration may limit leasing and occupancy of units (La. R.S. 9:1124.115, 9:1122.105(B)(8)); check them before you lease.

Planned communities (the Louisiana Planned Community Act, which applies to existing and future planned communities but does not affect the validity of community documents recorded before January 1, 2025, and does not apply to condominiums): the association may require an occupant, including your tenant, to sign and file with it a lease or occupancy agreement containing language the association requires, and may deny access to an occupant who does not; it may enforce those required provisions directly against the occupant, impose reasonable fines on owners and occupants for violating the community documents, and suspend an occupant's privileges, though it may not cut off services if that would endanger health, safety or property (La. R.S. 9:1141.3, 9:1141.20). An amendment that sets or raises a minimum lease term or bans renting less than the whole lot needs the supermajority vote for more burdensome restrictions, and it does not stop an existing rental use that began before the amendment was recorded unless that use stops for 12 consecutive months (La. R.S. 9:1141.14(C)).

Louisiana has no statute capping association lease-approval or application fees, governing an association-held tenant deposit, or letting an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you owe dues. Your lease should require the tenant to follow the association's rules (the library's association-compliance clause does this) and, where the documents require association approval, make the lease depend on it (the library's optional association-approval clause).

title: No Association Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require a lease of a condominium unit or a lot in a planned community to disclose the association's obligations, or require you to give the tenant a copy of the declaration, bylaws or rules. Louisiana's disclosure duty for association documents runs only to buyers: a condominium unit owner who resells must give the purchaser the declaration, bylaws and a certificate on assessments and the association's finances (La. R.S. 9:1124.107). Even so, give your tenant the association's rules before signing and make compliance a lease term: a planned-community association may require your tenant to sign and file a lease or occupancy agreement with language the association requires and may fine occupants for violations (La. R.S. 9:1141.20), so a tenant who never saw the rules is a problem for you. See the condominium and HOA guidance in the library.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to disclose a unit's bed bug history to an applicant or tenant, to give a bed bug information sheet, or to follow any statutory treatment timeline. The general lease rules apply: you must deliver the property in good condition and keep it suitable for its purpose (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2684), and you warrant it against vices or defects. Disclosure still matters to you: a lease waiver of that warranty is ineffective for defects the tenant did not know about and you knew or should have known about, and in a residential lease it cannot waive defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). So if you know of an active or recent infestation, tell the applicant in writing. See the pest and bed bug guidance and the optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause in the library.

title: No Pest Control Notice Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell tenants about a pest control service contract, to give notice before pesticide is applied in a unit or common area, or to post pesticide notices in a rental building. Pest control companies are licensed and regulated by the state's structural pest control laws and agency rules. If treatment requires entering a unit, your right of entry comes from the lease (Louisiana has no entry statute), so use the library's optional Pest Reporting and Treatment clause, which also requires the tenant to prepare the unit. One state program can reach your rental directly: the agriculture commissioner's agents may enter property to inspect for and treat Formosan termites on reasonable notice, at reasonable hours, with the consent of the owner, renter or lessee, or under a court order if consent is refused (La. R.S. 3:3391.9).

title: Louisiana Lead Paint Duties
bodyText:
Louisiana adds no lead notice, certificate or information packet that must be given with a lease; for housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet still apply (see the library's lead disclosure clause).

Louisiana does put duties on you as owner. If a child under six, or a person with an intellectual disability, lives in your rental and its paint, plaster or other accessible materials contain dangerous levels of lead, you must remove or cover them so they are out of reach: all peeling paint inside and out, and paint on surfaces a child could chew, such as window sills, door frames, windows, doors, stair treads, spindles and rails, and porch railings. Repainting over lead paint does not comply. The duty applies whether or not the unit has been inspected, and also to a new owner when a sale results in such a child or person moving in.

Once notified of a violation, you must start the work within 15 days and finish within 30 (La. R.S. 40:1285.7). You are liable for all damages caused by failing to do this (La. R.S. 40:1285.10), and violations are enforced like health-code violations and treated as emergencies (La. R.S. 40:1285.9).

When a child is lead-poisoned, the state health officer may inspect the dwelling with the occupants' consent; a dangerous lead level must be reported to you and to all affected tenants, and a notice is posted on the main entrance warning that young children should not live there, which may not be removed until the work is done (La. R.S. 40:1285.4). Lead hazard assessment and abatement must be done by a state-licensed contractor or certified worker; the exemption for doing your own work covers only a home you own and live in (La. R.S. 30:2351.2, 30:2351.12).

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: Louisiana has no lead-safe or lead-free certification for rental housing and no certificate that must be obtained or attached to a lease. For housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet apply. Louisiana's own lead rules are owner duties, not a certificate: remove or cover dangerous lead where a child under six or a person with an intellectual disability lives, and use a licensed lead contractor for abatement; see the Louisiana lead paint guidance in the library (La. R.S. 40:1285.7, 30:2351.2).

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell a tenant that a rental was once used as a methamphetamine lab, and sets no remediation-before-renting rule or habitation ban for landlords. Three related rules apply. First, when law enforcement learns that a residential property was contaminated by use as a clandestine meth lab, it reports the property to the Department of Environmental Quality, which keeps a public list on its website and removes a property once it confirms proper remediation and notifies the owner; failing to follow these steps creates no cause of action (La. R.S. 9:3198.1). Second, a seller's property disclosure must state whether a meth lab was ever located on the property, and that disclosure law also covers a lease with an option to purchase; once a remediated property is removed from the state list, the owner need not disclose the past contamination (La. R.S. 9:3198, 9:3198.1(F)). These provisions as printed take effect in their current form on January 1, 2027. Third, an undisclosed lab you knew or should have known about is a vice or defect: a lease waiver of your warranty cannot cover defects the tenant did not know of and you knew or should have known of, or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). If the property is on the list or you know of past lab use, disclose it in writing and remediate before renting.

title: No Mold Disclosure Requirement
bodyText:
Louisiana does not require you to disclose mold to a tenant or to give a mold information sheet. One statute is optional: the Louisiana Real Estate Commission has approved a mold informational pamphlet that real estate licensees may hand out in any real estate transaction; a licensee who chooses to give it must do so at or before the time the lease or rental agreement is entered into. A licensee who gives it need not provide more information about mold and is not liable for errors in the pamphlet that were not within the licensee's personal knowledge or that came from the commission, a public agency or an expert's report obtained and passed on with ordinary care, but the statute does not change any party's existing disclosure duties, including a licensee's duty to disclose a known material defect (La. R.S. 37:1470).

The pamphlet protects only the licensee, not you as owner. Your own exposure comes from the Civil Code: you warrant the property against vices or defects that prevent its use, and a lease waiver cannot cover defects the tenant did not know of and you knew or should have known of, or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). So disclose known mold in writing and fix it. If a licensee prepares your leases, the optional mold pamphlet acknowledgment records the delivery.

Mold remediation contractors are licensed separately (La. R.S. 37:2156.1).

title: No Radon Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Louisiana has no radon law for rentals: no duty to test for radon, disclose radon test results or a radon hazard to tenants, or give a radon information sheet, whatever the floor level of the unit, and no radon-resistant construction mandate in its statutes.  If you have tested and know of elevated radon, your warranty against vices or defects applies: a lease waiver cannot cover defects the tenant did not know of and you knew or should have known of, or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699).

title: No Flood Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell a tenant whether a rental is in a flood zone or special flood hazard area, whether it has flooded before, or whether you carry flood insurance, and has no flood disclosure form or flood-based termination right for tenants. Flood insurance for a tenant's belongings is the tenant's to buy; Louisiana's residential flood insurance rules recognize renter's and tenant's flood coverage but put no duty on landlords. Two general rules make disclosure wise anyway. Your warranty against vices or defects covers the property, and a lease waiver cannot cover defects the tenant did not know of and you knew or should have known of, or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). And if a flood damages the home, the lease ends on total destruction and the tenant may get a rent reduction or dissolution for partial loss (see the disaster guidance in the library). If a lease gives the tenant an option to purchase, the seller's property disclosure law may apply; see the required-disclosures guidance in the library.

title: No Owner Identity Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give a tenant, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the owner, a property manager or an agent authorized to receive notices and legal papers, and no statute bars or delays an eviction because you did not. Put this information in the lease anyway: the tenant must give you written notices (for example, the written termination notice for a month-to-month lease and the tenant's prompt notice of needed repairs), and the library's notices clause sends them to the address the lease states. If the property is sold or management changes, see the sale and management-change guidance in the library; Louisiana requires no notice of the change, but a tenant who has not been told may keep paying the former landlord. A company that manages other owners' rentals generally needs a real estate license; an owner managing its own property does not (see the landlord registration guidance in the library).

title: No Occupancy Certificate Disclosure
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell a tenant whether the rental has a valid certificate of occupancy, give the tenant a copy, or state it in the lease, and no statute makes a lease of a unit without one unenforceable or bars collecting rent for it. Certificates of occupancy are issued under building-code enforcement by the state and local governments for new construction and major work, and some cities and parishes require them, or a rental permit, before a unit is occupied; check local ordinances. Your general duty still applies: you must deliver the property in good condition suitable for the purpose for which it was leased (La. Civ. Code art. 2684).

title: No Drywall Disclosure Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on defective, corrosive or sulfur-emitting drywall in rentals: no disclosure duty, no remediation standard and no tenant remedy specific to drywall. The words do not appear in Louisiana's statutes. Drywall that corrodes wiring or fixtures, or that harms health, is a vice or defect covered by your warranty; a lease waiver cannot cover defects the tenant did not know of and you knew or should have known of, or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). If you know the property has defective drywall that has not been fixed, disclose it in writing before signing.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Louisiana does not require a lease disclosure for a rental near a military base or airfield, or in an aircraft noise zone or accident potential zone, and gives tenants no right to end a lease because of such a location. The only related rule binds local governments: before acting on a zoning request affecting property within 3,000 feet of a military installation (including a military airport), the city or parish must notify the installation's commander and publish notice at least 90 days ahead, and give 30 days' notice for a variance (La. R.S. 33:4734, 33:4780.52). Louisiana's military rules for tenants are about service members' rights to end a lease, covered in the servicemember guidance in the library.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Meter Disclosures
bodyText: Louisiana requires none of the three pre-signing disclosures some states group together. Ordnance: no duty to disclose a former military ordnance or munitions site near the rental. Demolition: no duty to tell applicants or tenants that you have applied for a permit to demolish the unit; historic-district and local permit rules regulate demolition itself, not notice to tenants. Shared meters: no statute requires you to disclose that a tenant's utility meter also serves other areas or to make a written allocation agreement; if you split a shared bill, state the method in the lease (see the utility apportionment guidance in the library). If you plan to demolish, remember that a fixed-term lease binds you for its term and a month-to-month lease needs the ordinary written termination notice.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no law like California's Proposition 65: no duty to warn tenants about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm on rental property, and no warning-sign requirement for rentals. Specific hazards have their own rules, covered elsewhere in the library: lead paint (federal disclosure and Louisiana's lead duties), smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and smoking. Your warranty against vices or defects covers hazardous conditions you know about, and in a residential lease it cannot be waived for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699).

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring a lease of waterfront or shoreline property to disclose public access rights along the shore, public servitudes across the property, or coastal zoning matters. Louisiana's shore and water-bottom statutes concern state lands, mineral and oyster leases, levee districts and public waterways, not residential leases. If public access or a servitude affects how your tenant may use the property, say so in the lease so the tenant's peaceful possession is not disturbed by surprise.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to test a private drinking-water well serving a rental, or to give tenants well test results. The state health officer may test the purity of a private well's water at the owner's request and reports the results to the owner (La. R.S. 40:5.4). If the home's water comes from a private well, test it, share the results, and say in the lease who maintains the well; see the well and septic guidance in the library. Water that is unsafe to drink is a defect that seriously affects health or safety, which a residential lease cannot waive (La. Civ. Code art. 2699).

title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: Louisiana has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no notice telling tenants whether such a law covers the unit, and nothing to put in the lease about one. A fixed-term lease ends at the end of its term without notice unless it is extended or reconducted, and a month-to-month lease ends on written notice (ten calendar days before the end of the month); see the for-cause eviction guidance in the library, which also lists the situational limits that do apply, such as the protections for domestic-abuse victims in buildings of six or more units. Some public and federally assisted housing has its own good-cause rules under federal law.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to carry liability insurance on a rental property, to register proof of insurance with a city or parish, or to tell tenants whether you are insured. Insurance is still wise: you are liable for injuries caused by defects you knew or should have known about, and a lease clause cannot exclude liability in advance for causing physical injury (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). Some local rental-registration programs may require insurance; check local ordinances. Louisiana's insurance-related lease statutes concern leases of movables (cars and equipment), not homes.

title: No Contamination Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell a tenant that a rental is or was contaminated with hazardous or radioactive material, and no state cleanup law requires recorded environmental use restrictions to be written into residential leases. What Louisiana does have is on the land records: when the Department of Environmental Quality approves a partial voluntary cleanup, the owner must record an agreement giving the state access and the use restrictions the secretary requires; both bind later owners and appear in the parish records (La. R.S. 30:2286). If your property is subject to such restrictions, your tenant's use must respect them, so say so in the lease. And a contamination problem you know of is a vice or defect: a lease waiver cannot cover defects the tenant did not know of and you knew or should have known of, or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). Methamphetamine-lab contamination has its own rules; see the meth-lab guidance in the library.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give tenants a copy of a variance from the State Sanitary Code or any housing or health code, or to attach one to the lease. The State Sanitary Code is a Department of Health rule, and variances under it and under local housing codes are governed by those rules and ordinances; follow any conditions a variance imposes.

title: No Rights Guide Delivery Duty
bodyText: Louisiana does not publish a state guide to landlord and tenant rights that you must give tenants before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one. The Attorney General publishes a consumer guide to Louisiana landlord and tenant law, "Moving In, Moving Out", which you may share with tenants (check it against current law; for example, its deposit penalty figure is out of date), but nothing requires you to. The only state-approved handout tied to leasing is the Real Estate Commission's mold pamphlet, which real estate licensees may choose to give (see the mold guidance in the library). Because Louisiana's residential lease rules are spread across the Civil Code and the Revised Statutes, a plain-language summary in your welcome materials is good practice, but it is not required.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether annually, when the rent changes or otherwise, and gives renters of a house or apartment no property-tax credit that depends on such a statement. Louisiana's only renter-related property-tax relief is narrow: the constitution lets the legislature give residential lessees credits or rebates similar to the homestead exemption, and the statute implementing it defines a residential lessee as a person who owns and lives in a residence, such as a mobile home, on land he does not own, and gives that person a credit against the ad valorem tax on the residence (La. Const. art. VII, § 20(B); La. R.S. 47:1710). It does not involve landlords of rented homes. If your lease passes tax increases through to the tenant, see the tax escalation guidance in the library.

title: No Code Order Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give applicants or tenants copies of outstanding code-violation citations, inspection orders or condemnation orders, or to disclose them before signing. Condemnation notices reach occupants through the local government instead: before a parish or municipality condemns a building, the owner is notified and given a hearing at least ten days later; if the owner is out of state or unrepresented, the notice is served on the occupant and on an attorney appointed for the owner, and in a grave emergency the building may be condemned on 24 hours' notice to the owner, agent or occupant, which may be posted on the door. The notice is recorded with the recorder of mortgages and binds later buyers (La. R.S. 33:4762). A similar procedure in some municipalities requires notice to both owner and occupant (La. R.S. 33:4770.9). A known violation affecting the home's condition is a defect under your warranty, which a residential lease cannot waive for defects seriously affecting health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); see the condemned-premises and rental-inspection guidance in the library for rent and inspection rules.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no meter conservation charge: no statute lets a utility add an energy-efficiency or conservation charge to a rental's meter, and no landlord notice or rent deduction for such a charge. Utility rates and any on-bill programs are set by the Louisiana Public Service Commission and local utility regulators; if a utility bill for the unit carries a special charge that the tenant will pay, say so in the lease.

title: No Submetering Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana does not require a lease disclosure when you submeter electricity (or other utilities) to tenants, and sets no submeter billing rules in its statutes. The rules that do apply are described elsewhere in the library: if you use a third-party billing company for an individually metered unit, the tenant may request copies of the utility's original bills (Tenant Bill Transparency law); money you collect from tenants for utility service must be applied to the bill within 60 days; and if you split a master-metered bill, the lease must state the method.

title: No Occupancy Presumption Notice
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule requiring a notice at the top of the first page of a lease, in large type, about a tenant's lawful occupancy, and no presumption that a tenant lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized, signed by a licensed property manager or states your address and phone number. Louisiana also sets no general type-size rule for residential leases; see the lease type-size guidance in the library. Removing people with no right to be there works differently in Louisiana: a person with no right of possession or lease can be removed under the criminal trespass law after being told to leave, while anyone claiming under a lease, written or oral, must be evicted through the court (see the occupant-removal guidance in the library). A written lease signed by both parties and kept on file is still your best proof that a tenant is lawfully in possession.

title: Louisiana Lease Disclosures
No Window Unit Right
bodyText: Louisiana gives tenants no statutory right to install a window, portable or floor air conditioner, heat pump or other cooling device, and no statute requires a lease to say whether such units are allowed. Louisiana also sets no indoor cooling standard you must meet. Your lease decides: you may allow, limit or ban tenant-installed units, and a lease that requires your consent before alterations covers window units. If you supply air conditioning, it is part of the leased property: you must deliver it in good condition and make the necessary repairs, except for damage the tenant causes (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691, 2692). If a tenant installs a unit with your consent, the lease's improvements terms (or, absent them, the Civil Code's default rule on removal at the end of the lease) govern it (La. Civ. Code art. 2695). A tenant with a disability may ask to install a unit as a reasonable modification or accommodation under fair housing law; see the disability-modifications guidance in the library. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness at the Property
bodyText: You do not have to tell a prospective tenant that the property is or may be "psychologically impacted": that a past or present occupant has or was suspected of having HIV or AIDS, or any other disease that medical evidence shows is highly unlikely to be spread by living in a dwelling, or that the property was, or was suspected to be, the site of a homicide, another felony, or a suicide. Louisiana law says those facts are not material facts that must be disclosed in a real estate transaction, and no one may sue an owner or the owner's agent for not disclosing them (La. R.S. 37:1468). The statute sits in the real estate license law, whose definitions make leasing and renting a "real estate transaction", a lessor a "seller" and a lessee a "buyer" (La. R.S. 37:1431), so on its terms it covers rentals, whether or not a licensee is involved. It removes a duty to volunteer; it does not let you lie. If a prospective tenant asks, answer truthfully or decline to answer: fraud includes a misrepresentation or a suppression of the truth meant to gain an unjust advantage, and a lease rescinded for fraud exposes you to damages and attorney fees (La. Civ. Code arts. 1953, 1958). Never volunteer or discuss a person's HIV status or other health condition. Other disclosures stand on their own rules: the sex offender database notice in licensee leases ("Sex Offender Registry Notice" clause) and methamphetamine labs ("No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule"). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute on housing you provide to your own employees: no required disclosure of when the employee must leave, and no duty to offer a regular lease when the job ends.

What the employee has depends on the deal. If the employee pays rent, the arrangement is a lease, and rent can be money or "services", so housing given in exchange for work can itself be a lease (La. Civ. Code arts. 2668, 2675). A lease can be written to end when the job ends, because a lease term may end on a designated event (La. Civ. Code art. 2678); the library's optional clause ("Employee Housing" clause) does that. When it ends, you still need a written notice to vacate giving at least five days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, unless the lease contains a written waiver, and then a court eviction if the employee stays (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701; "Louisiana Eviction: Notice to Vacate and Court Timeline").

If instead the employee lives there free, only by your permission or as an accommodation, the employee is an "occupant", not a tenant; once the purpose of the occupancy has ended you give a written five-day notice to vacate (again not counting weekends and legal holidays) and, if needed, evict (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4702, 4704). Which category applies to a given arrangement is a case-law question, so put the arrangement in writing.

Public housing authorities may let police officers and maintenance and management employees live in their developments (La. R.S. 40:500). Deducting housing from wages is governed by wage laws.

title: No Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to give tenants a state-prepared statement, summary or bill of tenant rights, to attach one to the lease, to have tenants sign or initial it, or to provide one before you may sue or evict. The notices Louisiana does require are specific ones: the pending-foreclosure disclosure, the sex offender database notice in written leases a real estate licensee executes ("Sex Offender Registry Notice" clause), and, for rentals of a tenant's primary residence other than owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units, the application-fee notice. The Attorney General's Consumer Protection Section publishes a free landlord and tenant guide, "Moving In, Moving Out"; sharing it is optional and it is not law. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Louisiana has no statewide tenant protection act like California's: no cap on rent increases, no just-cause eviction law and no general right for tenants to buy the property when you sell. So there is no state notice telling tenants such protections apply, and none belongs in your lease. The details are in "No Rent Control", "No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in Louisiana" and, for condominium conversions, "Condominium Conversions". Do not copy another state's rent-cap or just-cause notice into a Louisiana lease; it could be read as a promise you have made. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states require a lease statement telling tenants a property is exempt from statewide rent caps or just-cause rules. Louisiana has neither law to be exempt from ("No Tenant Protection Act Notice"), so no exemption notice is required and none should go in your lease. The Louisiana rules that do turn on building size or owner occupancy, such as the domestic abuse protections, the application-fee notice and the fair housing exemptions, are listed in "Building and Business Size Thresholds". The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: Louisiana has no truth-in-renting law. No statute requires your lease to state that it must comply with state law, to warn tenants that some clauses may be unenforceable, or to come with a state statement of rights, and no statute penalizes you simply for offering a lease that contains an unenforceable term. Such a term still fails: a contract term that departs from a law enacted to protect the public interest is an absolute nullity (La. Civ. Code art. 7), any waiver of a tenant's deposit rights is null and void (La. R.S. 9:3254), and in buildings of six or more dwellings (except owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units) a clause limiting or penalizing calls for police or emergency help is null, void and unenforceable (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)). Unclear wording in your own form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). The full list of terms Louisiana law voids or limits is in "Lease Terms Louisiana Law Voids or Limits". The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Louisiana requires no utility disclosure attached to the lease: no form explaining how a shared bill is split, no submeter certificate, and no notice of energy-improvement charges on a tenant's utility bill (Louisiana has no statute creating such on-bill or assessment financing). If you split a shared bill, say in the lease how you calculate each tenant's share, because the amount must be determinable by a method the parties agreed ("No Rule on Splitting Shared Utility Bills"). If you use a third-party billing company for individually metered units, the tenant may ask for copies of the utility's original bills, which you must send within thirty days ("Utility Bill Copies for Tenants (Third-Party Billing)"). Utility money you collect must be applied to the bill ("Utility Money You Collect from Tenants"). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText:
Louisiana has no law that authorizes, sets or caps a lease fee for a tenant who removes, disables or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide detector, and no statute makes tampering with a detector inside a home a separate offense.

Your remedies are the ordinary ones. The tenant is liable for damage caused by the tenant's fault or by anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent, and must repair it (La. Civ. Code arts. 2687, 2692), so you can recover the reasonable cost of replacing or repairing a detector the tenant removed or damaged. A lease may also stipulate damages in advance, and a court may change them only if they are so manifestly unreasonable as to be contrary to public policy (La. Civ. Code arts. 2005, 2012).

This library does not offer a fixed tampering fee for Louisiana: you could not collect both the fee and the repair cost for the same breach (La. Civ. Code art. 2007). The library's optional detector clause ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors" clause) uses actual costs instead.

Remember the duty that is yours: a one- or two-family dwelling must have an operable ten-year sealed-battery smoke detector and a carbon monoxide detector when leased ("Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors at Lease (One- and Two-Family Homes)"). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Asbestos: No Rental Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute requiring you to inspect a private rental for asbestos, to disclose asbestos to a tenant, or to notify tenants before asbestos work. The state's asbestos statutes cover other buildings: a detection and abatement program for public buildings owned or leased by the state (La. R.S. 40:1749.1) and the school asbestos abatement law (La. R.S. 30:2341 et seq.). Asbestos removal and abatement work are regulated through the Department of Environmental Quality's rules and federal law, so use qualified abatement contractors if renovation will disturb materials that may contain asbestos. Your general duties still apply: you warrant the property against vices or defects that prevent its use (La. Civ. Code art. 2696), and in a residential lease that warranty cannot be waived for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699; "Warranty Against Defects: What a Lease Can and Cannot Waive"). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Louisiana does not require you to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, when it was last inspected, or that it has none, and it prescribes no sign or lease notice for an unsprinklered building. The sprinkler rules that do exist run to the fire marshal, not to tenants: an owner of a building with a sprinkler or other life safety system must have it inspected and certified at least once a year, and the inspector attaches a copy of the inspection and test report in a conspicuous place on the sprinkler system itself (La. R.S. 40:1646(B), 40:1646.2(B)). Whether your building must have sprinklers is covered in the library's fire sprinkler note ("Fire Sprinklers in Louisiana Rentals"). If you choose to describe the building's fire protection in the lease, describe it accurately. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Louisiana Rentals
bodyText: Louisiana has no general duty to add fire sprinklers to an existing rental. Four rules apply. (1) High-rises built before 1975: every existing building with occupied floors more than 75 feet above the lowest level of fire department vehicle access, built before January 1, 1975, must be protected throughout by an approved sprinkler system; the deadline was January 1, 1999 (with limited fire marshal extensions), and a violation is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of $100 to $500, up to six months in jail, or both (La. R.S. 40:1642(2), 40:1643, 40:1645). (2) Upkeep: if your building has a sprinkler or other life safety system, you must have it inspected and certified at least once a year, and you must fix a system the inspector finds inoperative or deficient by the date the fire marshal sets; failing to obey a second fire marshal order can bring a fine of up to $500, up to six months in jail, or both (La. R.S. 40:1646(B), (C), (E), 40:1646.3). (3) One- and two-family homes: no state code, parish or city may require a sprinkler system in a one- or two-family dwelling (R.S. 37:3733(A)(3), as enacted by 2026 La. Acts No. 881, effective August 1, 2026; formerly La. R.S. 40:1730.28). (4) New construction and major work: new buildings follow the State Uniform Construction Code; a lawfully built existing building is not made to meet newer code unless the fire marshal finds a serious life hazard, but if you spend more than half the building's value on alterations or repairs within twelve months, the building must meet the code for new construction (La. R.S. 40:1578.6(A), (D), 40:1574(C)). Whether a particular apartment building needs sprinklers under the adopted codes is a question for your fire marshal or local fire prevention bureau. These rules are the same whatever the lease type.

title: Which Fire Code Applies
