bodyText: Louisiana's fire code is the State Uniform Fire Prevention Code, which is the National Fire Protection Association's Fire Code (NFPA 1) or the International Fire Code (La. R.S. 40:1578.7(B)). A parish or city that adopts a fire prevention code must adopt that code, and may add stricter local rules only with the state fire marshal's approval; places that had already adopted a model fire code by July 9, 1999 keep their own (La. R.S. 40:1578.7(C), (F), (I)). New buildings must meet the State Uniform Construction Code (the International Building, Existing Building, Residential and related codes), and the fire marshal enforces its fire protection, exit and accessibility provisions for every building except one- and two-family dwellings (La. R.S. 40:1578.6(A); R.S. 37:3733, 37:3735(C), as enacted by 2026 La. Acts No. 881, effective August 1, 2026, formerly La. R.S. 40:1730.28). The fire marshal, or a certified local fire prevention bureau, inspects apartment buildings and other structures, but not one- and two-family dwellings (La. R.S. 40:1563(B)(4), (C)). A lawfully built existing building does not have to be brought up to the current code unless the fire marshal finds a serious life hazard; then the fix follows the existing-building chapter of the 2015 Life Safety Code (buildings permitted before January 1, 2026) or the International Existing Building Code (permitted on or after that date) (La. R.S. 40:1578.6(D)). Remodeling that affects exits or fire protection needs fire marshal plan review first, and alterations or repairs costing more than half the building's value within twelve months bring the whole building up to the code for new construction (La. R.S. 40:1574(B), (C)). Detector rules for one- and two-family rentals are in "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors at Lease (One- and Two-Family Homes)"; sprinklers are in "Fire Sprinklers in Louisiana Rentals". These rules apply whatever the lease type.

title: No Accessory Dwelling Unit Law
bodyText: Louisiana has no accessory dwelling unit law. No statute requires parishes or cities to allow a backyard cottage, garage apartment or in-law unit, stops them from restricting one, or bars rules that the owner live on the lot or that the unit not be rented. Whether you may build and rent an accessory unit is a local zoning question: municipalities may regulate the size, density and use of buildings and land for residence and other purposes, and may divide their territory into zoning districts with uniform rules for each district (La. R.S. 33:4721, 33:4722). Check the local zoning code, any subdivision restrictions, and any homeowners or condominium association rules before you build or rent one. Once rented, an accessory unit is leased under the same Civil Code rules as any other home.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate
bodyText: Louisiana has no law requiring periodic engineering inspections of balconies, galleries, decks, porches, exterior stairways or other elevated exterior structures at rental buildings, and no required inspection report or repair deadline for them. Your general duties cover them. You must keep the property in a condition suitable for its purpose and make the repairs that become necessary during the lease, except those the tenant is responsible for (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691), and you warrant it against vices or defects (La. Civ. Code art. 2696); in a residential lease that warranty cannot be waived for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). If someone is hurt, an owner answers for damage from the ruin or a defect of the building when the owner knew or, with reasonable care, should have known of the defect, could have prevented the damage with reasonable care, and did not (La. Civ. Code arts. 2317.1, 2322). Even where the tenant has assumed responsibility for the premises' condition, you remain liable for a defect you knew or should have known about, or were told about and did not fix within a reasonable time (La. R.S. 9:3221). Regular inspections of elevated structures, especially older wooden galleries and balconies, are therefore good practice, and local building codes may require more. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Waiving Casualty and Mitigation Rules
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute saying whether a lease may waive the casualty rules or the duty to mitigate, and the lease library does not draft a waiver of either. The rules: if the home is totally destroyed without either side's fault, the lease ends and neither owes damages (La. Civ. Code art. 2714); if it is partly destroyed or its use is substantially impaired without the tenant's fault, the tenant may get a rent reduction or end the lease, plus damages if you were at fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2715). When a tenant fails to perform, you must make reasonable efforts to reduce your loss, or the tenant may have the damages reduced (La. Civ. Code art. 2002), and when the tenant has been constructively evicted and the home has become uninhabitable through no fault of the tenant, a statute separately requires you to mitigate (La. R.S. 9:3260). None of these provisions has its own waiver ban, unlike the military, sexual assault and deposit statutes and the termination-notice article. But a waiver would run into limits that do exist: a clause excluding liability for intentional or gross fault or for physical injury is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004); in a residential lease the warranty against defects cannot be waived for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); and no agreement may depart from a law that protects the public interest (La. Civ. Code art. 7). Whether a court would enforce a waiver of the tenant's casualty rights or of mitigation is a case-law question, so the library does not offer one. You may still give yourself a termination right after a casualty ("Landlord Termination After Fire or Casualty" clause); for early move-outs see "When a Tenant Leaves Early or Disappears". The rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: Louisiana does not require your lease to say anything about children: no required statement, no rule that children be listed as occupants, and no separate standard for them. You may list every occupant, adults and children, in the lease (the library's Permitted Occupants clause does this). What you may not do is treat families with children differently. Louisiana's fair housing law bars refusing to rent, or setting different terms, conditions or privileges, because of familial status, and bars advertising a preference against families (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(1)-(3)). Familial status means one or more people under 18 living with a parent or legal custodian, or with the custodian's designee who has written permission, and it also covers anyone who is pregnant or in the process of getting legal custody of a child (La. R.S. 51:2603(8)). So do not charge more rent or a bigger deposit for children, restrict children to certain units or floors, or set occupancy limits stricter than the local code in a way that keeps families out; reasonable local, state or federal occupancy limits are allowed (La. R.S. 51:2605(C); "Occupancy Limits Are Local"). Exemptions: the familial status rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons, meaning housing intended and operated for occupancy by persons 55 or older (at least 80% of units with one such person, with published age policies and significant facilities and services) or occupied solely by persons 62 or older, or state or federal elderly housing programs (La. R.S. 51:2605(C)); and the state act's rental rules do not reach a single-family house rented by a private owner of no more than three such houses without a broker or a discriminatory advertisement, or a building of four or fewer units where you live in one (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)), though the advertising ban still applies to them. Federal law applies separately. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Do not put a confession-of-judgment clause (a clause in which the tenant agrees in advance that a judgment may be entered against the tenant without a contested case) in a Louisiana residential lease. Louisiana prohibits confessions of judgment made before the obligation sued on is due, except for executory process (La. R.S. 9:3590). Executory process is a special procedure for seizing and selling property to enforce a mortgage or privilege that is evidenced by an authentic act (a notarial act) in which the debtor confesses judgment (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 2631, 2632, 2635); it is built for mortgages and security agreements, not for collecting rent or evicting a tenant. For rent and damages you sue in the ordinary way, and to recover the home you use the eviction procedure: a written notice to vacate (unless the lease waives it in writing), then a rule to show cause heard no earlier than the third day after service, not counting weekends and legal holidays ("Louisiana Eviction: Notice to Vacate and Court Timeline"). The only advance waiver the eviction articles allow is the notice to vacate ("Waiver of Notice to Vacate" clause). To reach the tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, use the lessor's privilege and sequestration ("Lessor's Privilege on the Tenant's Belongings"). The library does not offer a lease written as an authentic act with a confession of judgment to enforce the lessor's privilege by executory process; whether that works for a residential lease is a case-law question, and many household goods are exempt from seizure anyway. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Unfair Trade Practices Law and Leases
bodyText: Louisiana's Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law (LUTPA) makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in any trade or commerce unlawful (La. R.S. 51:1405(A)). Trade or commerce includes advertising, offering, selling or distributing services and any property, immovable or movable, and a "consumer" includes anyone who leases goods or services (La. R.S. 51:1402(1), (10)). Whether LUTPA covers a residential lease is decided by the courts, so treat your advertising, application, leasing and collection practices as if it does. Unlike some states' acts, LUTPA has no list of specific landlord practices (it does not, for example, name blank spaces in a lease or failing to give a copy; see "No Blank-Space Rule" and "No Lease Copy Rule"). Exposure: a person who loses money or movable property because of an unlawful practice may sue for actual damages, tripled if you knowingly continued after notice from the Attorney General, plus attorney fees and costs whenever damages are awarded; the suit must be brought within one year of the act (La. R.S. 51:1409(A), (E)). The Attorney General may seek an injunction and civil penalties of up to $5,000 per violation where there was intent to defraud, plus up to $5,000 more per violation against a person 65 or older or a person with a disability (La. R.S. 51:1407). A consumer contract made in violation of the law is an illegal contract on which no recovery may be had (La. R.S. 51:1403). If LUTPA applies to your lease, terms in a consumer's signed writing choosing another state's law, consenting to another state's courts, or fixing venue are invalid (La. R.S. 51:1418(C)); the library's governing-law clause names Louisiana law. Separately, any doubt in your own lease form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Victim Information and Address Confidentiality
bodyText: Louisiana's tenant protections for victims of domestic abuse, stalking, cyberstalking and sexual assault do not say what you must do with the documents a tenant gives you, and no statute requires you to keep them confidential. Those protections are the early termination and eviction rules for abuse victims, which apply only in buildings of six or more dwellings and not in an owner- or lessor-occupied building of ten or fewer units (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A)), and the early termination right for sexual assault victims, which has no unit threshold (La. R.S. 9:3261.2). Keep the certification forms, protective orders and any abuser's name the tenant gives you private anyway, share them only with staff who need them or a court, and never give them to the person named as the abuser. One statute does reach you. Louisiana's Address Confidentiality Program lets a victim of abuse, sexual assault or stalking use a substitute address designated by the Secretary of State (La. R.S. 44:52). If a tenant is a program participant, legal papers must be served on the Secretary of State; service made at the tenant's physical address or on the tenant personally, by someone who knows the tenant is a participant, is invalid, and all legal delays for service are extended ten days (La. R.S. 44:57). Plan eviction or collection filings accordingly ("Eviction Protections for Domestic Abuse Victims", "Proof for Abuse and Sexual Assault Protections"). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Right to Call for Emergency Help
bodyText: Louisiana protects a tenant's right to call for help in two ways. In a building of six or more dwellings (except a building of ten or fewer units in which the owner or lessor lives), a lease may not limit the tenant's or anyone else's right to call the police or other emergency help in an emergency or after domestic abuse on the premises, and may not impose a penalty for the call; such a term is null, void and unenforceable, and the right cannot be signed away (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)). And no parish or city may fine you, or authorize you to evict a tenant, because the tenant called the police or emergency officials about domestic abuse or another crime at the property (La. R.S. 33:9701(E), (F)). For smaller buildings no statute voids a lease term penalizing emergency calls, but do not use one: it would undercut a public policy the legislature has declared and invites a challenge. Details and related police-cooperation rules are in "Police Cooperation and Calls for Help". The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute aimed at lease clauses that impose a fee or penalty because you served a notice to vacate or filed an eviction, and no statute bars passing your eviction filing costs to the tenant. Other rules limit such clauses. Court costs are for the court to award, ordinarily against the losing party ("No Notice Fees"). Attorney fees for unpaid rent and other sums are recoverable if a written lease sets a fixed or determinable amount (La. Civ. Code art. 2000; "Attorney Fees in Louisiana Leases", "Fixed Attorney Fees for Unpaid Sums" clause) or, under an oral lease, as reasonable fees if you win after a written rent demand goes unpaid for 20 days (La. R.S. 9:3259). A flat "eviction fee" is stipulated damages: it cannot be collected on top of the performance it stands for, unless it is for mere delay, and a court may reduce it if it is so manifestly unreasonable as to be contrary to public policy (La. Civ. Code arts. 2005, 2007, 2012; "Agreed (Stipulated) Damages in a Lease"). The library does not offer an eviction-fee clause for Louisiana; recover your actual losses, court costs and any lease-based attorney fees instead. Remember that any doubt in your own lease form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Limits on Liability Waivers
bodyText: Louisiana has no landlord-tenant statute that voids every exculpatory or indemnity clause, but the Civil Code sets firm limits that apply to leases. A clause is null if it excludes or limits, in advance, a party's liability for intentional or gross fault that damages the other party, or for causing physical injury to the other party (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). Your warranty that the property is fit and free of defects may be waived only in clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention, and the waiver does not work for defects you knew or should have known about and the tenant did not, or, in a residential lease, for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699; "Limited Waiver of Warranty Against Vices or Defects" clause). The one statutory shift: if the lease makes the tenant assume responsibility for the premises' condition, you are not liable for injuries a defect causes to the tenant or the tenant's household and guests, unless you knew or should have known of the defect or were told of it and did not fix it within a reasonable time (La. R.S. 9:3221; "Tenant's Assumption of Responsibility for Condition (La. R.S. 9:3221)" clause). Any doubt in your own form is read against you (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). The library does not offer a broad release or a clause making the tenant indemnify you for your own fault: within these limits only a narrow release could stand, it would overlap the warranty waiver already offered (see also "Vehicle Damage and Theft" and "Storage Space Leased With the Home"). A tenant's own duty to answer for damage the tenant or the tenant's guests cause is already law (La. Civ. Code art. 2687). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Louisiana Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Louisiana's Equal Housing Opportunity Act (La. R.S. 51:2601-2614) bars housing discrimination because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status (children under 18, pregnancy, or securing custody), national origin, military status (service members of the uniformed forces or reserves, and their dependents), or a natural, protective or cultural hairstyle such as braids, locs, twists or afros (La. R.S. 51:2603, 51:2606). You may not, on any of those grounds: refuse to rent after a bona fide offer, refuse to negotiate, or otherwise make a home unavailable; set different terms, conditions, privileges, services or facilities; publish any notice, statement or advertisement indicating a preference, limitation or discrimination; or falsely say a unit is not available for inspection or rental (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(1)-(4)). For disability you must also allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense and make reasonable accommodations in rules and policies (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(6); "Disability Accommodations and Service Animals", "Disability Modifications"). You may not coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising these rights or helping others to (La. R.S. 51:2609). You need not rent to a person whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property (La. R.S. 51:2606(C)). Exemptions: the rental rules (but not the advertising ban) do not apply to a single-family house rented by a private owner who owns no more than three such houses, rents without a broker or agent and without a discriminatory advertisement, or to rooms or units in a building of four or fewer units where the owner lives in one (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)); an owner of a building for five or more families, or someone who made three or more rentals in the past twelve months, is treated as in the business and cannot use the single-family exemption (La. R.S. 51:2604(C)); religious organizations and private clubs have limited exemptions, reasonable occupancy limits are allowed, and qualifying housing for older persons may exclude children (La. R.S. 51:2605). Enforcement: a person may complain to the Attorney General within one year, or sue within two years, and a court may award actual and punitive damages, injunctions, costs and attorney fees (La. R.S. 51:2611(B), 51:2613(A), (E)); the Attorney General may also sue (La. R.S. 51:2614). Parishes and cities may adopt broader anti-discrimination ordinances (La. R.S. 51:2236). Source of income is not protected ("No Source-of-Income Protection"). Federal fair housing law applies separately and has its own exemptions. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Foreign Adversary Leasing Restrictions
bodyText: Louisiana bars a "foreign adversary", or a person connected with one, from buying, leasing or otherwise acquiring immovable property in Louisiana under contracts made after August 1, 2023 (La. R.S. 9:2717.1(A)). A foreign adversary is an individual or government identified as one in the federal list at 15 CFR 7.4(a) and in the Treasury Department's OFAC database; a connected person includes an agent of a foreign adversary and an entity a foreign adversary controls (La. R.S. 9:2717.1(G)). The ban does not apply, unless the person is an agent of a foreign adversary, to United States citizens, to non-citizens who are permanent residents or otherwise lawfully present, to entities wholly owned by such persons, or to property leased by a natural person and used as a one-to-four family residence (La. R.S. 9:2717.1(F)). So it rarely touches an ordinary home rental, but it can reach a lease to a company or a lease of a unit in a larger building. Since August 1, 2026 a second rule bars foreign adversaries and "prohibited foreign actors" (their agents and entities they control) from owning, leasing or otherwise obtaining any interest in land within 25 miles of listed military installations, with the same kinds of exceptions, including a natural person's one-to-four family residential property (La. R.S. 9:2717.1.2-2717.1.4, 9:2717.1.8). What this means for you: you have no duty to investigate whether a tenant is a foreign adversary and are not liable for failing to identify one (La. R.S. 9:2717.1(E), 9:2717.1.7); you may rescind a contract to lease before the transfer if you learn the lessee is covered (La. R.S. 9:2717.1(A)(2), 9:2717.1.5(B)); and you may rely on the person's affidavit that they are not covered, unless there is actual fraud (La. R.S. 9:2717.1(A)(4), 9:2717.1.2(C)). The Attorney General enforces these rules, and a lease you made is not affected by a forfeiture against someone else (La. R.S. 9:2717.1(B), (D), 9:2717.1.6(B)). The library does not offer a lease clause asking tenants to certify their status: you need not ask, the statutes' reliance rule is for a sworn affidavit, and questions about citizenship or nationality risk national-origin discrimination claims under fair housing law ("Louisiana Fair Housing Law"). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: Louisiana's building and fire codes mostly follow current national editions, with two fixed editions that matter for older buildings. Building code: the state Uniform Construction Code Council adopts only the latest editions of the International Building, Existing Building, Residential, Mechanical, Plumbing, Fuel Gas and Energy Conservation Codes and the National Electrical Code (R.S. 37:3733(A), as enacted by 2026 La. Acts No. 881, effective August 1, 2026; formerly La. R.S. 40:1730.28); the former statute limited the Residential Code to new construction, reconstruction, additions and extensive alterations, and the re-enacted paragraph (R.S. 37:3733(A)(3)) no longer states that limit, so ask your building official which work it reaches. Fire code: the State Uniform Fire Prevention Code is NFPA 1 or the International Fire Code, and the fire marshal may adopt later editions and amendments by rule (La. R.S. 40:1578.7(B), (E)). Fixed editions: when the fire marshal finds a serious life hazard in a lawfully built existing building, the fix follows the existing-building chapter of the 2015 edition of the NFPA Life Safety Code for structures permitted for construction before January 1, 2026, and the International Existing Building Code for structures permitted on or after that date (La. R.S. 40:1578.6(D)(1)); and pre-1975 high-rises without full sprinklers were measured against parts of the 1967 Life Safety Code (La. R.S. 40:1643(C)(5)(e); "Fire Sprinklers in Louisiana Rentals"). Which edition applies to a given project is set by the fire marshal's and the code council's rules and by local adoption, so confirm it with your building official before renovating. These rules apply whatever the lease type.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText:
Louisiana has no statute that bars, or expressly allows, passing a government fine imposed on you to your tenant, and none that limits pass-through to fines the tenant caused.

The general rules decide it. Charges that burden the property are yours unless the lease says otherwise, except those arising from the tenant's use (La. Civ. Code art. 2689), and the tenant answers for damage the tenant or the tenant's guests cause (La. Civ. Code art. 2687). So a lease may make the tenant reimburse a fine that results from the tenant's own violation, such as a trash, noise, parking or nuisance citation issued to you as owner; the library's optional clause does this ("Fines Caused by Tenant" clause).

Fines for conditions that are your responsibility, such as code violations from repairs you must make, stay with you: shifting them would undercut your duties to maintain the property and make repairs (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691) and, for defects that seriously affect health or safety in a residential lease, could amount to a waiver the law does not allow (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). Never charge a tenant for a penalty arising from a call to police or emergency help; parishes and cities may not impose one on you for that reason (La. R.S. 33:9701(E)).

Fees such as rental registration are covered separately ("Passing Government Fees to Tenants"). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases. Parish or city ordinances set most fines.

title: Immigration Status and Renting
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute on a tenant's immigration status in housing. It does not bar you from asking about status, does not require you to verify it, and does not make it a crime to rent to someone who is unlawfully present. The state's 2024 law creating the crime of unlawful entry or reentry into Louisiana by an alien, effective August 1, 2026, punishes the person who enters, not a landlord who rents to that person (La. R.S. 14:112.11, 14:112.12, 14:112.14). Two related rules matter. Louisiana's fair housing law bars refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of national origin (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(1)-(2)), so if you screen for citizenship or immigration documents, apply the same standard to every applicant and do not single out people by accent, name, appearance or birthplace; the act's exemptions for small owners and owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)) do not reach discriminatory advertising. And the foreign-adversary property law exempts citizens and non-citizens who are permanent residents or otherwise lawfully present, and does not require you to investigate anyone ("Foreign Adversary Leasing Restrictions"). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Jury Trial Waivers
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that allows or forbids a jury-trial waiver in a residential lease, and none that makes a waiver in a standard-form contract presumptively unfair. In practice a jury is rarely available in a lease dispute anyway. An eviction is a summary proceeding, and summary proceedings are tried without a jury; there is no jury at all in parish, city or justice of the peace courts, where most evictions and rent suits are filed; and no jury is available in a suit where no plaintiff's claim exceeds $10,000 (excluding interest and costs), or in a suit on an unconditional obligation to pay a specific sum of money unless the defense is forgery, fraud, error, or want or failure of consideration (La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 1732, 4871). Where a jury is available, a party must demand it in a pleading and post a bond (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 1733). The library does not offer a jury-waiver clause for Louisiana: it would add little, its enforceability in a landlord's standard form is a case-law question, and doubt in your own form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). For arbitration clauses see "Arbitration Clauses in Leases". The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Penalty for Including a Void Term
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that penalizes you simply for putting a prohibited term in a lease or for knowingly using a lease that contains one. The term itself fails: a term that departs from a law protecting the public interest is an absolute nullity (La. Civ. Code art. 7), any waiver of a tenant's deposit rights is null and void (La. R.S. 9:3254), and in buildings of six or more dwellings (except owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units) a term limiting or penalizing calls for police or emergency help is null, void and unenforceable (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)). Money exposure comes when you act on a void term or break the underlying rule: for example, willfully failing to return a deposit as the law requires can cost the amount wrongly kept plus the greater of $300 or twice that amount (La. R.S. 9:3252; "Returning the Deposit: One Month, Itemized Statement, Penalties"), and retaking an apparently abandoned home without following the eviction article's rules can cost $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater; the penalty sits in the article's disaster paragraph, but its words are not limited to disaster parishes, so assume it can apply anywhere (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4731(C)). A tenant may also try to use Louisiana's Unfair Trade Practices Law, whose reach to residential leases is a case-law question ("Unfair Trade Practices Law and Leases"). The full list of terms Louisiana law voids or limits is in "Lease Terms Louisiana Law Voids or Limits". The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Lease Terms Louisiana Law Voids or Limits
bodyText: Louisiana has no single list of prohibited lease terms. The limits are spread across the Civil Code, the lease statutes and other laws, and the general rule is that a term departing from a law enacted to protect the public interest is an absolute nullity (La. Civ. Code art. 7). The main limits: (1) Any waiver of the tenant's security deposit rights is null (La. R.S. 9:3254); a "nonrefundable deposit" is not available ("No Nonrefundable Deposits"). (2) A service member's early-termination rights and a sexual-assault victim's early-termination rights cannot be waived or modified under any circumstances (La. R.S. 9:3261(E), 9:3261.2(E); "Service Members: Early Termination and Eviction Stays", "Early Termination for Victims of Abuse, Stalking or Sexual Assault"). (3) In buildings of six or more dwellings (except owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units), no term may limit or penalize calls for police or emergency help (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)). (4) A reserved right to end the lease early requires the longer of the lease's notice or the Civil Code's notice, and that right to notice cannot be given up in advance (La. Civ. Code art. 2718). (5) A waiver of your warranty against defects must be clear, unambiguous and brought to the tenant's attention, and never covers defects you knew or should have known of or, in a residential lease, defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). (6) No term may exclude or limit in advance liability for intentional or gross fault or for physical injury (La. Civ. Code art. 2004; "Limits on Liability Waivers"). (7) No confession of judgment before the debt is due, except for executory process (La. R.S. 9:3590; "No Confession of Judgment"). (8) Stipulated damages, such as late fees, cannot be collected along with the performance they replace unless they are for delay, and a court may reduce them if manifestly unreasonable (La. Civ. Code arts. 2007, 2012; "Agreed (Stipulated) Damages in a Lease"). (9) A lease term for attorney fees on unpaid sums is enforceable only if the written lease fixes them or a way to compute them (La. Civ. Code art. 2000); without such a term, fees come only from statutes such as La. R.S. 9:3259 (oral leases, after a 20-day written demand). (10) The rent must be certain or determinable by an agreed method, so a rent you alone may reset is doubtful (La. Civ. Code art. 2676; "Rent Increases During the Term"). (11) A term may not exceed 99 years (La. Civ. Code art. 2679). (12) Waivers of seizure exemptions are addressed in "No Homestead or Exemption Waivers in the Lease", and electronic-notice limits in "How to Deliver Notices". (13) If Louisiana's Unfair Trade Practices Law reaches the lease, terms choosing another state's law, consenting to another state's courts, or fixing venue are invalid (La. R.S. 51:1418(C); "Unfair Trade Practices Law and Leases"). Some terms are allowed only in a particular form, such as a waiver of the five-day notice to vacate, which must be a written waiver in the lease ("Waiver of Notice to Vacate" clause). Any doubt in your own form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code art. 2056). Other statutes may also bar terms, and courts may refuse other terms under general contract law. The rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: Louisiana's fair housing law does not protect a renter's source of income. The Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act bars refusing to rent, or setting different terms, because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, military status, or a natural, protective or cultural hairstyle (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)); income source, a Housing Choice (Section 8) Voucher and other rental assistance are not on the list. So state law does not require you to accept a voucher or sign a housing authority's payment contract. If you do accept rental assistance, the subsidy is not rent: applying for or receiving rent-subsidy funds is not payment of rent and is no defense to an eviction (La. R.S. 9:3259.2). Three cautions. Parishes and cities may adopt their own anti-discrimination ordinances covering "all forms of discrimination" (La. R.S. 51:2236(A)), so check local law where the property is. Apply any income or screening standard the same way to every applicant, because a voucher policy used to screen out a protected class is still discrimination under the state act. The state act exempts, and so does not reach, a single-family house rented by a private owner of no more than three such houses without a broker or a discriminatory advertisement, or a building of four or fewer units where you live in one (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)); federal law applies separately. The rule is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: What a Louisiana Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Louisiana has no list of terms every residential lease must contain, and a lease may be oral or written (La. Civ. Code art. 2681). A lease exists once you agree on the thing and the rent (La. Civ. Code art. 2668); if you do not agree on how long it lasts, a lease of a home is month to month (La. Civ. Code art. 2680). What the law does require falls into three groups. (1) Disclosures: the sex offender database notice in every written residential lease a real estate licensee executes ("Sex Offender Registry Notice" clause), the pending-foreclosure disclosure, and, before you accept an application fee for a tenant's primary residence other than in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, the application-fee notice. (2) Terms that work only if the lease states them, sometimes in a set form: a waiver of the five-day notice to vacate (a written waiver in the lease), solidary liability of co-tenants (a clear expression of intent), a ban on subleasing or assignment (express, and read strictly against you), attorney fees (a fixed or determinable amount in writing; an oral lease carries a statutory fee for unpaid rent after a written demand, La. R.S. 9:3259), an automatic dissolution for a stated default, a reserved early-termination right, and a waiver of your warranty against defects (clear, unambiguous and brought to the tenant's attention) (La. Civ. Code arts. 1796, 2000, 2017, 2699, 2713, 2718; La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701; see "Where Louisiana Law Lets Your Lease Decide"). (3) Recording: a lease binds a buyer or lender only from the time it is filed in the parish records (La. Civ. Code art. 2681.1; "Oral Leases and Recording"). State-prescribed wording exists only for a few side documents. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases, except that the term itself is the lease's choice.

title: No General Non-Waiver Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no rule making all of its landlord-tenant law nonwaivable. Most Civil Code lease articles are defaults the lease may change, within the limit that no agreement may depart from a law protecting the public interest (La. Civ. Code art. 7). Non-waiver rules exist only for particular rights: the security deposit Part, where any waiver of the tenant's rights is null (La. R.S. 9:3254); the service-member and sexual-assault early-termination statutes, which cannot be waived or modified under any circumstances (La. R.S. 9:3261(E), 9:3261.2(E)); the right to notice before an early termination under a reserved termination right, which cannot be renounced in advance (La. Civ. Code art. 2718); and the warranty against defects, whose waiver is limited (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). The full list of lease limits is in "Lease Terms Louisiana Law Voids or Limits", and the terms your lease may choose are in "Where Louisiana Law Lets Your Lease Decide". The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Pool Safety Is Local
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that requires a residential landlord to fence a pool, install barriers or alarms, follow pool drain-safety rules, or give tenants a pool safety notice at lease signing. Pool fencing is local: parishes and cities may adopt ordinances regulating the enclosure of residential and commercial swimming pools, with minimum fence or wall heights and locking or limited-access gates, and may regulate draining pools into the street (La. R.S. 33:4875.1, 33:4883); the fencing statute does not apply where the parish or city already has a pool-fencing ordinance or a home rule charter, which typically act under their own powers. Health rules for pools open to residents of apartment complexes may come from the state sanitary code. Your general duties still apply: you must keep the property suitable for its purpose and free of defects (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2696), you answer for injuries from a defect you knew or should have known about and could have prevented with reasonable care (La. Civ. Code art. 2317.1), and a lease clause cannot excuse you in advance from liability for physical injury (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). Pool hours and rules may go in your property rules ("Property Rules Are Lease Terms"). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Questions About Protected Traits
bodyText: Louisiana's fair housing law has no separate ban on asking applicants or tenants about race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, military status or hairstyle, or on keeping records of those traits. It bans the discrimination itself and bans making, printing or publishing any notice, statement or advertisement about a rental that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on any of those traits (La. R.S. 51:2606(A)(1)-(3)); that statement ban applies even to the small owners otherwise exempt from the act (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)). So questions about protected traits are risky: a question can itself be a statement indicating a preference, and the answer can become evidence that a refusal was discriminatory. Ask only what you ask everyone and need for screening (identity, income, rental history, the people who will live there). For disability, do not ask about the nature or severity of a disability; when someone requests an accommodation or a support animal, you may consider documentation of the need (see "Disability Accommodations and Service Animals"). Louisiana's explicit bans on disability inquiries and records are in its employment law, not its housing law. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Severability and Void Terms
bodyText:
Louisiana generally strikes a bad lease term on its own, so the library's severability clause works as intended: the nullity of one provision does not make the whole contract null unless, from the nature of the provision or the parties' intent, it can be presumed the contract would not have been made without it (La. Civ. Code art. 2034). The severability clause states that intent. The specific lease statutes also void individual terms, not the lease: a deposit-rights waiver (La. R.S. 9:3254), an emergency-call restriction in buildings of six or more dwellings other than owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)(2)), and a void stipulated-damages clause, which leaves the main obligation standing (La. Civ. Code art. 2006).

Three situations can still sink more than one term.
- If the agreed method for setting the rent proves unworkable and no third person fixes it, there is no lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2676).
- A contract whose object is illicit is absolutely null as a whole (La. Civ. Code art. 2030).
- And if Louisiana's Unfair Trade Practices Law reaches the lease, a consumer contract made in violation of it is an illegal contract on which no recovery may be had (La. R.S. 51:1403; "Unfair Trade Practices Law and Leases").

Use the shared severability clause; it cannot rescue a term the law voids. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Registered Sex Offenders as Tenants
bodyText: Louisiana restricts where certain sex offenders may live, but the restrictions are crimes by the offender, not duties or crimes of the landlord. A sexually violent predator may not reside within 1,000 feet of a school, early learning center, registered family child care home, residential home for children, playground, youth center, public swimming pool or free-standing video arcade (La. R.S. 14:91.1(A)(2)). An offender convicted of a sex offense against a victim under 13 may not establish a residence within 1,000 feet of a school, early learning center, registered family child care home, residential home for children, or public park or recreational facility (La. R.S. 14:91.2(A)(2), (4)), and offenders convicted of certain aggravated offenses or child sexual abuse material offenses against a victim under 15 face similar limits (La. R.S. 14:91.2(B)(2)). No statute makes it a crime for you to rent to a registered offender, to rent a unit where two offenders live together, or to fail to check the registry, and none requires you to evict. A registered adult offender must give you, as lessor, landlord or owner of the residence, written notice of the crime, name, address, physical description and photograph, and must post the residence number visibly outside (La. R.S. 15:542.1(A)(1)(c), (5)); this notice is the offender's duty. You may consider criminal history in screening; if you charge an application fee for a tenant's primary residence (other than in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units), your written notice must say whether you consider criminal history (La. R.S. 9:3258.1(A)(2), (C)). Written leases a real estate licensee executes must include the registry notice ("Sex Offender Registry Notice" clause); for crimes on the premises see "Criminal Activity" clause. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No State Single-Family Zone Rental Limit
bodyText: Louisiana has no statewide law limiting rentals of homes in single-family zones, such as a rule that the owner must live on the lot, and no state law stopping a parish or city from adopting one. Zoning is local: municipalities may regulate the density of population and the location and use of buildings and land for residence and other purposes, by district, with uniform rules in each district and judicial review for abuse of discretion or unreasonable use of the police power (La. R.S. 33:4721, 33:4722). So check the local zoning code (and any short-term rental ordinance) before renting a house in a single-family district. State law also protects your rights as lessor against change except by state law, subject to the reasonable exercise of the police power (La. R.S. 9:3258); how that interacts with a local rental restriction is a case-law question. Subdivision building restrictions and homeowners or condominium association documents may separately limit leasing ("Condominium and HOA Rules for Rentals"). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: Louisiana has no law requiring you to install radiator covers on request, to give tenants a radiator-cover rider or notice, or otherwise regulating radiators in rental housing. Louisiana's statutes on steam boilers deal with boiler inspection and installer licensing, not with tenant protection. Your general duties apply to any heating equipment you provide: keep the property suitable for its purpose and free of defects, and make necessary repairs (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691, 2696); in a residential lease, a waiver of the warranty does not cover defects that seriously affect health or safety, such as an exposed hot radiator that burns a child (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). Local housing codes may say more. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Because Louisiana's fair housing law does not protect source of income, state law does not stop you from declining a Housing Choice Voucher or other rental-assistance tenancy, including because of the program's unit inspection, lease addendum or paperwork ("No Source-of-Income Protection"). No Louisiana statute governs program inspections of private rentals or a tenant's refusal of one; the program's own rules and your housing assistance contract control once you participate. If you do participate, remember that rent-subsidy money is not rent and is no defense to an eviction (La. R.S. 9:3259.2). Apply any voucher policy the same way to everyone: refusing vouchers selectively to screen out a protected class is discrimination under the state act (La. R.S. 51:2606), whose small-owner exemptions (a private owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a broker, or an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units) do not cover discriminatory advertising (La. R.S. 51:2604(B)). Parish or city ordinances may protect voucher holders; check locally. For inspections by local officials see "Government Inspections of Rentals". The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Sharing Tenant Information
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute that generally bars a private landlord from disclosing information about applicants or tenants, or that requires a tenant's consent before you share it. What does apply: if you keep Social Security, driver's license or bank or card account numbers electronically, you must protect them with reasonable security, destroy them properly and give breach notices ("Protecting Applicant and Tenant Data"); a tenant enrolled in the state Address Confidentiality Program has a protected physical address, and legal papers must be served on the Secretary of State ("Victim Information and Address Confidentiality"); and public housing authorities' files on residents and applicants are exempt from public-records disclosure (La. R.S. 40:526), a rule for housing authorities, not private owners. Share tenant information only for a legitimate purpose, such as a reference the tenant authorized, a court order or subpoena, or a lawful request from police with legal process ("Police Cooperation and Calls for Help"), and say in your application and lease how you will use and share applicant data. Federal credit-reporting law governs consumer reports you obtain. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Tenant Organizing Statute
bodyText: Louisiana has no statute giving tenants of private rentals a right to organize, form or join a tenants' association, or to meet in common areas, and no statute barring you from retaliating against tenants who organize (see "No Anti-Retaliation Statute"). The only statutory support for resident organizations is for public housing: a local housing authority may help form and run resident organizations (La. R.S. 40:457). Related limits still apply: you may not coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising fair housing rights or helping others do so (La. R.S. 51:2609), and federal labor or program rules may apply to federally assisted housing. Your lease and property rules may set reasonable, even-handed rules for use of common areas ("Property Rules Are Lease Terms"). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: Screening Applicants in Louisiana
bodyText: Louisiana has no tenant-screening statute: no limit on income tests, no required order of screening steps, no look-back period for criminal records, no rule that criminal history may be checked only after a conditional offer, and no statute shielding a landlord from negligence claims for renting to someone with a criminal record. A few rules apply. (1) Before you accept an application fee for a rental that will be the tenant's primary residence, you must give written notice of the fee, whether you consider credit scores, employment history, criminal history or eviction records, and the applicant's right to submit a short statement about hardship from a declared disaster or emergency; owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units are exempt (La. R.S. 9:3258.1; "Application Fee Notice"). (2) An expunged arrest or conviction is confidential, is not a public record, and need not be disclosed to you by the applicant (La. C.Cr.P. art. 973(A), (C)); do not ask about expunged records or treat silence about them as a false application ("Accuracy of Rental Application" clause). (3) Your criteria must not discriminate because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, national origin, military status or hairstyle (La. R.S. 51:2606; "Louisiana Fair Housing Law"), so apply them the same way to everyone. (4) If an applicant has frozen his or her credit report and will not lift the freeze for you, you may treat the application as incomplete, and a credit freeze does not reach databases of adverse information, including criminal records, used for tenant screening (La. R.S. 9:3571.1(L)(4), (Q)). Federal credit-reporting law governs the reports you obtain and the notice you must give if you reject an applicant based on one. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Unconscionability Statute for Leases
bodyText: Louisiana has no unconscionability statute for residential leases. Its only general unconscionability rule is in the Consumer Credit Law and applies to consumer loans and credit sales, not to leases of a home (La. R.S. 9:3551). The Civil Code reaches the same ground in other ways: contracts must be performed in good faith, and good faith governs both sides' conduct (La. Civ. Code arts. 1759, 1983); a term that departs from a law protecting the public interest is an absolute nullity (La. Civ. Code art. 7); a clause excluding liability in advance for intentional or gross fault or for physical injury is null (La. Civ. Code art. 2004); a court may modify stipulated damages, such as a late fee, that are so manifestly unreasonable as to be contrary to public policy (La. Civ. Code art. 2012); a warranty waiver must be clear and brought to the tenant's attention and never covers defects that seriously affect health or safety in a residential lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2699); and doubt in your standard form is read in the tenant's favor (La. Civ. Code arts. 2056, 2057). Whether a Louisiana court would refuse a lease term as unconscionable under general contract law is a case-law question. Louisiana has no statute declaring any particular lease clause, such as a default for misrepresenting an animal, fully enforceable. The full list of lease limits is in "Lease Terms Louisiana Law Voids or Limits". The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Veteran Landlord Incentive
bodyText: Louisiana has no tax credit, payment, deposit guarantee or other incentive for landlords who rent to veterans, and no statute requiring a veteran preference in private rentals. Related rules: Louisiana's fair housing law protects "military status", meaning current members of the U.S. uniformed forces or their reserve components and qualifying dependents (La. R.S. 51:2603(10), 51:2606); a veteran who has left service is not covered by that term, so treat veterans like any other applicant and do not set terms by service history. The Louisiana Military Family Assistance Fund pays need-based claims of family members of activated or honorably discharged military personnel, which may help a family meet expenses, but it is not a landlord program (La. R.S. 46:122). Service members' lease-termination rights are in "Service Members: Early Termination and Eviction Stays". The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Louisiana has no law setting a maximum (or minimum) hot water temperature for rentals and no requirement to reset a water heater before each new tenant moves in. Your general duties cover a water heater you provide: keep the property suitable for its purpose and free of defects that prevent its use, and make necessary repairs (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691, 2696); a dangerous scalding setting could be a defect that seriously affects health or safety, which a residential lease cannot waive (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). Setting a unit's water heater at a safe temperature (many codes and manufacturers use about 120 degrees Fahrenheit) at each turnover is good practice. See also "Heat and Hot Water". Local plumbing and housing codes may say more. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Louisiana has no law requiring window guards, window stops or fall-prevention devices in rentals, and no window-guard notice for the lease. The only statute touching windows and children in dwellings is the lead-poisoning program, which treats lead paint on surfaces such as window sills that young children may chew or touch as a hazard ("Louisiana Lead Paint Duties"). Your general duties apply to windows you provide: keep them in repair and the property free of defects (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691, 2696), and in a residential lease the warranty cannot be waived for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699). If a tenant asks to install child-safety window devices, your lease's alterations terms govern; agreeing is usually wise. Local building and housing codes may say more. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Louisiana has no plain-language law for leases. Write clearly anyway: any doubt in your own form is resolved for the tenant (La. Civ. Code arts. 2056, 2057). See "No Plain-Language Lease Law" for the full answer and what the search did and did not cover; it did not cover case law, agency rules or local ordinances.

title: Leasing as a Usufructuary
bodyText: If you hold a rental home as a usufructuary rather than as its full owner (common when a surviving spouse inherits the use of a home and the children own it), a lease you sign ends when your usufruct ends, for example at your death or remarriage if the usufruct was granted until then (La. Civ. Code arts. 567, 2716). If you did not tell the tenant you were a usufructuary, you are liable for the tenant's loss when the lease ends early (La. Civ. Code art. 2716). Say so in the lease: the optional Landlord's Status as Usufructuary clause does this. The exception: if the act creating your usufruct expressly gave you the right to dispose of the property, you may lease it for a term that runs past the end of the usufruct, but you then answer to the naked owner for any loss of value caused by the lease (La. Civ. Code arts. 568, 568.2). This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: Louisiana's statutes do not require you to supply a stove, range or refrigerator. Whether appliances come with the home is up to you and the tenant. If you include them, they are part of what you lease, so you must deliver them in good condition, repair them (except damage the tenant causes) and answer for defects (La. Civ. Code arts. 2682, 2691, 2696); see the appliances note ("Included and Excluded Appliances"). This applies to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Lease Terms
bodyText: No Louisiana statute requires, authorizes, sets the wording of or bars a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, so such a term is an ordinary lease term. The library's optional criminal-activity clause covers illegal drug manufacture, sale and distribution. In buildings of six or more dwellings, except owner-occupied buildings of ten or fewer units, such a term must not limit anyone's right to call the police or emergency help in an emergency or after domestic abuse on the premises, or penalize such a call (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(A), (C)), and you may not end, refuse to renew or give a notice to vacate because domestic abuse (domestic abuse battery, stalking or cyberstalking), or activity directly related to it, occurred on the premises against a tenant or household member, except under the statute's narrow exception for repeated violence (La. R.S. 9:3261.1(B)(2), (D)(1)(b)). Separately, parishes and cities may not penalize you, or authorize an eviction, because a tenant called for help (La. R.S. 33:9701(E), (F)); that law binds local governments, not your lease, but do not treat a call for help as a default. Federally assisted housing has its own federal rules.

title: Ending a Lease for a Breach: No Statutory Cure
bodyText: Louisiana has no statutory notice-and-cure period before you end a lease for a breach. For unpaid rent, you may dissolve the lease under the general contract rules (La. Civ. Code art. 2704); a lease clause that says the lease ends for nonpayment lets you end it by notice, with no time to cure (La. Civ. Code art. 2017). For other breaches, you may serve a notice to perform within a reasonable time, warning that the lease will be dissolved if the tenant does not (La. Civ. Code arts. 2015, 2719). Either way, to get the tenant out you then give a written notice to vacate of at least five days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, unless the lease waives it (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701), and file for eviction if the tenant stays. The library's Default by Tenant clause sets these terms. These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike. Courts can refuse dissolution for a minor breach.

title: Other Rules Louisiana Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states are not in Louisiana's statutes. (1) No statute bars leasing the same home to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it. You are bound to deliver the home to the tenant (La. Civ. Code art. 2682), so a tenant you cannot deliver to has the ordinary contract remedies, and between competing tenants a lease filed for registry in the parish records has effect against third persons from the time it is filed (La. Civ. Code art. 2681.1). (2) No statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false; the library's application-accuracy clause ("Accuracy of Rental Application" clause) makes accuracy a lease term, and an applicant may lawfully stay silent about an expunged arrest or conviction. (3) Louisiana has no rule of its own on a tenant's bankruptcy; federal law governs ("Tenant Bankruptcy"). (4) Louisiana has no general type-size rule for residential leases; a waiver of the warranty against defects must be brought to the tenant's attention (La. Civ. Code art. 2699), and automatic-renewal terms have their own rules ("Automatic Renewal and Reconduction"). One rule Louisiana does have: for one- or two-family dwellings, which must have smoke and carbon monoxide detectors when leased, failing to comply is not a reason for an insurer to refuse a claim (La. R.S. 40:1581(D)).

title: Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: (1) Squatters: Louisiana has no fast squatter-removal procedure, but remaining on or re-entering a dwelling without authority after being forbidden is a crime, and an occupant who never had a lease is removed with a five-day notice to vacate and an eviction ("Removing Squatters and Other Occupants"). (2) No statewide rental license or registration is required to rent a home or to win an eviction, but an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business here may not present any judicial demand, an eviction included, until it has a certificate of authority, and an individual renting under a name other than his own must file an assumed-name certificate (La. R.S. 12:314, 12:1354, 51:281); parishes and cities may have their own programs ("No Statewide Landlord Registration"). (3) No statute requires you to give a receipt for rent, including cash rent ("No Rent Receipt Duty"); give one anyway.

title: Penalty for Keeping a Deposit Wrongfully
bodyText: If you willfully fail to return a security deposit or account for it as Louisiana requires, the tenant can recover the part you wrongfully kept plus $300 or twice that amount, whichever is greater. Failing to pay within 30 days after the tenant's written demand for a refund counts as willful. The court may also award costs and attorney fees to the winner, and a lease term waiving these rights is void (La. R.S. 9:3252-3254). The return rule does not apply when the tenant abandons the home without the required notice or before the lease ends (La. R.S. 9:3251(C)). See the deposit return note ("Returning the Deposit: One Month, Itemized Statement, Penalties"). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: What a Lease Can Shift on Condition and Repairs
bodyText:
Louisiana has no list of habitability duties a lease may or may not shift.

Two Civil Code tools let a lease move some of the risk to the tenant, each with limits.
- (1) Your warranty that the home is fit and free of defects may be waived, but only in clear and unambiguous language brought to the tenant's attention, never for defects you knew or should have known of and the tenant did not, and, in a residential lease, never for defects that seriously affect health or safety (La. Civ. Code art. 2699; "Limited Waiver of Warranty Against Vices or Defects" clause).
- (2) If the tenant assumes responsibility for the home's condition, you are not liable for injuries from defects unless you knew or should have known of the defect, or were notified and did not fix it within a reasonable time (La. R.S. 9:3221; "Tenant's Assumption of Responsibility for Condition (La. R.S. 9:3221)" clause).

Neither lets you escape liability for causing physical injury or for intentional or gross fault (La. Civ. Code art. 2004). Specific repairs can be shifted by agreement ("Tenant-Performed Repairs" clause). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: No Statutory Pay-or-Quit Notice
bodyText: Louisiana has no pay-or-quit notice, no required wording and no notice-service fee rule for unpaid rent. When rent is not paid, you may dissolve the lease (La. Civ. Code art. 2704); the library's Default by Tenant clause lets you end it by written notice. Then you deliver a written notice to vacate of at least five days, not counting weekends and legal holidays, unless the lease waives it (La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701; "Louisiana Eviction: Notice to Vacate and Court Timeline", "Waiver of Notice to Vacate" clause). For a primary residence, send eviction and default notices on paper, because Louisiana's electronic-transactions law does not cover them (La. R.S. 9:2603(B)(4)(b)(ii)). These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Claims Against the Property
bodyText: The tenant must tell you without delay when someone disturbs the tenant's possession, for example by claiming the property, and you can recover damages caused by a failure to tell you (La. Civ. Code art. 2688); the shared clause asking the tenant to forward papers about the property reflects this. You, in turn, protect the tenant against anyone who claims ownership of or a right in the property (La. Civ. Code art. 2700; "Claims and Lawsuits Against the Property"). On your side, the notices about a pending foreclosure are in "Pending Foreclosure Disclosure" clause, and what a foreclosure sale does to the lease is in "Tenants When Your Rental Is Seized and Sold". These rules apply to fixed-term and month-to-month leases alike.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Louisiana follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (La. R.S. 10:3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (La. R.S. 10:1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. Louisiana's Civil Code adds that where a money debt is disputed only in part and the debtor is willing to pay the undisputed part, the creditor may not refuse that part and keeps the right to claim the disputed part (La. Civ. Code art. 1861); how Louisiana courts fit that article together with the check rule is case law, so follow the cautious course below. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Louisiana's Civil Code imposes a duty of good faith on every obligation, a lease included: good faith governs the conduct of both sides in whatever pertains to the obligation (La. Civ. Code art. 1759), and contracts must be performed in good faith (La. Civ. Code art. 1983). In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: No State Approval Rule for Leases; Tribal Trust Land Is Federal
bodyText: No Louisiana law makes a residential lease of private land wait for a government officer's approval, and Louisiana has no communal land system: a lease binds once you and the tenant agree on the thing and the rent, whether oral or written (La. Civ. Code arts. 2668, 2681). Land held in trust or restricted status by the United States for a tribe or an individual Indian is governed by federal law instead. Restricted Indian land may be leased for residential purposes by its Indian owners only with the approval of the Secretary of the Interior (25 U.S.C. § 415(a)). Anyone who is not an owner needs a lease from the owners before taking possession, and possession without a required lease is a trespass that the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) may act to end, including by eviction (25 C.F.R. §§ 162.005, 162.023). A residential lease of such land takes effect on the date BIA approves it (25 C.F.R. § 162.342). Practical step: if the property may be tribal trust land, check its status with BIA or the tribe before you sign, and don't let a tenant move in until any required approval is given.

title: No Louisiana Rule on a Tenant's Hunting Rights
bodyText: No Louisiana law says whether a tenant who rents a home with land gets the right to hunt or fish on that land, or keeps that right with the owner. A lease gives the tenant the use and enjoyment of the thing leased (La. Civ. Code art. 2668); whether that use includes hunting is not settled by statute. The Civil Code lets the owner of a tract of land forbid entry to anyone for hunting or fishing (La. Civ. Code art. 3413). The trespass laws make it a crime to enter immovable property owned by another without express, legal or implied authorization (La. R.S. 14:63(B)(1)), and to go onto or stay on property after being forbidden, orally or in writing (including by posted signs or purple paint marks), by the owner, lessee, custodian or other authorized person (La. R.S. 14:63.3(A)). Because a lessee can forbid entry, your tenant may be able to keep hunters off land the lease covers. So settle it in the lease: say whether the tenant may hunt or fish or let others do so, where and when, and whether you or others will keep hunting the land.

title: Recording a Lease or Notice of Lease in Louisiana
bodyText: Louisiana doesn't require you to record a residential lease to make it valid: a lease may be oral or written (La. Civ. Code art. 2681). Recording decides whether the lease binds third persons. A lease of an immovable has effect against third persons from the time it is filed for registry (La. Civ. Code art. 2681.1), and the rights and obligations created by a written lease of an immovable are without effect as to a third person unless it is recorded in the parish conveyance records (La. Civ. Code art. 3338). Instead of the lease itself, you and the tenant may record a signed notice of lease giving the parties' names and addresses, a description of the property, the lease date and term, any extension or renewal terms, and any option or right of first refusal; it has the same effect as recording the lease (La. R.S. 9:2742(A)). If you sell, the sale doesn't end the lease, but you answer to the tenant for any loss the transfer causes (La. Civ. Code art. 2711), and the buyer isn't personally bound by your obligations under the lease unless it assumes them (La. Civ. Code art. 2712). No Louisiana statute ties notice to a relative's lease the way Nebraska's does. Practical step: for a long lease, or one with a purchase option or right of first refusal, record a notice of lease; when you sell, have the buyer assume the lease in the act of sale. See also "Oral Leases and Recording".

title: Time Limits (Prescription) to Sue for Rent or Damages
bodyText: Louisiana calls its time limits 'liberative prescription'. An action for arrearages of rent prescribes in three years (La. Civ. Code art. 3494(2)), and the period runs from the day each payment is due, separately for each missed payment (La. Civ. Code art. 3495). A personal action with no other period set by law prescribes in ten years (La. Civ. Code art. 3499), and delictual actions (claims for wrongful injury or damage) prescribe in two years from the day the damage is sustained (La. Civ. Code art. 3493.1). Whether a claim for damage to the unit is a contract claim (ten years) or a delictual one (two years) is case law, so treat two years from the damage as your deadline. Prescription is interrupted when the tenant acknowledges your right, and then it starts over from the acknowledgment (La. Civ. Code arts. 3464, 3466). Whether a partial payment counts as an acknowledgment is case law, so get any acknowledgment in a signed writing. The landlord-tenant articles set no shorter period of their own. The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month leases.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a Louisiana Lease
bodyText: No Louisiana law requires a residential lease to say that the property lies in a special taxing, assessment, improvement or other special district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges or rules. Louisiana law creates many such districts, but none of the laws found puts a disclosure duty on a landlord. Any district taxes or fees on the property are yours as owner unless the lease passes them on. If you pass a district charge through to the tenant, state it in the lease as a fixed amount or part of the rent.

title: Renting to Students in Louisiana
bodyText: No Louisiana law is written for student leases: nothing on parental guarantees, academic-year terms, roommate matching or disclosures to student tenants, and no student-housing exemption from the lease articles, which apply to student rentals like any other lease. The one student-housing statute found is about public colleges' own housing: a public postsecondary institution that offers student housing may adopt a plan giving current and former homeless and foster youth access to housing during and between terms, including first priority for placement (La. R.S. 17:3399.24). It puts no duty on private landlords. If a student tenant is under 18, have an adult sign or guarantee the lease.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Louisiana gives you two trespass tools to keep a non-tenant (a former tenant, a troublemaker, a tenant's ex) out of parking lots, hallways and other common areas. First, it is a crime to go onto or stay on any property belonging to another, or any part or area of it, after being forbidden to, orally or in writing, by the owner, lessee, custodian or other authorized person; a posted sign, or purple paint marks on trees or posts placed as the statute describes, also counts. The penalty is a fine of up to $500, up to six months in jail, or both (La. R.S. 14:63.3). Second, it is a crime to enter or remain in a structure or on immovable property owned by another without express, legal or implied authorization (La. R.S. 14:63(A)-(C)), and a person who had such authority has a defense (La. R.S. 14:63(D)). A first offense carries a fine of $100 to $500, up to 30 days in jail, or both (La. R.S. 14:63(G)(1)). Delivery people, solicitors and people with a legitimate reason to talk to a resident may come onto the property unless specifically forbidden (La. R.S. 14:63(F)(3)). Your tenant is a lessee who can also forbid entry, and a guest the tenant invites has implied authority, so a ban that reaches into the tenant's own unit is enforced against the tenant through the lease, not by trespass. Practical step: give the banned person a written notice, keep a copy, post signs in common areas, and tell the police.
